A woman can keep a secret, but she doesn't like to. ' 'Why is a beggar like an attorney I—He is a solicitor. ' There its,a soul in friendship which is eternal as love , itself. Why is a tiresome orator like a whale?—Because he I often rises to spout. "What struck you most in :the equatorial regions ?" 1 asked a gentleman of a traveller. "The sun," was the reply. None are so fond of secrets as those who do not mean to keep them; such persons covet secrets as a spend- thrift does money. "Please to dive me something. sir," said an old woman. "I had a blind child • he was my only means of subsist- ence, and the poor boy haerecovered his sight." On hearing that the lost tribes of Israel had been dis- covered, Sheridan wittily remarked;:" I am very glad to hear it; for I have long exhausted the patience of the ethers !" Mother: "Now, girls, as you've finished your7daily quarrel suppose you go and eat some dinner. Arabella (sarcastically) : "Oh, I suppose you want us to swallow o•kL feud." She (eagerly): "Well, dearest, did you speak to papa this morning?" He: "Yes, I spoke to him." She (excitedly): "What did he say ?" He "He said Good mommy.'" Cosmos, Duke of Florence. was wont to say' of perfi- dious friends- that "we read that we ought to forgive our enemies, but we do not read that we ought to ,for- give our friends." • "I thought I should snicker right out," said Mrs. Cash- ton, "when, at the circus to-day, Mrs. Smith called an -animal a seraph. Of course she meant giraffe; but the fun of it was, it wasn't a giraffe. It was a camomile." A witty, as well as a soft answer, will sometimes turn away wrath. Charles Burleigh, the abolitionist, in the midst of an anti-slavery speech, was struck by a rotten egg full in the face. Pausing to wipe away the contents of the missile, he said calmly, "I have always contended that pro-slavery arguments were very unsound." The -crowd roartd, and:he was no longer molested. To SUPPORT TRH FAMILT.—A boy of four climbed up on the Pillow beside his mothet, who was bitterly weep- ing over the death of her father. Alter smoothing her hair and,caressing her, he said, "Don't cry, mamma, I'll be a fodder to you." The boy grew in years and in worldly wisdom, and came to twice the age when he had offered to act the part of a father. Seeing his mother weary with work, for she supported her three children, be said, "I tell you what, mamma, you sha'n't work when I grow up." "Well, what will you do for me, son?" "I'll marry a rich wife." How TiPPO Tie GOT His num—Hamad ben Mohanie med—Tippo Tib—accompanied Mr. Stanley down the Lualaba to the Seventh Cataract in 1876. The origin of the latter sobriquet is peculiar. It was applied to him ty the people at Kansongo in consequence of their hear- ing the sharp, distant rattle of the bandits' guns when on some of their slave-catching excursions. The crack of the rifle-shot sounded in their ears like "tip—tip— tip." Another name that has been given to this re- markable man on the eastern side of Central Africa is " M'Kango Njaa "—" A f raid of Hunger "—for the natives in the famine-stricken regions declare that that is the only enemy of which Hamad, with his large cara- vans traversing their barren country. is in dread. This man's life for the past thirty years has been one con- stant succession of adventures. He 4at the present moment the strongest and most formidable ruler in the Congo regions of Equatorial Africa.—Life Among Congo Savages, in Scribner. GORDON'S OPJNIONS ON DRESS AND MARRTAGS.-- Gordon's reasons for so suddenly throwing up the envi- able appointment of private secretary to Lord Ripon, as Governor-General of India, have hitherto been a mys- tery. They will be a mystery no longer after the enter- taining article, "A Voyage with General Gordon,"sn the February number of The Contemporary Review. The writer of the article has had access to the diary of a • skipper who, inlBB2, conveyed Gordon in a small trad. trig schooner from Mauritius to the Cape. Gordon was very communicative! on the voyage, when he was not prostrate with sea sickness—which, by the way, he bore no better than Marius—and one evening he told his nautical host why he had resigned. He simply could not endure the manners and customs "of the high social circle in which he was expected to move.fili` Dress for dinner, dress for evening parties, dress farsballs, dress and decoration, decoration and dress! day:after day. I could not,' said Gordon, 'stand the :worry of it, and, Tether than do so, I gave up the appointment." In his talks with the skipper, he did not fail to touch on those curious practical questions connected with the Fall which so frequently engage his attention in the 'published correspondence with his sister. He was firmly persuaded that the site of the Garden of Eden is one of the islands of the Seychelles, and that the coca-dc-seer of that region is the true Forbidden Tree. He carried amid his otherwise scanty luggage a box full of chips of the wood, and offered them to persons who had won his particular regard as the most precious gifts itlwas in his power to bestow. His reason for not marrying' as stated on the same occasion, was only less original than his reason for throwing up his appointment in India. "I never yet have met the woman who for my sake, and perhaps at a moment's notice, would be prepared to sacrifice the comforts of home -and the sweet society of roved ones, and accompany me whithersoever the de- mand of duty might lead." This, of course, was simply his misfortune, and by no means the fault of the other

sex. . "BRITONS NEVER WILL BE SLAVES !"—(A Scene from a Domestic Comedy.)—Mrs. Bob Bull was the wife of a Br tish workman, and she got up at four o'clock in the morning. "Must rise early," she said, "to see that my man has his breakfast." So she lighted the fire, and put the kettle on to boil, and laid the cloth, and swept nut the rooms. Then down came Bob rather in a had humour, because he had been late over-night at the ."Cock and Bottle," detained (as he explained to his wiFe) by a discussim about the rights of labour. "Ot course," said Mrs. Bull; "and why shouldn't you, after. .41 hard day's work, enjoy yourself?" But Bob contended that he had not enjoyed himself, although he bad un- doubtedly expended two shillings and eightpence upon ' refreshment. What Bob wanted to know was, why there was a button off his coat, and why his waistcoat had not been properly mended. "Well. I was busy with -.the children's things," replied Mrs. Bob; "but I will put all straight when you have gone to work." "Gone :^ work, indeed 1" grumbled Bob. "Yes, it 's I that dOes au . e And worn luck to it rThe. moment Bob was out of u hellte, Mrs. Bob got the children up and dressed them, and gave them their breakfasts ea sent them off to school. When they were gone, she 44 tidied up" and dressed the baby. Then !he did one -of "the bits of washing," that came from a family in whose service she had been before she married Bob, Inni that family's connection. And this occupied her fully, what with soaking, and mangling and ironing, until it was time to carry Bob his dinner. In the pauses of her work she had been able to cook it, and it was quite ready to go with her when she was prepared to take it. It was a long walk (in the rain) to Bob's place of work, and it seemed the longer because she could not leave the baby. But both got there, and the dinner, without any accident. And then Mrs. Bob hurried hack to give the children, now home from school, Their midday meal. And Mrs. Bob had plenty of work to do afterwards. She had to mend, and to scrub, and to sweep, and to sew. She was not off her legs for a moment, and had she been a weaker woman she would have been the,. rouohly done up. Then came the children's evening toilette and thocooking of Bob's supper. Her lord and master entered in due course, and she helped him off , with his coat, and (when he had finished his food) ' lighted his pipe for him. "Mended my clothes?" asaed Bob. "Of course I have.", "And washed my linen, and drug nails into my boots, and baked the bread, and i pickled the walnuts, and all the rest of t?'' "'Yes., Bob, 1 have done them all—every one of them." This put Bob into a better temper. and he took out an erening raper, and began to'read it. " I say," said .he: "what ,do you think! They have got. white slaves in Turkey!' "You don't say so, Bob!" replied Mrs. Bob, lost in I .amazement. Then she said as she paused tidying up 1 the room, "Ahl they wou/dn't 'allow anything of that sort in England !—would they, Bob?" And Bob, amok,. lag his pipe, and sprawling befOXelthe ret,..agk'eed with: her !—Punch.

A DEAR LITTLE MAID OF TWO.

I'll sing you a song to a nursery tune, Of a dear little maid of two, Who has peachen cheeks and rosebud lips, And eyes of a soft sea-bine; With charms of a gleeful innocence, That are ripe at the age of two. She is not an angel, no, no, no. And heaven be praised for that; She is tairily human from top to toe, With limbs that are daintily fat, ' And where she trots, be it high or low, There is wealth of surprising chat. Somebody's heart is-strong and brave, And Somebody's love is true, By day, by night, they are amply tried By this little maid of two; But Somebody's love would never tire, Had it ten times more to do. What reward does Somebody get Dear dreamer with eyes of blue ' A:kiss, a smile, from the roguish pet, t A tender caress or two. Why, each of these is a heaven of bliss, From a sweet little maid like you. Come, happy maid, with the sea-bright eyes, And prattle:about my knee, Then lay that soft round cheek to mine, And laugh in innocent glee; That childish talk and downy touch Give joy and strength to me. • Theregrow, my sweet, as well as you may, And be like Somebody, true, For high-born dames of noblest heArt Have been as tiny as you— And in the maiden of twenty-one May we find the maid of two! —Good Words. HENRY Jonas Torr.

div.p: NED WAUGH'S BIRTHDAY.
BY Tina 0' Dlcic 0' Bon's.

Last Wensde wer th' .birthday o one o' Lanca- shire's gm:tett pootiv:when Ned Waugh reyclied seventy-three. Id wer Stedman as said his Vidorsan Poets as Waugh wer "by far the best of Lancashire's recent dialect poets." an' he could ha' said "English" • for "Lancashire," an' added "deceased or" at after id, . an' still ha' towd,nowt but th' truth; for aw could ne'er see owt wonder- ful P Tim Bobbin, an' th' only other two dialect writers as is fit to mention i' th' same breath as Ned are Tennyson, an' WiWain Barnes., 49, wodn'd say as Come whoam to thi Childer an' lie is a lot better nor The Northern Farmer, but aw think id'll be a long time afoor owt, so sweet sin' tender as Come whoam 'll be written'; it's a song as gooas to th' heart, an' werms id,. becos ev'rybody knows or feels ia to be genuine. Ned wer born at Rochdale, an' he worn'd born wi' a silver spoon in, his meawth, noather: wod he'S tlone ,hes bin done. wi persever- ance an' herd werk, an' ther's mony a lord wod be fain to swap his title an' his wealth forth' honour o receivin' ninety peawnd a year fro' Govern- ment, an' bein' th' author ,pv elevewsich vollumg as Ned's written'. Aw con fancy seethyth' owd throstle this Minute jut as aw see him'for ' th' fost time abeawt ten year sin' a th' Kersal Hotel, Manchester. He coom into th' room wi his shoon under onelrni, his clock honkt on th' finger o' one hand, an'. hie canary an' cage-i' th' other hand; then ther wer his 'cheery greetin' an' his werm handshake: an' as for th' chat we bed—well, aw dorn'd know as aw'ever laughed as mich o' mi life as aw dud at his ' ackeawnt o' wod took place between him an' th' poet Laureate to George, King ov Grand Bonny— a bit o' descriptive writin' as doesn'd appear in his Lake sketches. An' then ther wer bits gbeawt 1 Harrison Ainsworth as interested me, an' a look at th' han'some card presented to th- guests at th' Ainsworth banquet; aw've nooan fergetten a bit o' criticism en a line or two o' Tenneyson's Dream of 1 Fair Women, noather : thad Sunda' afternoon ..wer one o' th' red-letter days i' mi life. Aw've sin' th' owd Enid a time or two sin' then, an' bed a tooathri letters fro' him, too, an' 0' as aw've sin' on him an heeard fro' him, hes strengthened mi love an' admir- ation for him an' his. werk. ' • DIONY HAPPY RETURNS.
TO NED WAUGH on his 73rd birthday, 29th Jan.,

1890. Here's health an' plenty to the, Ned, For mony a year to come; Tha'rt one o' to' finest lads we've hed I' Lancashire, bi gum! , -Ay, long may the. be spared, owd Brid, Thi " wood-noosts wild" to sing; For th' Brid as cheers a tooathri hearts Does moor nor queen or king. We ill con part wi' men like thee, Fro' this throng world o' eawrs ; A mon "should never awse to dee " As grows us Fancy's fleawerg. An' nooan so mony men con grow Sich pooasies as thisel,— Sich good owd, gradely, hooamly sooarts, Or wi' so rare a smell.

One smell, an' o' mi pulses thrill— Aw feel the moorland breeze; Aw see the sun rise o'er the hill, Aw hear the hum o' bees; Aw bear the mowers' cheery song As they spread the new-mown hay; Aw hear the skylark up aboon Bid welcome to the day. Ther's magic i' these fleawers o' thine— They're grown i' Fairyland, But th' way they cherm this heart o' mine Tha couldn'd understand; Ther's a fragrance lingers reawnd 'em, Ned, 'At's crept into mi heart, An' kept i' check id hot young blood, An' saved id mony a smert. It's a fragrance like to thad as clings To love's young dreeam so sweet. Or fro' a mother's fond heart springs When her childer pray at net ; An' may id creep into other hearts . An' mek 'em better grow ;- Then when it's done id appointed werk They'll bless thee for id o'.

Id wer nobbut last fleet 'as aw geet a letter fro' th' owd nightingale written yesterday mornin', an' as id hes some good news in id as'll suit his Lancashire admirers, beside throwin' a bit ci leet on his correct age, aw mek no apology for quottn' a bit on it : With respect to the date of my 1 birth, the certificate of my baptism is dated in the year 1818, but my sister always asserted that I was born on the 29th of January in the year before the year of my baptism. Of course I cannot swear to the fact, although Iwas there at the time; but I am inclined to think that my sister was right. You kindly enquire about the state of my health, and although I must confess that I am better than any- body expected after what I have gone through, yet I feel that the shock of this last operation has left its mark; nevertheless I have much to be thankful for, aS my general health is good, for a man of my time of life. I am busy at present preparing my next book for publication, the matter for which only needs careful revision before going to the printer. The title will be "An old man't. memories of his early days." But so wodever his correct age is it's as "Festus " Bailey—another Manchester poet—says: “We live in deeds not years; in thoughts, not breaths ; In feelings, not in figures on a dial; We should count time by heart-throbs. Ii most lives Who thinks most, feels the noblest, acts the best." —From "The Blackburn Standard and Weekly Express."

THE EXAM INER, SATURDAY FEBRUARY 8, 1890. LIBERALISM IN SOUTH 'WALES. MR. O'BRIEN IN MANCHESTER. The annual meetings of the Council of the South Wales / Liberal Federation were held on Tuesday at Cardiff, and were largely attended. At the morning sitting Mi. Albert Spicer, candidate for the Monmouth district boroughs, presided, and delivered an address in which he dealt with one or two of the more important questions now engaging general Attention in Wales. Afterwards a number of resolutions covering the whole field of Welsh politics came on for diScussionisomdbf those relating to tithes and some Rule forthe principality —were received with much enthusiasm. The Federation unanimously declared its convict-on that the people of Wales should be entrusted with the management of the purely domestic affairs of the 'principality, and recog- ni i sed n the movement for Welsh Home Rule the solution of the grave difficulties under which Wales suffers by reason of the neglect of succeeding Governments. With no less vigour and unanimity was it resolved that,. no legislation providing for the tithe being paid by the land- lord, or which would have the effect of depreciating the value of the national property in tithe, would meet with approval. By resolution also Sunday closing was upheld and its extension advocated, while disestablishment in Wales was regarded as a question so pressing. as to demand legislative attention concurrently with or imme- diatoly after Irish Home Rule. Many other reforms— educational, Parliamentary, industrial, and relating to taxation and registration—were approved in a group, Mr. Dillwyn, M.P., was elected president for the ensuing year. A great public meeting was held in the evening, of which Professor Bryce, M.P., was the principal speaker. , emir

Mr. William O'Brien, M.P., and the Rev Canon Keller, were entertained to dinner at the Manchester Reform CluWon Tuesday, and they afterwards addressed a large gathering of the members. In the absence of Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., the President of the Club (owing to the death of his sister), the meeting was presided over by Mr.-It. Prestwich. Canon Keller dealt mainly with the cases of hardships occurring on the- Ponsonby estate for the purpose of showing that although Unionists might say the law was the same in Ireland as in England and only differed in procedure, yet so vitally differ that what was just and equitable in England was cruel in Ireland. Mr O'Brien, who seemed very weak, addressed himself to what he described as the higher aspects of the Irish ques- tion. He declared that if Home Rule were ever so long delayed the good feeling evoked by Mr. Gladstone's con- duct would not pass away. The Irish never had any ill-will against the working millions of the Ehglish people ,—only against the governing classes,—and the fact that they did not conceal their fallings in the old days nor cringe to their rulers should,he submittede accepted as some proof at any rate of the sinceritvof their utterances now, when the prospect was so much brighter. The English people might rest alsured that the Irish leaders were speaking- for their country and their race when they said that if Mr. Gladstone's policy were accepted cheerfully, generously, and loyally-by the British nation at the next general election, the day on which the Home 'Rule Act was inscribed on:the statute book would witness. the disappearance of the Irish difficulty, which had been our weakness and our shame and the blot upon our escut,checn, and there would have been created across the Irish Channel a nobler and more enduring garrison in a friendly, happy, and contented Irish nation. Mr. O'Brien, and Canon Keller addressed a great meeting held on Wednesday night in the Free-trade Hall, under the auspices of the Manchester Liberal Union. Speaking first of Mr. Balfour's administration, Mr. O'Brien said there was a certain airy and sublime auda- city about the Chief Secretary which his admirers mis- took for courage and sometimes for truth. Mr. Balfour' took credit for the revival of trade in Ireland, but this was just as if Mr. Matthews were to take credit for the revival of English trade. Canon Keller gave details with regard to the state of things on the Ponsonby estate. Both gentlemen were received with great enthusiasm. In the afternoon Mr. O'Brien opened a new club in Hulme for the Father Sheehy Branch of the Irish National League.

div.head: "LA GRIPPE,"
div.p: "LA GRIPPE,"
THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC. PARISIAN CHEMISTS INTERVIEWED.

Since the eruption of this epidemic in Paris, the corrOs- pondent of the New York Herald "in that capital has diligently endeavoured to ascertain by means of the leading Chemists of the City what prescriptions are given by eminent medical men to allay or prevent the 'ravages of the disease. We lu re insert the result of his interviews with some of the chief Pharmacists of the French capital. M. Herat said :—" We never take our hands off the quinine bottles nowadays. The most popular and simple remedies are quinine and anti-pyrin. We sell quite as much to people who think they are going to have, the malady as to those who have already: taken it." Mr. Roberts, the fashionable chemist in the Reu de la st.ted :—" An exceedingly good mixture is com- posed of quinine with a small quantity of aconite. I think men do not suffer as much as women, because a woman's nervous system is more readily disturbed than that of a man." _ _ _

Mr. Swann, Chemist, the Rue 'Castlglion4- said "Most of our customers have had the epidemic inn mild form. Some of them havetaken Simply doses of quinine. In all such cases the patients have either etikaped it altogether or have had it in a very slight form. , It appears also that 'quinine is taken during the convales- cent period, and when taken with food it will never dis- agree with the stomach." Dr. Hogg, the Champs Elysees, Chemist, in reply to inquiries, declared :—" So far, quinine and anti-pyrin is the general prescription." The correspondent, with some difficulty, Qbtained an interview with M. Jacquignou, Director of the Phar- macie Normale, in the Rue Drout. ills statement was : —" The medicines most frequently prescribed for the epidemic are : Sulphate of quinine and anti-pyrin. The doses vary according to the age and constitution of the patient." At the Pharmacie Boinet, in the aristocratic Faubourg St. Germain, the Chemist said :—" The remedies most frequently called for are anti-pyrin and sulphate of quinine. _ The latter drug probably produces the most rapidly efficacious results." The Chemists of the Faubourg St. Honore were all found as busily employed as their confrers is other parts of the city. The consumption of quinine and anti-pnin in Paris during the past fortnight is astonishing. It will , be seen from the above testimonies that the Parisian doctor l with one accord prescribe quinine in conjunction with some other drug, but most frequently with anti- pyrin, as a remedy for this epidemic which has spread so rapidly from Russia over Europe. The objection to anti- pyrin is that patients who have reason to apprehenel that they are subject to any affection of the heart dare not take it. div.head: BRITISH DENTAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: BRITISH DENTAL ASSOCIATION.

A meeting of the Midland Counties branch of this association, was held, at Warrington, on Saturday. The members were received at the Art Gallery by Mr. John Taylor and Mr. Thomas Fletcher, and afterwards a number of them made an inspection of the latter gentleman's Works. Tea was served in the lecture-room at the Museum, and Mr. R. H. Pearson's band played selections .01 music befo*e and during the meal. Mr. Chantrey was the caterer, and Mr. Fletcher and Mr. Taylor were res- plnsible for the arrangements; 'whia were admit' aßly carried out. At the busineis meeting the chair was occupied by Mr. Quinby, of Liverpool, and representatives were present from London, Manchester, Liverpool, Leeds, Preston, Rochdale, Ches- ter, York, Halifax, Sheffield, Bradford, Southport,Stock- port, Hanley, Shrewsbury,.oldham, Huddersfield, Hull, and other towns. The Chairman announced that it would be necessary for the branch to investigate certain cases of alleged fraudulent registration, and it had been suggested that a guarantee fund should be raised for the purpose of meeting any expenses that might be in- curred. £72 had been guranteed by those present.'.. Since the last meeting a circular had been drawn up with the object of informing the general public of the objects and *jibs of scientific dentistry; it would be in the hands of the members in a few days. Since their last meeting at Halifax, the late honorary secretary, Dr. Waite, of Liverpool, had resigned owing to ill-health, and Mr. Renshaw (Rochdale), had been appointed hon. secretary in his stead. On the proposition of Mr. Storey (Hull), a resolution of sympathy with Dr. Waite on his illness was passed. The Hon.' Secre- tary stated that it had been decided to hold the annual meeting of the branch at Derby in May next. Mr. Rowkins (Hull) then read a paper on • Some Improvements in Tubes and Pins for Pivot .Teeth." Afterwards the president congratulated_ Mr. liowkins upon his remarks, and Mr. Brunton (Lis), exhibited and .explaiped several dental appliandes. Mr. T. Fletcher followed With an interesting paper on "Coal gas in the laboratory,", which was interestingly illustra- ted by experiments. As in the case-of Mr. Howkins's paper, that of Mr. Fletcher dealt purely with technical subjects, and the members seemed to much appreciate it. In conclusion he expressed his pleasure that, although he had deserted .the profession for the last fifteen years, he felt that he was not quite forgotten, and that he was as much at home amongst them as if the desertion had not taken place. The President, in pro- posing a vote of thanks to Mr. Fletcher and Mr. Taylor for entertainine the branch, said that the meeting had been a very interesting one, and the experiments had been a source of instruction. The motion was carried by acclammation, and Mr. Taylor, in reply, said they had been very pleased to see the members of the branch at Warrington, and he did not think they had exceeded their duty in providing fer their wants. If the members had been pleased with the catering, both Mr. Fletcher and himself were thoroughly satisfied. With regard to Mr. Fletcher, he would like to say that when he mentioned to him that the branch intended to hold a meeting in Warrington he very willingly and cordially promised to assist him in making the arrangements for the visit. The members did not know Mr. Fletcher as Well as he did, and he could assure them that out of the abundance and kindness of his heart he was wilting to do All he could to promote the interests of the profession. They might depend upon it that what Mr. Fletcher did he did well and willingly. They accepted the vote of thanks, and could assure the Midland Counties Branch that they would be glad to again welcome them to War- rington. (Applause.) A vote of thanks having been accorded to Mr. Howkins for his paper, the proceedings were brought to a conclusion.

div.head: TAF, LATE MR. BLECKLY.
div.p: TAF, LATE MR. BLECKLY.

On Wednesday morning, at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, the presiding magistrate, Captain Withington, referred to the death of the late Mr.' Henry Bleckly, whose loss, he said, they deeply regretted. Mr. Buckton (magistrate's clerk) said chat Mr. 131eckly was an experienced mairisttate, and had a conipetent knowledge of a good dal of criminal and other. law. His loss was a great one. REFERENCE AT ST. PAUL'S. •

In his sermon at St. Pail's Churth, Warrington, on Sunday morning, the Rev. S. Wilkinson, vicar, made a brief reference to Mr. Sleekly, who he said; had been lately laid in his grave. He was a hard worker for many, years in the town of Warrington; he was one of the founciers of the colossal works at Bewsey, an active member of the Board of Guardians, a magistrate and chairman of Quarter Sessions, and in each capacity he had worked very hard for the benefit of his fellowmen. He had now passed away, and had been laid with his fathers. A large number of workmen in the employ of the Messrs. Pearson and Knowles Coal and /ran Com- pany, who had attended the funeral at Bowdon, were among the congregation. MAGISTERIAL REFERENCE AT ALTRINCHAM.

Before the commencq,ment of the ordinary business at the Altrincham Petty Sessions, on Monday, the presiding magistrate, Mr. William Armitage, said that it was his duty to inform the Court of the death of their friend and brother, Mr. Bleckly. He was not very frequently in that Court at the usual sittings of the Petty Sessions, but on other occasions his services were,always available. He had met him very often and had always found his fair and impartial in his judgments. They would greatly miss his assistance.—Mr. J. Overend Evans, barrister, said, as a member of the bar, he felt it his duty ta emphasize as far as he was able the expressions which, had fallen from the Bench for their extreme regret at the passing away of the magistrate to whom reference had been made. Though his presence at Altrincham was not as frequent as that of others, yet his attention and courtesy when he was there had endeared him to all who had the opportunity of appearing before him.

SHOCKING CASE OF CHILIi STARVING AT WARRINGTON.' On Wednesday, at the .Warrington County Petty Sessions, Thomas Gavin, a puddler, living in. War- burtbn.-st., and his wife, Sarah Gavin; appeared in answer to- a summons charging them with havistg wilfully ill-treated, neglected, abandoned, and exposed their son, James Gavin, a boy of the age of seven years.—Mr. Basil Shearer, relieving Officer, said he appeared on behalf of the Guardians of Warrington Union t« prosecute the defendaftts for neglect of their child. The proceedings were taken under the Prevention of Cruelty to and Protection of Children Act, 1889. On the 21st ult. the defendant's house was visited by the Nuisance InspectortiVlr, Frank Kerfoot, who found the child lying on an pld settle amongst a lot of dirty 'rags near to the fireplace; but there was no fire in the grate. Later the saine'dity Dr. Peacocke, Mr. Harbourne Mr. Kerfoot, and. the speaker visited the house, and found the child suffering from burns, which it had received some weeks previously, and starvation. The doctor ordered its removal to the Workhouse, but the i mother would not allow it to be taken away. The father was afterwards seen, and on the following morning the child was taken to the Workhouse, where it now remained. The father was a peddler, and his average wages for the last four weeks had Leen 29s.—Frank Kerfoot, inspector of nuisances fes the Rural Sanitary Authority, said when he went to the house of the defen- dants he found several warners standing near a child which was lying by the empty fireplace. The mother was net there at the time, and he was told that she had not been home since the previous day. The child—a boy —appeared to be in a very neglected and filthy condition; in fact, it was unpleasant to look at. There was no food in the hcuse, and the child, who was wretchedly clad, looked more like a baby than a seven years old boy. Her legs, arms, and fingers were just like bones. —Mr. Thomas Harbourne, relieving officer, said that on the afternoon of the game day he visited the house. The female defendant was there, with one or two other women. Resew the child, which was lying close to the fire, and was hpparently comfortably placed. There was, however, a great want of comfort about the house, and scarcely any furniture. The child was in a dreadful state; it was one of the worst cases he bad ever seen. It was nearly seven years old,, and was actually crying for food. The family consisted of the two defendants, a son about 18 years, a daughter about 18, both of whom were earning their own litangt; and twins nearly seven years old, of which the child in question was one.—Dr. Peacocke, Union Medical Officer(No. district), said that he examined the child, and found it suffering from excessive burns on the chest and abdomen. It was in a very emaciated condition;, its limbs and arms were almost fleshless. At the back of the child's heed a portion of the hair and skin had worn elf, as if by a hard substance on which the child had been lying. The boy seemed to be suffering from starvation and neglect. The dressings on the burns were decomposed, showing that they had not been changed for some time. The child cried for food whilst witness was in the house. The ordinary weight of a child about ei years of age should.be about four stones.—A child weighed from 7 to 111bs. at birth, and from 25 t0,301b.5. when 12 months old.—Nurse Daniels, Warrington Workhouse, stated that when the child was received on the 22nd January it was in a very dirty and neglected condition. When admitted he was bleeding from wounds en the back and hips. They were bed sores. He was, weighed, and found to be only 241b.e. (Sensation.) Round the thick part of the arm he measured 2a inches„ and the circumference of his thigh was only 3-1 inches. Witness had never seen- a child reduced to such. a skeloton.—The male defendant: said that he had always been a good father to his child- ren, and the female deferment denied, that she had neg- lected the child, and called a neighbour, named Ellen Terry, Veho Said that she (Terry) sat up with the child for eleven nights after it had been burned. Another neighbour, Ann Floyd, said that on Sunday,,the• 19th ult., the male defendant asked her to look after the child. She told him that she wanted a blanket to wrap it in, and he.sa:nd that he had bought blankets pleisty of times, but that they had been pawned. He fetched some clothes and wideefer the child. He cried when witness *Mowed him the state the child was in, and said he lied not thought it was neglected in such a manner. He said that his wife had the pawntickets, and he would get them from her, borrow some money, and redeem- the things.—The Chairman said that the Bench bad been pleased to fincUrorn the evidence of two of hi's. children that the male defendant nail been a good father to them generally, and for that reason they were going to make a distinction between him and his wife. He would be lined 20s. and costs, or have to go to prison for a month, in default. The female defendant had been neither a good wife nor a good mother, and she deserved the full penalty which the law prescribed, which was three months' hard labour. The magistrates had, however, decided to reduce it to two months' hard labour, and they hoped she would come out of gaol a better woman.

div.head: CATHERINE'S MISTAKE,
div.p: CATHERINE'S MISTAKE,
%O.OP"'
from Catherine's BiCi) at her first exclamation, and sat down near the table, his head supported on his hand. His face was ashy white, and a clammy sweat had burst out ovlr his head and features. _

"It is coming," he muttered; "it is coming! Eighteen years now, and it is coming to light ! " " Catrina," continued the creole, "for years now I have never once lost sight of you and yours. Un- known to yourself, you have been watched over and protected by me; your movements regulated, and your actions influenced indirectly by my will. When you came to England. a year ego, it was through my agency you entered the house of George Ingestre, as men call him. I was the author of that letter, and I it was who received your monthly journal—received it for a purpose of my own. Shall I nano it? It was, then, to discover whether you would penetrate the fraud of that man's life, whether—" _ - _ "Stop," cried Ingestre, starting up; "stop! Now I know why God has rescued you from the grave; why fi4 has permitted the dead man to walk the earth again.' It is to denounce the crowning guilt of a guilty life; to expose the lie that has given me name. weaith, and position, instead of the heritage of shame that was mine by rights. You have come to expose it; do it. Yet, wait one moment; Maxall and my girl shall know it—all the world shall know is. While the iron is hot, let it strike." - He walked out into the hall, and called Maxall: He was there, utterly brazen and utterly shameless, look- ing defiant, insolent, and fully determined to see the end of the affair. Cleland, the baroness, and Lino were walking up.and down the bail, wondering when dint door would open. Ingestre stood on the threshold, and called them all in. He looked calm, and there was a half smi:e on his lips. "Cleland. Maxoll, and the rest of you, come in here; I wish you to know something, this man has talked out of his grave to tell the world. Come!" They followed him in, all wondering what strange 'ale was to be heard next. _ _

_ "A *I now. say ,your say, Fernando Ponti—fiendi ghost, or whatever you are !" The man turned to Catherine, and said: "Are you willing to hear what I have to tell you?" " Say what you choose; I think I have no wish of any kind WO " Then 1, tell . you this man: who calls himself George 'foss Ingcstre, is an impostor George Ross Ingestre died of the small-pox. in Jamaica., eighteen pion ago: and this is his elder, and illegitimate brother, Edward Maxall," "True, Catherine; true, my own love! I am Edward Maxall, and your hustiand George is in his grave ! I never saw you before—l never loved you before you came into this houSe. You have received no such injuries as you imagined from mt. That devil there Put it into say head, Catherine, to bury poor Cworge, and take his name and inheritance. He urged `tipiin'nte, by what had-I to suffer for the wrong- doing of my parents? for George had no heir but his brother, and I coeld dot claim a thing, for the stain that was on me. • Fe., tempted me! Send! Nom laid the dainty bait! You said we were both so like—the same height; the stune‘. make, the same in everything but birth— and there the younger had the. advantage —we were both knocked down with the small-pox, , and tvhoWould.know which lived and which died of the two? And Iconsented, iii an evil hour—l consented to rob my dead brother of his name, and give him' mine instead. And, Catherine, that is the tale I've 70 tell. Can you love me in spite of it?" The poor lady rose from her seat, and looked at every face in the room. All were alike astonished and cositounded, but not one exhibited a doubt of tbe truth of what they heard. She wrung her hands, andOttok- ing at the baroness, murmured something in a bourse voice. The kind lady heard the, words and interpretea them. "'She asks for her children."
_ Then Fernando spoke

"The b(:).y did net die of the disease, as you *rem told. There he staiads, Catrina ; that youth is your son !" She was clutching the baroneSs's hands for support, but wen she heard this, he flung them away and walked up to Ingest:v. "Is this true? Is that your brother's son ?" "Yes,. Catherine; as I stand here, that boy is George's sem!' She cast her hands up in a gesture of utter despair:: "TheriHod has given me a murderer for a child! His will be done. I am a wretched woman!" "Wait, wait one moment," broke in a sweet voice —it was tinal, who stood pale and shivering close to the door—" do not believe one word that wicked man says, unless it is- confirmed by some one else—some one else who will be here- presently—some one else who is here now' And she opened the door wide at the erund of rapid footsteps striding up the stone-flagged hall. Ingram Ingnitre,,booted and spurred, hot and breath- less, entered without ceremony, and clrised the door after him. "Am lin time; Lina? I have ridden hard. What is it?" _ .

"You are in time, Ingram Ingestre,'' cried the girl," to say all you know of that man yonder—of his—" "Of his-plottings, disgeleas, and all the rest, of it? Very well; Icon de that. I havo not traced hen like a wild Indierethese heti three months for nothing. When and where shall I begin ?" "Begin by letting my poor mother know where my brother is—whabewas. Tel} her, pray tell her, or she will believe that creature te be him." And she pointed to Noxell, who seemed half dead at the words- which, had fallen from Catherimes' lips. I "Mrs„ Ihgestrei your son did not die of the small- pox, as you were told," said Ingram, bowing respect- fully to Catherine. "Nor," turning to Ingestre, "did re bring him to England- as you supposed. The little George Ferdinand! the SOD, and heir, was stolen by the creole Ponti, and brought up as his brother, for the purpose of future revenge upon the went. You hove all seen and know the. poor fellow—he now lies ar, rest in a churchyard two' miles out of Naples; he died of a broken heart, r believe, but in ignorance of wheze I tell you.. Ile who was-the true heir of Redfern is dead, but his sister lives.—there she stands !" He pointed to bins, who had walked up ,to Catherine's aide. Then followed a- dead silence. Edward Mexall turned his bloodshot eyes on young Maxall, and the creole, with, fokied maims, stood by the window- and. smiled. Catherine alone remained an image of mute andi frozen despair. "And now for you,' said Ingram, glaring -at' the- figure leaning so carelessly in the recess formed by the. window, "Doctor Crouse, Count de Resiment, Ponti, or by whatever name you call yourself, I warn you to look out, for I know what you are." Here the-man started a little—just a little. Ingram was-on the point of bursting forth again, when Ingestre as we will still call him) arrested the furious tide. "Fprelleavenra sake let the man go! open the door and let him go.!: Who cares now who or what he is? Catherine will die, she will die, if you. do not all of you go away," Andle walked up to the door and threw, it wide open. Maxall was the first to rush out, but no one thought of him or his flight just then: "No, noe I will not have it so !" cried Ingram. " I have-worked like a horse to find out all that fellow's knavery, and now lam determined you shall all hear it. First and foremost, the man is one of a. secret society, er, rather, he is the secret spy of a certain 'order, of whom Dr. Riga is the head. Riga was in Jamaica when Ponti was executed for the attempted murder of my cousin there. He did not die,,for he had a- quill in his throat ; and Riga restored him to life, on condition he should take a horrible office upon him- self, which had been vacant two years then. This is simple truth. A holy father in Naples- swore it to me, thinking I was about to enter his church. Ile told me that, and gave me abo a list of the sickening duties the fellow had to perform—the knavery, de- ception, and trickery his whole life had. to practise, in order to render him worthy of note- itt his abominable profession; for if his abominations are even so much as suspected by the world, he forfeits his own life. There, there, Madame Bernstein, stands your- beloved Doctor Creusa, who frightened out of you the- secret of Line's birth. There, Mrs. Ingestre, stands the false friend, who, by a forged letter, took from you name, children, and peace. There, Edward Maxall is the man—the demon, rather—who held your secret, and meant to make a trade by the hold- ing. Ah ! it has cost me almost life itself to find out all his subtletieo—all his complicated machinery—his wheel within wheel of secrecy and mystery. But, thank God!" he exclaimed, wiping his heated brow, "thank God I haveldone it, and saved you, as far as, lay in 'my power—saved you, poor child ! from his dreadful clutches." Here he took Lines hand, and pressed it between his own. " That demon wanted to kill her, poor little soul! wanted to make hor his wretched dupe and tool, as he did the poor boy; but-- Ah !" The cry wee wieisted from him by a feet of dexterity suddenly practisel by the creole, who, in the flash of a moment, flung toe window wide open, and leaped down on to the lawn below, a distance of at least twenty feet. •

div.head: SECRET FOR YEARS.
div.p: A SECRET FOR YEARS.

CHAPTER LIT. , atu re • SAITNCR'S STORY. BEWAIL FATINCE told the magistrates her tale in her own fashion, turning her back on George Ross, hut every now and then casting her eye on the dismayed countenances of Maxall and Mrs. Ingestre. ~•.'My name is Keziah Faunre. lam e married woman, but i %%tido* now. Fifteen years ago I was ladys'-maid to Mrs. Ceterfq Ross Ingestre. She was a drunkard, and had a vile temper as well. She wed her husband very badly at those times—l mean wire' the fit was on her; but when she was quite right, Was pleasant and lady-like enough. I was fond Of her in spite of her faults, and I consider I was a good friend to her in those days—aye, and many a time since. 1111,1 e husband didn't like her taking part against him with his ward and the blank thing Domingo. Those three hung tagetheir, and brewed a deal of mischief and scandal in the place, one way and another. Then he sent her away to the North— I her and me—and paid handsomely for ,her in a doctor's family; but she broke out so dreadful that they would notkeep her; and it was the same thing over and over again, twenty—aye, forty and fifty timen, he Corte him no end of mon7. I believe - A generous man---e - Here the woman stopped. Something seemed to rise in her throat and choke the sr rds. Only for a moment; she recovered herself, and continued— "Yes, he is a generous man, and he never grudged the money she cost him in the hope of making her better; but it did not, and he began to hate the shame and tali; of the thing; for she was so given to low company when these fits were on her, that oftentimes the house he lived in was no better than a den of thieves and vagabonds. She was not living in Redfern then, but in London, and round about it. She 4ad a strange fancy for stealing, too, at those periods; and it Wars while- she was staying in a clergyman's family at Dublin that, in one of her worst Ate, she took a gentleman's watch:, She was counted. and 'sentenced to seven years' transporta- tion, under my name—for she always went by it. In order that I might be her scapegoat in these affairs. Then it was that her husband swore he'd give out to everYbody she was dead, He did; he went hack to Redfern with the two children (who had always been kept from her), and the tablet was put Up in/the church to confirm the tale. It is nat for me to say what 'thy master has been since then, or what life he led at Redfern, but I believe his wife drove him to it in the beginning, and then it came very easy to him afterwards. It is not my business to repeat the -erindals that have taken place, but .stilir I tumid enough of _ them to know that my late rnaw.a.• 'sac a reckless and godless man, and WAS bringing his children up in his own bad ways. e I heard that he was madly attached te this last governess of his daughter's, and wanted tO.Marry her, spite of his wife being home again, and dette. mined to annoy him as much as possible. I wartird him through his lawyer of her intentions, for core to me she meant to work his ruin some way or other—swear his children were not legitimate, and that she had never been his wife, if she could injure

him no other way; and she was glad enough when Ma-sall, the spy, told her what his guardian Till.B going to do—marry the lady, and dare her to come forwatd. I walked all the way to L-7 to tell Miss Waco what I knew. The poor soul thought Mr. Ingestre was a widower, and her grief was sad to see when I told her the truth. She left the house that same night, for 81m passed me on the road. walking like one isle-p. I spoke to her, but she did not answer, only moaned and went on. No fear of her marrying- him after that. Miss Wace is in the room : yo.: had better her if I have not told the truth.! And then Miss Waco was politely asked to come forward, and the last wit- ness fell back to :slake room. She was in front of Mr. Ingestre, and as she lifted her veil, looked at him for one moment. That look! ah ! that man seldon-: had tasted such real suffering as when he encountered its silent woe. He stood up, and folded his arms across his massive chest; it heaved up and down in giant throes, and the veins on his forehead and clAwn his hands stood out in knotty joints, llity,emetion was painful for those other men to vritneerts; they turned their eyes Away from, his facet and gazed at the lady's. She tol4 r simple fain simply enough, and in a low, unfalteffnevoine. She had lived in his hon:se, been Ibved by him' and offered marriage; their wed- ding was fixed for the 24th, but had been delayed by Mr. Ingestre's non-arrival at Redfern. She was not married now. Keziah Faunce had warned her not to marry Mr. Ingestre, and. told her that his wife was livipg; she had left the house that night in con- ' Se When her voice ceased; his burst forth. It seemed utterly beyond his control, and he stood there before them aft, a colossal figure of grief and despair. "Alt, Catherine! dicnt think I would injure thee? Did'st think out of very wantoness I would bring this shame upon thy dear-head?' No: no, think it not! re- proach me not. I looked upon myself as free. lam, 'in Gres sight. That woman yonder is none of mine. Catherine, hear me--" • But with& sickening shudder she turned away, and taking the arm of the baroness, left the room. Ingestre followecrher with greedy eyes, and thou turned them on Maxall. "This is your doing" be cried out; "but I forgive you; ats:l have forgiven _all the rest, I forgive this, too. Keziah Faunce,.l thank you. And now, gentle- men, aml a free man once more ?" There. was little doubt about that. He had not married the lady, that was certain; therefore the crime was not committed with which he stood there charged: Whatever the intention might have been, he WAS guiltlesa of the fact, and., therefore, Colonel Towersi,with a hearty shake of the hand, told him a. highly unpleasant business was agreeably got rid Of, and he was free of St. David's Gaol. Ingestre, in spite of his strong emotion, forgot not the courtesy of the gentlemen. Ile turned round, and with a low bow, addressed a few words of thanks to the assembled magistrates for the good feeling evinced in the examination he had' been subjected to, and then, with a second and haughtier bow to Maxon and Ws wife, marched out of therooni, Cleland at his side, mad Mr. Kent following:
CHAPTER LIM
GEORGE INGESTRE S SECRET.
found

lifs went in search of Catherine.instantly, and f( her in a small room, at the side" of the large hall, fainting in the arms of the baronage. fie lifted her up in his own without a word, walked down stairs, and placed her in the carriage which stood waiting at the door. Madame Bernstein .followed with Cleland, and they, too, entered, much, against the master's wish. He stood over her, as. though he expected every hand would be raised to snatch her from him, and he breathed a sigh of infinite relief as the horses started forward at the word "borne" The unfortunate lady did' not remain long uncon- scious, but when she saw on whose bosom she lay, whose arms embraced her; she hrank with cihnost abject terror from hint; ' "Baroness, oave me !"' she, implored, an& then wrung her batch, and gobbed hysteri. ally. The usually calm woman had lost the even balanee ,of her mind—her grief-was beyond control—her utter misery beyondi silent endurance. She wept most wildly, most mournfully.. The tears felbfrom Tegestres eyes as he beheld her suffering. "Oh, my- own Q..therites! my darling 1. my best love He called" her his,, and appeared to have no idea she was no lainger- so.. for be .turned fiercely on the baroness when she remonstrated with him for carry- ing her back to Redfern with him. "And where etse eau she go, madatal- What other home hgs she, pay ?" And when Cleland attempted to draw CatherinVh. rigid hand. from his grasp, he asked her how she. dared, and thrust her away. "Redfern at last r and he bore her out of the. carrisge, into the little room he called his ewn, stretched her tenderly on the sofa, and turned round to bolt the doer on all the rest. Upon the threshold of that door stood the, man Philippe de Regiment. George Ingestre started Ina with a terrible. oath won his lips. "Who, in IleavAt's name, are you?" The man only smiled, and came further into the room, his dark eyes fixed intently on Catherine. "Look at me," hs said to her; "look at me well and earnestly, and answer this question Catherine Franchi, have you forgotten me?" Her white face could become no whiter, but her eyes distended, and she raised her trembling hands, as if to abut out a dreadful sight. "If a dead man can come to life again, you are Fernando Ponti."

"Yes, Lam Fernando Ponti," echoed the man with a smile ; "but I was never dead—never out of this life; and I have never loved another woman than you. I love you 11.0 W ; and I have come to save you iron that man." That man was George Ingestre, who had moved

PEE 'LANCASHIRE COTTON TRADE. A North-east Lancashire correspondent says :—At Present there appears a disposition to increase rather than to decrease the number of looms at srork in East Lancashire, and it is stated that at the first favourable °PPortunity the weavers, through their organisation, 'will apply :for an advance of five per cent. ,LANCASHIRE MINERS' WAGES. The miners .and day wagemen in the Lancashire 'niers" Tederation have issued circulars to their eLalPloyers asking, owing to the selling pricesSf coal hat-, gone upso high, for a further advance of 10 per , in wages, and also expressing regret that selling .I;cices were put up so rapidly, as they are afraid it will, "0 much towards killing the present good trade. The Dean of Manchester, speaking at a social meeting at miners at Mosley Common on Saturday night•referced to recent discussions on the proposed Eight Hours Bill, and expressed-the opinion that an eight hours day would Probably go a long way to bring about an equilibrium of Work and of workers. He commended the principles and practice of trade unionism, but held that the per- inanent success of labour combinations would not be aft, tired until Boards of conciliation and arbitration had neen established.
