THE' LATE MR. ,LcIIINI\TIES:
THE FUNERAL,

The remains Olitie-itti.e7a-1-r., john Gordon Mc &Unties were interred at the Warrington Cemetery, on Tuesday, in the same grave to which, years ago, was consigned the body of the late Mrs. MeMinniee. There was no elaborate display, no "pomp and cere- naony," but the deceased was display, wed to the grave by a large body of prominent townsmen who,having esteemed him in life, attended to pay a kst open to- ken of respect. The signs of mourning were general, Drawn blinds and business places closed, on the route to the Cemetery, evidenced how widespread was the sense of the loss sustained in the death of one who was in his lifetime so +devoted to the interests of his fellows,and whose benevoleet and genial nature made him liked by all who kneiv hli Before the procession was formed the representatiVes of the Liberal Association and liberal Club met in the darkened rooms of the building in Bewsey-st, and sorrowfully went about the task of preparing to follow to the grave all that was mortal of their departed leader. Beautiful wreaths were placed on the table in the reading room. One was the tribute of the Liberal Askociation, one was from the club members, and the other was from Councillor F. A. Roberts. When the cortege left the late resi- dence of the deceased, it was headed by a possii of borough police, of whom Inspector %maks was in charge. "The Mayor, who wore his gold chain of. office, and with him other representatives of the • civic body to which Mr. McMinnies formerly be- longed, came next, The Aldermen who walked were Messrs. Sutton, Wright, Holmes, and Davies, and Alderman Harrison joined the procession in his carriage. The Councillors were Messrs. Ashten, Blackhurst, Bolton,Cannell, J. Fairclough, T. Flood, J. Garner, J. Shaw Green, J. Hepherd, W. H. .T. Jenkins, R. W. Marsh, J. Muir, and N. B. Percival, and the following corporate officials also walked : Messrs. W. H. Brook, (Town-clerk). J. Lyon Whittle (deputy town-clerk), G. F. F. 'White (deputy magistrates' clerk),T.H.Longdin (borough surveyor), C.4Madeley (librarian), and F. Taylor (gas office.) The 1 succeeding order of the procession was observed as undera—Deputation from the Conservative Associa- tion, consisting of Messrs. John White and Henry 'Green all (who occupied a carriage).Messrs.W.W.West- well, 'J. Hampson, Thomas Crozier, A. Jolley. James Smethurst, and R. D. Topliss ; deputation from Con- servative Club, consisting of Messrs. S.Higham, G. Pllkington, and E. Aukland ; the Revs. S. Wilkinson and E. C. E. Carleton ; the representatives of the Liberal Association and Club,' consisting of Coun- cillor F. A. Roberts and Councillor 3. H. Fleming, Who carried wreaths, , Conncillor William Pierpoint, Rev. J. W. Varley, Rev. E. Moore. Messrs. H. Brown, A. Browne, Corney, Joseph Titchett, D. Tinnion, John Harrisoi, ThOmas Kiernan, Thomas Mather, James Strange, William Roberts, C. J. Holmes. Jabez Plinston, Thomas Birch- all, John Craik, Thomas Morris, G. T. Brown, E. 3. Guest, J. E. Warren, William Jones, W. Winstanley, Thomas Critchlev, Samuel Jones, Joseph Owens, George Weaver, Felix Loughlin, Henry Eyes, A. Stir- rup, George Wallington, John McConville, • W. H. Dutton, Thomas Evans, S. Dunbobbin, T. Caldwell, John Gandy, ',John Walker, M. Shepherd. G. Moly- neax, E. J. Mitchell, John Oritehley, John Clayton I Liberal agent), Albinson,FraneisDickson,W. Diggle .W.Walker, Haynes, S. Kenyon, E. Place, T. S. Birtles, R. Siddall, &c. Afterwards came the hears. and then carriages bearing the principal mourners. In the first carriage were Mr. W. McMinn' es (Farrington), nephew of the deceased, Colonel Fagan (London), Mr. G. B. Dewhurst and Mr. Barnsley (Liverpool). The second contained Aldermen Crosfield and Burgeks, and Messrs. T. G. Ryland; and Ziba Armitage; the third;: Conncillors , F. Monks and • H. Roberts, and Messrs. William Crosfield (Liverpool), and C. S. Burgess; fourth : Rev. John Yonge, Dr. Starkey Smith, Mr. T. J. Ridg- way, and Mr. C. Morris; 'fifth:: Messrs. W. T. Threlfall and R. Payne (Farrington) ; sixth: Dr. Gornall and Mr. David Garnett,. seventh: Messrs.. Samuel Rigby and Charles Choriey .• other carriages held the Rev. F. Roberts, Rev. F. K. Freeston, Mr. Thomas Jones, and the following deacons of Wyc- liffe Congregational Church, of the congregation of which the late Mr. Merlin/ries was a member : Messrs., William Beswick, Joseph S. Garland, J. Pod- more, Henry Spencer, Richard Roberts. Thomas Haw- thorn, A. H. Lee, William Wallington, and the Rev. J. Davies minister at Cockhedge mission, the Rev. W. Graham, Messrs. ITitchett, J. Podmore and William Crampton were present as representing the . Primitive Methodist denomination. The mourners left Summer House, Bewsey-road, at about half-past eleven o'clock, and the procession moved slowly and reverently through the streets to the burial ground. The route taken was by way of Bewsey-street, Horsemorket-street, B tattertoarket- street, and Church-street, and large crowds watched as the cortege passed. As the hearse containing the coffin, which was covered with beautiful wreaths, passed on its way, heads were uncovered, and there were general manifestations of sorrow. Work was suspended at the large establishment of Messrs. Rvlands Bros. in Church-street, until after the funeral ceremony had been completed. AT TUB CEMETERY. " 'When the cemetery was reached the coffin was borne to the chapel, where the chief mourners and as many others as could, accommodated as- sembled. 'Here the Rev. John longe, the pastor of Wycliffe, impressively read the burial service, and as he did so, and as he efterwards made fitting allusion to the virtues of the deceased, the heartfelt sorrow of some found expression in tears. The scene was one of great solemnity, and the words of the rev, gentleman found a response in the hearts of all present. He said : 'We have met hero to-day to pay a last token of respect and affection, to cele- brate the last Christian rite for one whom we have all held high in honotir, one whom many of us have held in true affection and esteem. Mr. Mc Minnies has been for many long years one of the most conspicuous of Warrington men. His intel- lectual capacity and social position have madehim a leader' in this town. Long years Of devoted service to the welfare of the community, according to his views Of truth, right, and duty, have given him a position'in the esteem and confideoce of the Whole town which has been strikingly illustrated by the marvellous impression whi eh his funeral has crested to-day. He has been trilled to hold municipal office, and to hold the high and hotmurable position of political representative of this borough. Ithink we all know that he recognised what is at least one of the cardinal doctrines of the Christian faith—that a man is not to live ,unto himself. Therefore, he gave his thought, energy, time, and means very largely to the service of hie fellow-men. Thus he haebeen conspicuous. This gathering to-, s day, of all parties and creeds, is a further token that le has been highly respected and esteemed. Few • -men, certainly few men it has been my privilege to ' 'know, have been so true to their own personal con- • atictions and yet made so few enemies in the course of their career. I very much doubt whether, in the • actual and libselute sense of the word, MIT departed friend had an enemy anywhere to be 'found. He 'had political opponents. but I believe there is not a single political opponent of his who does not hold him in the highest honour and esteem. If the ptrblic have learned thus to esteem him, those in the circle of his private life have learned to love him. We have found him a genial friend, gracious, courteous, and considerate to others, carefttl of the comfort of everyone, free and generous in his hospitality. We have found him also a generous friend to every good 'and true cause, whether reli- gions ,or philanthropic; and he has been a 'helper, comforter, friend, andbrother to nasory a needy one in the time of need end 'distress. The town is; poorer by his death. The religions denomination into which he was born, and to which to the 'last he was a faithful adherent, loses greatly in his death, and a large circle of friends will never cease to cherish the memory of John' Gordon McMinnies with affection and esteem. He haa gone,eB 'you arid I will have to go in our turn, and when that day may come may God, in His infinite mere, receive ris into His glory everlasting.. The enflin was then borne to tie grave, into Which ' it . vias lowered in the presence of a large concourse of people, many having, come to the Censetery to witness' the interment who had not joined in the procession. Amongst them were Mr. Robert Dairies, Major Litton, and Mr. S. Davey. The inside of the vault was made beautiful by flowers and ferns sent from Walton Lea by Mr. John Crosfield. The coffin was of fumed oak with brown oak panels, and gilt brass mountings. On the breast-plate was the simple inscription—" John Gordon McMinnies, born May 27th. 1817 ; died February let, 1890." Messrs. R. Garnett and Sous had 'charge of the funeral arrangements, which were carried out under the supervision of Mr. Ay. C. Nicholson. The bearers were Messrs. Buck (coachman), Bonehill, Tinsley, Bloomfield, and Longshaw. In addition to the wreaths forwarded by the Liberal Association and Club, others had been received from Aldermin and Mrs. John Crosfield, Alder- man and Mrs. Burgess, Mr. and Mrs. W. McMinnies, Councillor and Mrs. F. A. Roberts,Councillor and Mrs. H. Roberts, Mrs. George Crosfield, Dr. Gornall, Miss Hood, Mrs. Earle, the porters at Bank Quay Station, Mr. C. S. Burgess, Mr. Milne Barnsley, the Rev. G.S. Reaney and Mrs. ReaneY, the servants at Summer House, the teachers and scholars at Farrington Day Schools, Mr. tri4 Mrs, ob Xiltiel the choir of Wycliffe Congrega- ,

gational Church, the workpeople at Farrington Mill, and Messrs. W. and J. Richardson. ,The wreath sent to Summer House by the lesrat Quay porters was accom- panied by a most sympathetic letter. We are informed that the Rev, George Sale Heaney, formerly pestor of We cliffe Church, was away in York- shire, andcould not return in time for the funeral. Mr. John Rytands was prevented by indisposition from attending. REFERENCES AT THE LIBERAL CLUB. On Monday evening a largely attended meeting of the General Council of the Warrington Liberal Association, was held at. the Liberal Club, the meeting having been called on account of the death of Mr. McMinnies, the late president of the Associ- ation. Alderman Burgess was elected to preside, and amongst those present were Alderman Molmes, Councillors F. A. Roberts, W. Pierpoint, Henry Roberts, J. 11. Fleming, J. Shaw Green, Garner, and T. Flood; Dr. Gornall, Messrs. T.' Birchall, C. S. Burgess. C. .T. Holmes, T, Morris, S. Kenyon, ...T. Gandy, J. Walker, Albinson, G. Wallington, S. Dun- bobbin, Kiernan, Strange, Tinnion, Clayton (Liberal agent), &c. The CHAIRMAN said that when he came into that room he did not suppose he should be asked to take the chair, but his long. associations with Mr. McMinnies, of such an exceedingly agreeable charac- ter as they had been, would not permit him to hesitate for one moment to take the chair they had' ' so kindly asked him to take, and to see if by any interchange of opinion they could improve the melancholy occiaion of his-(Mr. 1/IcMinntes') leav- ing them. He could have wished that Mr. McMin- nies could have been spared. (Hear, hear.) He was expressing the feeling of every gentflemanite saw before him when he said that there was not a man amongstthern they would not rather have seen pass away than their venerable friend Mr. McMinnies. (Hear, hear.) Few, perhaps none in that room—and there were very few left in Warrington out of the room—who had had the same life-long opportunities of knowing Mr., McMinnies that he had had, and from the earliest days of their association together to the last moment of his existence.he had always been the same kind genial friend of man wherever man wanted a friend (Applause.) The people in War- rington would Bye a long while before they found another man like Mr. McMinnies, or one as ready to do a grand work. They as Liberals could hardly hope to replace him in any way. (Hear, hear.) He (Alderman Burgess) thought it would be perfectly idle to suppose that within the ranks of the Liberal party there was a man to-day that was qualified to occupy the position that Mr. McMinnies had occu- pied. They all knew as well as they knew they were in that room, that Mr. McMinnies' great desire was for the 'extension of freedom, not simply of political freedom for he was equally earnest in his desire for the religious freedom of every creature on the face of the earth. He was equally ardent and enthusiastic in his desire that the utmost freedom of his cour try's commercial life should exist, and no man; either in this or any other toWn, knew better than Mr. McMinnies the advantages 'of having free inter- course with all the nations of the earth and how it addedtothe greatness of his own country. (Hear, hear.) But, the time had come when they must part with him, and that night they should try if they could to embody the sentiments and feelings of -their minds with - respect to their great and , departed 'friend in the shape of a resolution that , would convey what they felt on the subjett. He had -nodoubt that before they parted an oppor- tunity would be afforded of recording by vote their, sentiments as to the great loss they had sustained, as well as the great loss this community and the Whole human family had sustained in the shape of .ene of the most ardent and life-long workers for its well-being. He would not go into detail. He could speak to them of almostewery public act in Mr. McMinnies' life from 1840 up to the present rive, for it was in that year he first become politicagy associated with him. From that time to this that acsocie :ion had never had a break in it, and he liadsregretted that the seve-ance had come with such rapidity and haste, for, although Mr. McMinnies' health had not been satisfactory for a 'long time, they did not anticipate a week ago that 'they should be meeting that night on such a Imelancholy occasion. (Hear, hear.) They all knee/ what Mr. McMinnies' life had been, but this he would say in summing up, that as a politician, as a neighbour, as a townsman, and as a friend of the great human family, Mr. McMinnies discharged his dcties in such a way as ought to be an example to all of them to do, so far as in them lay, the same sort of thing according to the light and power that was in' them. (Applause.. 9 Alderman Houses said he could join with Alderman Burgess in every remark he had made. He had not been associated with Mr. McMinnies quite to the same extent as Alderman Burgess ; but he had been associated with him years ago in several public works and measures in which' he was engaged, and he well remembered the tact. ability and exceeding cleverness with which Mr. Mc Mienies entered into and conducted all these various schemes. He reeretted more than he could express the great loss the town had sustained, beginning possibly with his political party and going on to the Chapel over the way (Wycliffe) but finiehing with the whole of the inhabitants of Warrington. They could all see and feel that they had lost a grand '.and beneficent neighbour.' (Hear, hear). Oauncillor F. A.Ronears said a letter had been received from the Rev. W. Graham regretting that he was unable to be present at the meeting, for the cause of which he was deeply grieved, bet stating that he would be present at the funeral the next day. Mr. Z. Arrmitage-, also regretted he was unable to be present, and Mr. W. Long had serf,: a message that he was unable to leave his house. Continuing, Mr. 'Roberts said he felt Imbed lost something more ;than 41 political friend in Mr. Madinnies—he felt as though he had almost lost a father in his pelitical life. He had loclked up to Mr.' McMinnies and hall gone to him regularly for advice,and in adversity for comfort! and he knew he was not singular amongst their party in that respect,foranany of them, if anything had troubled them in their political or public life in the borough,had been in the habit of going to Mr. MeMinnies with their trouble, knowing when they went that he would fully enter into their troubles and try to extricate them fromthem. There was no truer friend than Mr. MeMintriee to any one who knew him (Hear hear). He did not know that he felt the death of any public man as much as he had felt that of Mr. McMinnies. Ele had grown up inthe town as a successful business man, and he was singled out as the man likely to, win the Liberal cause in Warrington. Long before he (Mr. Roberts) came to Warrington he had beard from his brother that if Warrington was to he won for the Liberal cause the only man to do it was Mr. McMinnies. He did win it and wen it-well, and if he had only been in good vigorous health he would have been member for War- rington to-day.. (Hear, hear.) But health failed, and finally death had come to take him from them. Even at that time they might perhaps take some comfort from the knowledge Of the general grief that was felt in the town owing to -the decease of Mr. McMinniee. They, the Liberal party, were not alone in feeling the loss the Borough had sustained. He had been pleased and grati- fied as a member of the Liberal party, that at once on the 'knowledge of the death the flh.g was hoisted half-mait high at the Censervative Club. ('Applause.) He was - pleased to think that even in the ranks of political op- ponents, there was sympathy with them and a feeling of regret that a great man had gone away from amongst them. From the sentiments expressed by a number of the Conservative leaders in the town he had met within the last day or two,it was evident that there was a wide spread feeling of deep regret that Warrington had lost one of its foremost citizens. (Hear, 'hear.) He could only hope that the memory of Mr. MeMinmes would be an incentive to all of them in the future to try and use' their beet endeavonrs when called upon to carry nut the wofit which it was his aim in life to promote. (Ap- plause.) Mr. T. BIRCHALL mast cordially re-echoed the senti- manta expressed by Alderman Burgess and the other speakers. He felt the less of Mr. McMinnies as a very deep personal loss. He remembered that as a lad of 13 in. It'e learned' from Mr. McMinnies' lips to love the cause at political freedom pleaded, as it always was by him, ee,eloquently. Eremitic° that he had looked upon him as a born leader of men, a man with whom they always felt perfectly in sympathy, and one who had the facullyolcnderstanding men to a degree that was not given to every man."( Hear, hear.) The tact he dis- played at all times of difficulty was really wonderful, and his genial humour and kindly countenance made them on all occasions feel perfectly at home with hire. And then when /licitness had laid it had upon him, end as he sakin his room aconfirmed invalid he was an example to all of there. (Hear, home-) Now that he was gone, the deeper was the responsibility that v lvasceon them, especially upon their younger men, to sap at the taloa he loved so well and so continually ad , not only by speech but also with his purse and In every possible way, did not fall to the ground for want of support. (Hear, hear.) Councillor W. INISRPOINT said he had never known his own father,and of alt the men he had ever met who came nearest to his ideal of a father that man, was he who,* loss these so much deplored that night. The eloquent speech that hat' been made by Alderman Burgess had, he thought, expressed everything that the Liberal party generally could have expressed with reference to Mr. McMinnies. He could only say Mat the Liberal party had been tossed about to some very considerable extent for the last few years. They had done all they could to keep the ship moving on in the direction indicated by Mr. McMinnies, and his name and memory should be a further incentive to them to see that the ship of Libera- lism, which some people expected would now be dashed upon the rocks,would not be allowed to suffer such a fate. (Hear, hear.) He had sufficient confidence in the Liberal party of Warrington to believe that that would make them use increased efforts, knowing that such incremed efforts would only be towards Currying out

the lifelong' work of John Gordon 'McMinnies. And although they had but few of their old leaders left, the younger members of the party must take a joint respon- sibility ia carrying on that', work. By doieg all they could to carry Out Mr. MeMinnies'ipolicy, they.would do something towards perpetuating, his name which would ever be a household word in Warringtop. (Applause.) Mr. T. Meatus said he could not leave the room with- out expressing his regret for the death of the" grand old man" of Warrington "%•-• He had never been se impressed in his life before as when he heard of Mr. McMinnies' death with those magnificent two: lines in Longfellows' poem" The Psalm of Life," Lives a great men all rernirol us. We can make our lives sublime. And if the young men of Warrington would follow Mr. McMinnies' example they would not be like "dumb- driven cattle but heroes in the strife." (Applaufse). Councillor H. ROBERTS moved the following resolution': "That the members of the Warrington Liberal Associa- tion Kaye learned with the profoundest grief of the death of their president, John Gordon McMinnies, Esq., and desire to place on record their sense ef the irreparable loss which Asa thereby been occasioned.. During a period of half d century his wisdom as a leader, his inde- fatigable courage, his unwavering faith in the principles to which his was a lifelong devotion, these were ever an inspiration to tkose whose pride it was to number them- selves amongst his attached co-workers. The great cause of Liberalism in this town and in the country at large, have lost in him an able advocate and a most generous benefactor, and to all of us his death presents itself as the loss of a beloved and trusted friend. To the surviving relatives of Mr. McMinnies we tender our heartfelt sympathy and condolence in this sad bereave- ment which has overtaken them." Mr. Roberts, con- tinuing, said words would fall far short of what the privilege of an acquaintance with Mr. McMinnies had been to him during the last 17 years. Seventeen years ago when quite a youth he first made the acquaintance of Mr. Minnies in his capacity as a candidate for the secretaryship of the Liberal Asso- ciation, and he received such kind sympathy from him, in what was to, him (Mr. Roberts) a critical period of his life, that from tilfat moment he felt he had secured a warm and thorough personal friend. During to the whole of the years that had passed since then, in times of depression Mr. McMinnies had been a great sup- port to him, and in times of encouragement and success they had rejoiced together, and there had never passed between them an unpleasant word. But he was not there to speak so much of the personal relationship between Mr. McMinnies and himself as he was to speak of the connections which existed between Mr. McMinnies and Warrington as a town. It was a very curious thing but he did not think that within the last fifty years there had been a man in Warrington whose death had been so much regretted as the death they deplored that night. (Hear, hear.) And the reason was not far to seek. It did not matter who the man woman or child was that approached Mr. McMinnies to ask his advice and sym- pathy upon any subject whatever, they were all treated with the same gentlemanly courtesy and the same kind geniality, and in numbers of cases with the same unosten- tatious but thorough pecuniary support. (Applause.) Ile knew of many cases where widows had cause to bless the name of Mr. McMinnies. There were young men today who a sew years ago where orphan boys and whose position was a very awkward one indeed, but Mr. McMinnies came to their rescue, and to-day they occupied honourable and prominent positions in this and other towns. Time would fail him to speak adequately of the private munificence of Mr. McMinnies. (Hear, hear). And more than all that was the remarkable devotion which characterised all his conduct towards the great principles of Liberal- ism. There never was any doubt as to where Mr. Me Minnies would be found in regard to all the great ques- tions of the day, and he was sorry to think that such a I doubt had entered into the mind of a single Conservative in the borough to suppose, because of Mr. McMinoies' repeated absences from Liberal platforms through physi- cal weakness. Those who had had the pleasure of meeting with him in his own house knew how false was the suggestion contained in one of Saturday's papers. (Hear, hear). He was in full and earnest sympathy with the grand old man in his efforts to redeem the Sis- ter Isle and in spite of great physical weakness in spite of great pain and inconveniences of all kinds:Mr. McMinnies never allowed those things to come between him and the loyalty he professed and showed to the great cause they all had at heart. (Applause). Dr. GORNALL, in aeconding the proposal made by Mr. Roberts, said that like Mr. Pierpoint he had never known his own father, but from the first time he knew Mr. McMinnies, 22 years ago, till the present he always felt that in him he had even a parental adviser. That was not an oecassion in which he dare indulge in many encominms on Mr. Mellinnies' work. But this he did knew : his Liberalism was a far higher Liberalism than many of them carried out. The Liberalism that he carried out was a Liberalism that transferred itself from his mind and from his pocket to the interests ef every religious body in the town. Dissenters found ia him an earnest friend, and their friends the Roman Catholics he knew, if there were any in that room, would say that they had not a better friend even in their 'own denomination than John Gordon McMinnies. (Hear, hear.) He (Dr. Gorna,ll) had had frequent opportunities of being present in the library at Summer House, and he could say as a medical man that he never knew a man who suffered pain with such patience as Mr. McMinnies. The patience with which he suffered was a sermon to every person in that room. (Hear, hear.) He never heard him grumble on any occasion. In all his recollections Mr. McMinnies was the manliest man he ever knew. (Hoar, hear.) He was pleased I. see such a large meeting that night, and he only wished there was •as large a meeting on every occasion in connection with the Liberal party. He did not see why there should not be. If they believed that Toryism was tyranny,tyranny- of the worst kind, there ought never to be a leader absent from their meetings, and if they acted in the spirit of Mr. McMinnies they ought to bury every diffi- culty and every division ea emancipate Warrington from society's strangulation and from Tory hypocrisy. (Applause.) Mr. S. DIINROBRIN referred to the pecuniary help Mr. McMinnies' had given to the Medical Association in the town, and to various friendly Societies. The working classes of the Town had, he said, received a severe blow by the death of Mr. McMinnies. (Hear hear.) Mr, C. S. Burtoess said that only those who had the nrivelege of being a personal friend of Mr. McMinnies could estimate him at his full worth. As the leader of the party in Warrington he was a very great force, and by his shrewdness, and tact he inspired a con- fidence in his followers which it was not given to many men to do. He was sure it would be a pride to many young men in the town to be able in the future to say that they had been followers and supporters of Mr. McMinnies. (Hear hear.) As a personal friend it was always a delight to be in his company ; his genial disposition led one always to him, and his charming manner of conversation was most delightful. (Applause). Mr. C. J. Hovers felt that the loss of Mr. McMinnies was a very great blow far outside the ranks of their own party. (Hear, hear.) Mr. W. ROBEars referred to the regret expressed by men of all parties at the death. He also mentioned that Mr. McMinnies had expressed to him his admiration of the rank and file of the Liberal party of Warrington, and that he believed they were loyal to Mr. Gladstone, and so earnest in their desire to support him that if they got a good candidate at the next election there was a very good chance of victory. (Hear, hear.) Councillor FLEMING said that since he was first intro- duced to Mr. McMinnies he had found him one of the most genial and warm-hearted friends it was the privilege of man to know. He was head and shoulders -above all the men he had known, and with another man like Mr. McMinnies Warrington would be safe for (Applause.) Mr. limmove referred to the high opinion of Mr. McMinnies expressed to him during the Northwich election by Mr. T. P. O'Connor. Be believed that all the Irish representatives had a thorough respect for the genuine character of the deceased gentleman. (Hear, hear.)

... , , Mr. G. WaLuxurox referred to Mr. McMinnies'connec- tion with Wycliffe Chapel, and to the high esteem in which he was held by the congregation there and the townspeople generally. Mr. ALBINSON gave a touching instance of the thought- ful sympathy of Mr. McMinniesin cases of bereavement. Mr. S. BAntow remarked that taking bins all in all he was afraid they should not see the like of Mr. McMinnies again. Mr. A. DROWN)? referred to the readiness of Mr. McMinnies to always give advice when asked for it by those who were younger and less experienced than him- self. The resolution was then put to the meeting and car- ried unanimously by a show of hands. The meetinc terminated, after a cordial vote of thanks had been given to the chairman. WARRINGTON CRICKET AND BOWLING CLUB. Reference was made to the death of Mr. McMinnies at the annual dinner of the WarringtonCricket and Bowling Club on Sear lay evening. Mr. William Owen, in giving "Success to the Club," a toast with which the name of the President (Councillor F. A. Roberts) was associated, said he was sorry to find that Mr. Roberts seemed rather under a cloud that even- ing, on account of the death of Mr. McMinnies. The speaker felt that that was, perhaps, an opportunity of which he might take advantage by saving that there was not a Conservative present who did not feel the very deep- est sympathy with Mr. lloberts—(hear, hear)—and he knew this from his very heart,—that there was not a Conservative amongst them who had ever respected anyone amongst their opponents snore than the late Mr. McMinnies. (Hear, hear.) In him the Conservatives had a foreman who was thoroughly worthy of their steel, and whom they were proud to fight— (hear, hear)—and if their friend, Mr. F. Roberts, op- posed them some day he was the sort of man also that ' they would be proud to fight. (Applause, and Voices : " Arid beat." " Maybe.") The Conservatives condoled very sincerely with Mr. Roberts and all on his fide on the loss which had that day befallen them. The man they had just lost had been a very strong man amongst them—strong because of the fact that he had engaged the attention and the affection of men on both sides. All, no matter what their political creed had been, had res- pected him, and they felt his loss very much. (Applause).

Councillor F. A. Rosters, replying; thanked Mr. Owen and the company generally most sincerely for the kind feelings to which expression had been given. Any Liberals who were present would, he was sure, join in the acknowledgment of the kindly feelings which had been shown them that evening in what, to them, was really a great bereavement. (Hear, hear.). When he first heard the flews he felt almost unable to come there that evening, and if it had not been that he knew so many friends had promised to come and that the absence of himself and others would have put a damper on the gathering, he would have been inclined to have stayed away. But after the kindly reference which had been made the Liberals must be pleased that they were pre- sent to mingle with the " other side in expressing deep regret at the loss which they felt Warrington had sus- tained by the death of Mr.. McMinnies. (Hear, hear.) To many of them Mr. McMinnies had been not only a political friend, but a dear friend, a social friend, in more senses than one. He had always been willing and ready to give help and advice to anyone who came for it, and the Conservatives could not have known a better col- league than the Liberals had in Mr. McMinnies. (Hear, hear.)

, WYCLIFFE CONGREGATIONAL CHURCH. At the conclusion of the morning service at this church on Sunday the organist played the Dead March in " Saul " as a mark of respect to the late Mr. McMinnies, who was a member of the congregation.

LEGH-ST. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL. At the Legh-st. Primitive Methodist Chapel, on Sun- day evening, the preacher, Mr. Samuel Owens, of Wid- nes, said : I have only this day heard of the great loss which the town, the Primitive Methodist Chapel, and the connexion have sustained by the death of Mr. McMitmies. By it we have lost a truly generous friend. Truly a noble-hearted son of humanity has fallen. Mr. McMinnins was endowed with two grand essentials, a good social position and a generous disposition. He was always ready to help those in need, and especially ready to give his help to the Primitive Methodists. You, the members of this congregaton, and the friends at Latchford, know this better than I can 'tell you, and I trust that the occasion will not be allowed to pass with- out some more fitting allusion being made than I feel I am capable of making, owing to only having heard a few hours ago and having had no time for preparation.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

A DODGE TO GET LODGINGS "ON THE CHEAP." At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday morning, two brothers named James and William McMullen were brought up on remand charged with being deserters from the Army. It transpired that they gave themselves up as deserters, but inquiries failed to bear out their state- ments. The Chief Constable (Mr. S. Hunt) said that it was very possible that the confession was a ruse on the part of the prisoners to get a meal and a night's lodging at the Biidewell: Prisoners were discharged. AN ASTONISHED LODGING HOUSE KEEPER. Henry Webber, summoned for keeping lodgers with- out having his house registered, at Rixton, on the g3rd of December last, told the magistrates at the Warrington County Petty Sessions, qn Wednesday, that:he should re- fuse to comply with the law. They thereupon fined him 40s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment, which seemed rather to astonish him. He was also informed that he would be subject to a penalty of 40s. a day if he took lodgers without having the house registered. ALLEGED THEFT IN THE MAE/OCT.

At the Warrington Police Courton Thursday, a youth who gives the name of Michael Seeles was charged in custody with having stolen 12 collar studs, the property of Louis Hart, smaliware dealer, of Liverpool, who has a stall in the market. Mr. Hunt (the Chief Constable) said that on Wednesday Constable Bell saw prisoner attempt to pick a woman's pocket and arrested him. In his possession were found the studs,which were supposed to have been stolen from the stall of the prosectutor.—A rernand was granted.

A VIOLNNT FEMALB IN COURT. Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, a well-known character named Emma Howard was sen- tenced to a month's imprisonment for breaking glass at the house of John Dixon, her uncle, who lives at Latch- ford. She threw a stone through the window. After the sentence had been passed prisoner threatened to kill her sister, who had given evidence against her, and com- mitted an assault on her uncle by clutching hold of his hair. The magistrates therefore increased the sentence to one of six week's imprisonment.

div.head: FOWL STEALING AT WALTON.
div.p: FOWL STEALING AT WALTON.

_ At an Occasional Court, held at Warrington on Thurs- day, two labourers named John Jackson, and Joseph Shawcross, were brought up on warrant charged with having stolen three hens, the property of William Bee- wick, Ship Inn, Walton. P.C. Dutton stopped the prisoners at Moore, and found in their possession a bag containing the hens, which Shawcross said they had found. The birds were subsequently identified as be- longing to Mr. Beswick. Prisoners were each sent to gaol for a fornight.

A BAD CHARACTER SENT TO PRISON. Edward Sauce, a young man, made his twenty-seventh appearance before the Warrington magistrates, on Monday. He was charged with having be n drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-et., on Saturday evening, with assaulting Constable Monoghan, and, on warrant, with having been drunk and disorderly on the Bth of last October. The Chief Constable (Mr. Hunt) said that Sauce had been twenty-two times in goal, and had paid ; fines four times. He was about as had a lad as any in Warrington. The magistrates sent Sauce to prison for a month, with hard labour. A QUARRELSOME DRUNKARD. On Tuesday, at the Warrington Police Court, John Burke, a yourtg man, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road, on Monday night, and also with assaulting George Billington, barman at the Norton Arms Hotel.—Billington said that the prisoner called for some beer, and on it being refused him, on account of his being drunk, he said he would not leave the hotel until he had been served. He afterwards struck witness, and became so quarrelsome that he had to be removed by a constable. The magistrates con- sidered it a bad case, and committed the prisoner for a month's hard labour. TATOORD PRISONER. At the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday, Francis Dawes, a man-o'war's man, 35 years of age, was brought up in custody charged with being an absentee from H.M.S. Revenge, lying at Queenstown.—r.c. Monaghan apprehended toe prisoner at Messrs. Monks, Hall, and Company's works on Monday. The warrant which had been issued by Captain Dyke, of the Revenge, described the prisoneras "a straggler," and mentioned that he bore the following tattoo marks :—" Free trade," and elapsed hands, on chest; flag, and woman's bust, on right forearm; tombstone with inscription, upper left arm ; crucifix, front left forearm' and " Prince Im- perial " on upper right forearm.—Prisoner was remanded to the naval authorities at Queenstown. • COMPLIMENTING A CONSTABLE. At Monday's sitting of the Warrington Police Court, Alderman Davies, referring to two cases in which Con- stable Monaghan had been engaged on Saturday night said that officer in the short period of a quarter of an hour assisted te lock up three persons who had been guilty of disorderly conduct in the streets. He men- tioned the fact to show the great trouble persons of the character who had been charged gave to the police. There was no desire on the part'of the police to interfere with people unless there was a necessity to do so ; it was no pleasure to them to be always concerned in these brawls. The Bench •could express their satisfac- tion with the manner in which the police dealt with
, - these difficult cases. STEALING FROM THE W08E1101:78E.

On Wedne;i:;;;i- the Borough POlice-E'-ourrt,Catherine Doherty, an old woman, was charged with stealing from the Union Workhouse, on Monday last, a skirt, of the value of 6s. 6d.; and Julia Noakley was charged with receiving the same knowing it to have been stolen. ' Doherty was an inmate of the Workhouse, and on Mon- day obtained permission to go into the town for a few hours. While in town she met Noakley, who pawned the skirt at Mr. Morton's shop in Winwick-st. The assistant communicated with the police; esquiries were made, and it was found to have been stolen from the Workhouse.---rrisoners were committed to gool for 18, days with hard labour. CIIEA—ING TICE RAILWAY COMPANY. Joseph Matthews, a young man, was summoned to the Warrington Police Court on Monday on a charge of having travelled by rail from Cross-lane to Warrington, ; on the 16th of November last, without having paid hit fare. Mr. Preston prosecuted on behalf of the London and North Western Railway Company, and said that the defendant had abused a privilege that the Company give to the public. He had when going on the station at Bank Quay procured a platform ticket, and next day, when he travelled from Cross-lane to Warrington, he gave up the ticket in question and said that he had not come by train. He afterwards admitted having come by train. Defendant, who told the magistrates that he had no , intention to defraud the Company, was fined 20s. and costs. or 14 days' imprisonment.

A VIOLTINT SORT OF A LOYER. John Cullerton, a young man, was before the magis- trates on Monday. on a charge of having been drunk and disorderly in Church-st.,on Saturday night. It was also alleged that he had assaulted three women, whose names were not known. A witness named Fern said that on Saturday night he saw the prisoner with two girls, in Church-st. He seemed to be trying to kiss one of the girls, but, changing his mind, he assaulted thcm. He also assaultei an elderly woman, supposed to be his mother. Another witness said that prisoner was "tick- ling the girls under the chin, and so-forth," but that he afterwards assaulted them. Prisoner called his mother and one of the girls, who denied that he had struck them, but the magistrates considered the case proved, and sent him to prison for six weeks. It was his fifth appearance.

WHAT 16 A LODGIVG HOUSE? On Monday, at the Warrington Police Court, Charles Jackson, 21, Brook-st., was charged with having, on the 20th November, kept lodgers without having his house registered. From evidence given by Inspectors Norman and Church, it appeared that there were nine persons in the house, of whom five were lodgers. The house was

I adapted for eight people..-2.11r.- Norman said the (iTien- dnnt, who refused to have therttquse registered, although he had been frequently asked `;) d o,sh, wed 10)1 ,Naf his visits a number of newspaper cuttings dealing with the question, "What constitutes a lodging-house?" —Defendant said he let the apartments at a rent of half-a-crown a week, and the lodgers providedtheir own furniture.—Mr. Norman : The bye-law says that" person shall let a house, or part of a house, in lodgings." —Defendant: I don'p furnish the rooms. The lodgers bring their own furniture, even their kitchen utensils.— Mr. Norman: The rooms are not separated from each other, and all use the same stairs. No part of the house is closed or barred from the other. The defendant had access all over the house.—Defendant: I should not like to keep a lodging-house.—Alderman Harrison: It is no degradation to do so.—A fine a 10s. and costs was inflicted.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.

MONDAY.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Aldermen Harrison, Davies, and Sutton. --17/nuNitzsNEss.—For this offence the following persons werelklealt with :—James Murphy and Ann Dillon' on Croppers-brow, each fined ss. and costs; Harriet Carter, in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night, dismissed with a caution; John Frain, in Buttermarket-st.' fined ss. and costs; Henry Bithell, in Mersey-et., fined ss. including costs; Joseph Bibby, in Rose and drown-st., on the 27th ult., fined ss. and costs; Elizabeth O'Brien, in Dial-st., dismissed. ,

DISTURBING THE PEACE.—John Burke and Thomas Flannery, for disturbing the peace by fighting in Butter- market-st., on the 25th ult., were bound over to be of good behaviour, and were ordered to pay costs. TUESDAY.—Before Messrs. E. J. Guest and E. M. Crosfield.

• BEGOING.—Peter Godfrey,-ai-arged with begging on the previous night, in Cockhedge-lane, was sent to prison for a week. , SCHOOL CASES.—The following cases were brought under the Elementary Education Act, Mr. George Riley prosecuting on behalf of the School Attendance Com- mittee :—Charles Goulding!, labourer, 01d-rd., fined ss. : Themas Hughes, mechanic, Pierpoint-st., 55.; James Eddie, confectienerrWinwick-rd., Zs. 6d., Thomas Pem- berton, forgeman; Watkin-st, ss. ; William Cowell, forgeman, Warburton-st, ss. ; Thomas Allen, decorator, Crossley-at., 58. ; George Jatindrell, forgeman, Winwick- rd., 2s, WRDNESDAY.—Before Alderman Holmes and Messrs.
John Fairclough, and E. J. Nicholson. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE CASE.—Thomas Amis was fined ss. and costs for neglecting to send his child regularly to school.
Tistrasney.—Before Captain Ridgeway and Mr. W.

Owen. DEUNKENNESS.—WiIIiam Henry Wells was fined 2s. ed., including costs, for this offence, and Henry Baker was fined Ss., including costs. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.—WiIIiam Spafford was brought up on warrant charged with having neglected to send his two children to school. As the defendant's wife has persistently refused to bring the children into Court, and as defendant had not brought them, the magistrates remanded him in custody until they are produced. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison and Dr. Gomall.

- - DRUNKENNESS.—For having been drunk and disorderly in Wilderspool-road. on the evoning previous, a woman named Mary Jane Wolstencroft was sent to prison for a a fortnight. ALLEGED ASSAULTS.—EIIen Malone and Mary Ann Mannion were summoned for having assaulted Bridget Bolton, on Saturday morning. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. The case was dismissed.

WARRLNGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Peter Stubs. ALLEGED THEFT.—Richard Cordon, a blacksmith, from Golborue, was charged with stealing blacksmith's tools, the property of Mr. Samuel Wilkinson. div.head: WIFE MURDER AND SUICIDE.
div.p: WIFE MURDER AND SUICIDE.

A terrible tragedy is reported from Higher 'Huxham, near Exeter. A man, named James Gosling, who is said. to have lived unhappily with his wife for some years quarrelled with her late on Tuesday night, and the dis- pute ended in the woman being murdered, the man after- wards committing suicide.
THE "TIMES " CdTVES IN AND PAYS MR. PARNELL Z 5,000.

The action by Mr. Parnell against the "Times" for the publication of the alleged facsimile letters was settled on Monday morning in the Queen's Bench. Mr. Asquith annotinced that Mr. Parnell had agreed to take a verdict for £5,000 damages. Mr. Murphy, tho leading counsel for the "Times," said his clients assented to this arrangement.,..A. formal verdict was then entered by the jury, and the Lord Chief Jiistibes gave judgment accord- ingly. This unexpected turn of affairs caused great sensation in court, which was crowded. Mr. Parnell was present, looking in better health than he has done for some time past, and all the " Times " coil:lse' was in court. • Mr. Lionel Hart afterwards mentioned the case of Mr. Henry Campbell against the "Times," and asked that therecord might be withdrawn, as the case had been settled; and Mr. Murphy consenting, it was withdrawn. We understand that Mr. Campbell has accepted a few hundred pounds in settlement of the action. THE COSTS OF THE 'COMMISSION. The difficulty as to the expenses of the Parnell Corn- missioa,writes a London correspondent. will probably be settled by a compromise. The Treasury, as in the case ,of all Commissions, pay the strictly official expenses of the. Special Commission. The Treasury will also, it is believed, make good the travelling expenses of witnesses e nbte are paid n not tnl itkheilsy way on both sides, and their hotel expenses in London during the period that they were required for cross-examination : nbeedut bLytonsadyththisatthtehGe mogyuernni s ti mere fraction of the expenses incurred by the "Times."

div.head: MR. BRADLAUGH'S INDIA COUNCIL BILL.
div.p: MR. BRADLAUGH'S INDIA COUNCIL BILL.

Messrs Caine, Justin M'Carthy, and W. S. B. McLaren have consented to back Mr. Bradlaugh's India Councils Amendment Bill. The' measure Practically leaves the Viceroy's Executive Council untouched, but proposes radical changes in the constitution of ,the supreme and provincial leglislatures. The number of the latter is to be increased to six' tkus distributed : tßengal, Bombay, Madras, Punjaub, North-West Provinces, and Central Provinces. Provision is made for the creation of a greater electoral body, four-fifths of the members of which are to be elected by duly qualified voters, and the remain- ing fifth by co-optation, in order to secure the proper representation of minorities. Mr. Bradlaugh has been busy preparing the draft since his return from India, and expects to complete his task in a few days.

div.p: WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT.

THIIRSDAT.—Before his Honor Judge Ffoulkes. THE CADSR List comprised 2 default summonses, /75 original plaints, 3 adjourned plaints, and 52 judgment summonses. A DISCHARGED SERVANT'S CLAM—John Wheeler, a coachman, formerly in the employ of Mr. Edward Greenall, of Grappenhall, but now living at Heath Road, Penketh, claimed from Mr. Edward Greenall the sum or £5 lOs Od, alleged to be due as damages for wrongful dismissal from his situation as coachman. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Swift, barrister, instructed by Messrs B•ickton and Green- all, was for the defence.—Mr. Browne said his client had been in the service of the defendant for thirteen years, first as odd man about the place, and afterwards as coachman. The understanding was that the situation was subject to a months notice, give or Like. About eighteen months ago plaintiff, in order to corroborate that understanding, gave a. month's notice, but remained in the situation on an arrangement being made that he should have an increase of salary. Ou the 9tltt of last December Mr. Greenall called. in the plaintiff' and asked him what about the scandal that was ve..41g7 about. Plaintiff asked him what he meant, but Mr.. Greenall refused to tell him and ordered him out of the. house. A second application for an explanatiork was unsuccessful, and the case was entered in Court. They claimed 225. for She portion of a week during which he workad, and the rest as salary in lieu of notice.— Evidfnee having been given by the plaintiff, Mr. Swift said that while Mr. and Mrs. Greenall were away from home the plaintiff, who had a house of his own, mis• conducted himself in going into the house at times when he should not be there, in eating and drinkirr, in the house, and in sleeping there. It was also alleged', but plaintiff denied it, that he had been under the influence of liquor_ in the house, both in the day-time and in the evening - He should call evidence in support of his contention that the conduct of the plaintiff was such as to give reason- able cause for his dismissal.—The case was not concluded at the rising of the Court.

Why, as Mr. EmmErr asked, cannot "the Party of gentlemen" take their defeat like gentlemen, and" not go whimpering to EUSTON to try to damage a man's character?" The Tories on the Board deny that politics have had anything to do with the advance in the price of gas to the London and North-Western Railway Company; but taking the case on its merits, what justification have they for raising the price to the largest con- sumer when they are lowering it to other large consumers ? They have certainly not made out any case for such an extraordinary proceeding. It does not cover the issue to say that all large con- sumers are now being charged at the same rate; for, if the Railway Company were entitled to a lower rate because of their vast consumption—and that has been admitted—they are still entitled to that consideratiOn. But to put up the price to them, whilst the price to others is actually being brought down, is inexplicable, except upon the assumption that there is something behind the acenes. That something is said to be political Spite ; but if it is not political spite let the Com- missioners speak out and justify their conduct, if they can, in the eyes of the ratepayers and of the

THE annual meetings and confer- Liberalism. Welsh ence of the South Wales Liberal Federation were held at Cardiff, on Tuesday, and it is gratifying to observe how thoroughly earnest and enthusiastic were the dele- gates in giving voice to their demands. Like the Scotch, they are ahead of the people of England in political education. They take to thinking rather than drinking, and they are all the better for it. Welshmen would be ashamed of sending brewers to Parliament whose chief merits are in their ales; and it is about time that 'Englishmen repented in this respect and reformed their ways. The programme which was adopted does not materially differ from that approved by the national Liberal Federation, except that it is more advanced—more Radical—a prelude, so to speak, of the lofty strain which will be frequently heard in " the good time coming." After Home Rule for Ireland, which is accepted as beyond discussion, the disestablishment of the Church of England in Wales is laid down as the first plank on their platform, and there is to be no waiting to see what will be done in the matter in Scotland. Wales has certainly the first Claim; but if two birds can be killed with one stone it will not be for Welshmen to object. There is an emphatic demand for Free Education, and the Pederation further " protests against any measure Which tends to endow denominational institu- tions, or to place public money at the service of bodies not subject to public control by popular representatives. On a resolution being submitted in favour of the principle of "one man one vote," it was strengthened by adding "and every man a rote This means Manhood Suffrage which is the only rational and logical stand point. Tithes it was affirmed should be "devoted to national purposes ;" and with regard to Home Rule for Wales it was "resolved : • . .

" That this Federation declares that the people of Wales should be entrusted with the management of the purely domestic affairs of the Principality, and recognises in the movement to secure self-govern- bent for Wales, which received Mr. Gladstone's support at Manchester, the solution of the grave difficulties under which the Principality suffers by reason of neglect of succeeding Governments to raeet the logislotive requirements of itd people, It further confirms the action of the executive in arranging for a Conference of Scotch and Welsh Rome Rulers, to consider what joint action shall be taken to further the cause of Home for Scotland and Wales.

There is nothing, it will be noticed, said of Home Rule for England; the fact is Englishmen are alto- gether slow in the matter, and there is no Asso- elation for that purpose in this country. It is next to impossible for Home Rule to be granted to Ire- land and to Scotland and Wales without being conceded to England ; but if the boon is wo,rth striving for England should take part in the strife, and not leave it to Welshmen and to Scotchmen to do her work. If, in the other hand, the depar- ture which is being taken is in the wrong direction, it is quite time for the people of this country to express an opinion upon the question. For our Part, we do net see any other solution of the Rome Rule problem. When we have established four subordinate Parliaments, with an Imperial ?ornament for Imperial affairs, we shall have legis - lative machinery which will be equal to the work to be done, anA there will be some hope of lessen- ing the largo pile of arrears.

div.head: "TOUCH AND 00."
div.p: "TOUCH AND 00."

Parliament opens on Tuesday; and, notwith- standing the disquieting rumours that have been current, it is understood that the Prime Minister will be found in his place. It is satisfactory to learn that, although Lord Salisbury suffers from weakness as a sequence of the attack of influenza, there is no reason to fear any further compli- cations

The trial of the Bishop of Lincoln is going to take a deal of time, and cost a deal of money. What a pity it is that he cannot be brought before a couple of Irish " Removables ! " They would soon dispose of him, without fussing about points of law. The points of law could be seen to after he had lain on a plank bed for a month or two; and meantime Mr. Balfour could be singing the praises of his minions.

Candlemas Day was observed, on Sunday, at St. Mary's, Warrington, by the candles being blessed before the high mass in the morning. It is asso- ciated with "The feast of the purification of the Blessed Virgin," and its institution goes as far back as the sixth century. A "Candlemas Crown " was a badge worn at some Scotch grammar schools by the scholar who gave the largest gratuity to the Rector. He was a wide-awake Principal, with both eyes in the main chance, who instituted that "honour."

The engine-winders in the St. Helens district are making a in-ive for a reduction of their work- ing hours • and they ought to be successful, for some of them are called upon to work 84 hours per wenk. They urge that if the hours are not reduced, the wages should be increased; but if they are wise they will take their stand on the main plank of their platform—lessened hours of labour. They will find that increased pay will follow in due course, if the state of trade continues prosper- ous.

The German Emperor has set his heart upon dealing with the labour question, and ameliorat- ing the lot of the workers. He " means business," for he is willing even to take part in a European conference on the subject. The difficulties to be grappled with are enormous; but they will never be overcome if they are not grappled with ; and "monarchs and statesmen " cannot be better employed than in seeking to improve the lot of the lowly. It is a great advance upon taking means to kill them.

The " Standard " frankly remarks that "the rank and 1e of the Conservative and Liberal Unionist parties do not iii all cases work together quite as cordially as could be wished, and that the time seems to be approaching when the expediency of forming them into one homogeneous party, with one name and under one flag, will have to be con- sidered more earnestly than it has yet been." This is hard on the old Tory and the new Conservative. Happily the Liberals are in no such difficulty ; they still faithfully follow the old cause, the old flag, and the old leader.

The Cheshire County Council are going the right way to work in seeking power for the formation of a Joint Committee of all the authorities interested the purification of the Irwell and the Mersey. It is a big job; the labour of Hercules in cleansing the Augean stables is as nothing to it ; but it must be done, or the Ship Canal, which wilt be fed from the Mersey, will become a great nuisance. If the river water could be washed, thirty-pound sal- mon might again take a fancy to it; and—picture it, think of it, rod-and-line man

"Tis strange; 'tis passing strange ! " Twenty ton loads of dead cats have been sold in Liverpool for manure. They have been imported from Egypt, where a cat cemetery has been discovered. Those who are learned in such matters fix the date of the interment at ",000 years before the Christian era." Poor Puss! This is worse than Imperial Omar dead and turned to clay, who stops a hole to keep the wind away. However, we are always learning something; we certainly understand now what is really meant by "Catacombs." Eh, Mr. Dig-at-the-root?

There has been a flagrant case of over-loading at Runcorn; and J. B. Higham, master of the steamer Musgrave, has been fined £lO and costs for the offence. The excuse was that a new engineer had taken in too much coal; and the result was that "it only left a clear 511, inches from the water to the deck." It is courting destruction to over-load in this style ; and the penalty was not at all too heavy, Had it not been for Mr. Plimsoll the over-loading might have gone on, and the Musgrave figured as a lost steamer. People must be saved at times from themselves.

A London correspondent says :—" Mr. H. H. Asquith, M.P., the new Queen's Counsel, is the first old boy of the City of London School who has reached the dignity of silk. He is a north-country- man by descent, and Went from the City School to Oxford as a scholar of Balliol. Mr. Lawson Walton, the other new silk, is the son of an ex- President of the Wesleyan Conference. For some years he was junior for Messrs. Lewis and Lewis." Mr. Asquith is moving up, and those who heard him at Warrington, a few months ago, will agree with us in predicting that he will go yet higher.

" The devil drunkenness" muit have taken possession of the woman who wassent, by the War- rington County magistrates, to gaol for two months, on Wednesday, or she would surely never have allowed her child to sink into the horrible condition in which it was found. Prison life will sober her; and, when sober, it is to be hoped she will realise how near she was of becoming a child murderer. There are other mothers in the town whom drink brutalises—but will they take warn- ing?

P.C. Monaghan was complimented, at the War- rington Police Court, on Monday, upon having in the short space of three-quarters of an hour assisted to lock up three persons who had been guilty of disorderly conduct. This still left some disorderly persons in the street, and there is a reason for their unreasonable behaviour. How if P.C. Monaghan was permitted to lock-up (say as "first- class" prisoners) Sir Gilbert Greenall and Sir A. B. Walker, each gentleman having the key of a locked brewery in his pocket? Would it make any difference to the streets, does anybody think?

Poor old bamboozled ".Times!" Its cup of misery is full; it has not only had to apologise to Mr. Parnell, but to pay £5,000, and all costs; and there is no one—not even a Tory or a Liberal Unionist— to shed a tear, or do it reverence. Indeed, Unionists of all sorts are the loudest in denouncing it for the injury it has done to " the cause." They forget that, in taking the forger to its bosom, it was doing its muddle-headed best to accomplish what they all aimed at—the politi- cal ruin of the Irish leader. The " Times " has 'fallen because it most perfectly embodied the stupidity of the Tory party, for not even the gods can save from stupidity.

Alderman Crosfield referred, at the Warrington Town Council meeting, on Tuesday, to the need there was of warming the mortuary chapels at the Cemetery; and it is promised that, at whatever cost, this shall be done. Mourners, depressed alike in mind and body, are especially susceptible to chills. People worn with watching and with grief should certainly have a well-aired chapel to enter when the last sad offices for the dead are being performed.

It is singular, but so, that the minutes referring to the resignation of Mr. W. H. Brook as Town Clerk, and the appointment of Mr. J. Lyon Whittle as his successor, were adopted without comment. It is true that the members of the Council had been furnished with the report of the sub-com- mittee, and the recommendation of the General Purposes Committee; but it is not every member of the Council who is on the General Purposes I Committee: and, besides, there are, after all, such people as ratepayers, who are entitled to know something of the reason or reasons for which any- thing is done. It is not creditable to the Town Council that a most important piece of business was treated, as "Mr. Toots" would say, as smatter of" no consequence."

THE EXAMINER.,6O4ITRDAY, FEBRUARY 8 1890 THE-PROPOSED GLAZIMILOOK.Ra.NaIt....- • After receiving; the rumoured decision of .the Government to withhold 0.4 grant of .£12,000 required for the Gbizebrook rifle range, the Mmt. chester Brigade Range Committee, which consists of Officers attached to the various diBtriCt corps, held a meeting at the rooms of the Volunteer Officers' Association in Market-st., Manchester. A letter was read in which Brigadier-General Blundell advo- cated the formation of a company to carry out. the proposed Works at Glazebrook, and it was stated that he would be Prepared to take shares. Such a scheme, was, however. thought scarcely feasible, as the land would only be held on lease, and it would be impossible for Lord ‘Vininarleigh to sell even if so disposed. With the stipreme impdrt mice of the range to Manchester volunteers in view, it was thought that those members of Parliament inter- ested in the mrivement might put pressure on :he Government in order to obtain so trifling a loan, and the meetittg was then adjourned until later in the month, whim General Blundell will be requested to attend. W1D1413.9 C.E.T.S. ' Under the auspices of this bociety Dr. McLennan, on Thursday evening, delivered a lecture bearing on the temperance movement, in the National Schools. There was a large audience and the Vicar presided.

BETHESDA BAND OP HOPE, RUNCORN. The members of this Band of Hope gave an entertain- ment, on Wednesday evening, to a large audience. A lengthy programme of songs, recitations, Sm., was gope through in capital style, and a pleasant evening was spent. Mr. T. Riley presided.

SUCCESSFUL RUNCORN MUSICAL S TIIDENT. At the recent local examinations (Liverpool centre) in instrumental and Vocal music, in connection with frinity College, London,Miss Augusta H. Jones, (Miss Isherwood, Runcorn) passed in the senior division with 79 marks. RUNCORN GOSPEL MISSION HALL. The members of the Band of Hope in connection with this mission, gave an entertainment on Monday evening last. The Rev G. Thompson presided, and delivered an address on the temperance movement. Songs, glees, recitations and dialogues were rendered by the children in an enjoyable manner. There was a • good attendance.

WIDNES IRISH NATIONAL LEAGUE. In connection with this league, a concert was given in the Drill Hall, on Monday evening, when a large audience assembled. The vocalists were Madame Mullen (soprano), Miss Layton (contralto), Mr. Beaumont (teßor), and Mr. Ludwig (baritone), and an admirable prbgramme of a miscellaneous character was presented. The audience was most appreciative. UNIVERSITY EXTENSION LECTURES AT RUNCORN. The third lecture of the pries on physiography will be held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Tuesday evening next, when Mr. Mac Kinder, will deal with the subject of " Rain." At the end of the lecture Mr. Mac Kinder will, on behalf of the University Delegates, present the certificates to the successful candidates in the recent examination on "English Social Reformers."

RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. The first rueeting of the new BoArd was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening. Presont the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, Rev. Ur. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. Taylor, J. J. Howitt, A. Salkeld, and G. Moss (clerk). The first business was _ _

THE ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN. The Rev. A. M. Wood proposed that Dr. McDougall be elected Chairman of the Ward for the ensuing year. —Mr. Salkeld seconded, and Mr. Pritbard support ,c 1 the proposition.—Dr. McDougall said he was most anxious that Mr. Pritchard should be chairman, and having personally no wish for the office, he desired his name to be withdrawn.--Mr. Taylor proposed that Mr: Pritchard be chairman for the ensuing three years, and Mr. Howitt seconded the proposition.—Dr. Ga.staldi supported the amendment. For the amendment there voted Dr. Gastaldi, Dr. McDougall, Messrs. Taylor and Howitt. For the original ;notion the Rev. A. M. Wood, Mr. Pritchard, and Mr. Salkeld voted. The amendment was declared carried.—Mr. Pritchard upon taking the chair, thanked the members for the confidence reposed in him, but personally he should have been glad if Dr. McDougall had been eleced to the position.

MYSTERIOUS ROBBERY AT RUNCORN. On Wednesday night a mysterious robbery took place at the Egerton-st. shop of Mr. Walter Collier of Church- St. After business the shop was properly secured and the keys deposited with Mr. Collin. Next morning the doors and windows were found to be fastened as usual, but the till had been completely cleared of its contents. Fortunately only a few shillings had been left there for change. There is no clue he the robber.

ROBBERIES AT RIINCORN. , At Runcorn Police Court on Wednesdiy before Mr. •James Handley and Dr. Steele two navvies named Henry Jackson and Henry Woodfield werecharged on remand with Stealing a bottle of whiskey the property of Mr. J. W. Lightburn from the Devonshire Hotel : a coat the property of Arnold Unsworth, High-st.' and a coat the property of Craddock and Son Church-St. Woodfield, was sent•nced to 7 days hard labour, and Jackson to 21 days' hard labour. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at an hours' notise.-7. & W. Dutton, Sankey-street. RREAXING A POLICEMAN'S FINGER AT WIDNES. , At Widnes Police Court on Monday, John Higgins, of Dock-st., was brought up on remand charged with hay- ing been drunk and disorderly, and assaulting P.C. Simpson. About midnight on the 27th inst. the prisoner was drunk and causing a great disturbance near St. Ambrose Church, Halton View, and the constable asked for his name and addresi. The prisoner told him to "find it out," and the constable thereupon took him into custody, but the prisoner resisted him and in the struggle which ensued both fell to the ground. Seizing hold of the constable's third finger on the right hand, and twisted it back until the bone snapped. The constable still held his man and with great difficulty got him to the police station. Dr. MacLennan, who had set the finger, great strength nifist have been used to break bthe bone. The constable would be unable to go on duty for a month.—Superintendent Johnstone said the charge had been reduced from committinclegrievous bodily harm to one of common assault in order to save the expense of sending the prisoner to the Quarter Sessions.—Inspector Keighley said the prisoner had been seven times before the Court and twice fined for assaulting the police.—The Bench sentenced the prisoner to three months hard labour.

WAYLAYING WO:N.11/N AT DITTO. At Widnes Police C,Ourt, on Monday, Walter Clarke, of 11, Walmsley-st., Widnes, was charged with criminally assaulting MargaretWright,a young woman, 21 years of age, who resides with her parents at Pit Ville House, Dit- ton. About half-past eight on Saturday night the prose- cutrix was walking along Cow-lane towards her home when she met prisoner who without the slightest notice Of his intention seizA her by the throat and threw her to the ground. She screamed " Murder " several times, and the prisoner threatened to choke her if she did not "atop it." After struggling, on the ground for sonic time, she got upon her feet, but he again threw her down and this occurred repeatedly At length Ebo'r Taylor, and Mark Longton, farmers,rame to the woman's assist- ance and captured the prisoner, who pleaded to be set at liberty because he. was drunk, and did not know what be was doing, and stated that he had a wife and three 'children. His captors, however, took him to the police station and gave him into the custody of P.S. Ross. In reply to the charge he replied "Yes, FIE not refuse it"— He was committed to the Assizes for trial.—On Tuesday the prisoner was brought up on a similarcharge in repra to Hannah Markley, a widow reeiding at Marsh End I Farm, Ditton. The prisoner committed this offence near Ditton Hall College at 20 past seven. The woman was struggling with her assailant for nearly ten minutes and was badly bruised about various parts of the body. The I prisoner hearing some person approaching decamped. When arrested on the previous charge Mrs. Medley recognised • him as the man who had assaulted her.— The prisoner was committed for trial on this charge also.

RUNCORN TONIC SOL-FA CHOIR CONCERT. The members of the Runcorn Tonic Sol-fa choir gave their second concert of the season on Monday evening last in the Public Hall, and it is to be regretted that the attendance of the townspeople was not commensurate with the musical fare provided. In the past the choir has done much good work, and it is to be hoped that a useful existence will not be terminated for the want of a little public encouragement. The choir, which numbered about 40 voices, was assisted by the following principals —Miss Heaton, soprano ; Mr. A.S. Kinnell. bass ; Miss Nunn. L.R.A.M., solo pianoforte; Miss Gordon Nunn, solo violin. The programme consisted of miscellaneous item., and was of a highly enjoyable character. The work of the choir was marked by the usual time preci- sion and tunefulness, and the audience did not fail to show their appreciation. The madrigal "Down in a flowery vale," was a charming piece of vocalisation, and was loudly encored. Miss Heaton possesses a sweet and expressive voice, wanting pprhaps, a little in power, and the various items set dewn to her name were ad- mirably rendered. Mr. Kinnell, who has a voice of capital range, made a highly successful first appearance in Runcorn, and sang with niuch harmony and power of expression. Miss Nunn performed two solos on the piano, and on each occasion the brilliancy of her execu- tion gained her an an enthusiastic recall. Miss Gordon Nunn was equally successful with her contributions on the violin. As a violinist she is a star of the first magni- tude, and the audience were quite carried away by the concord of sweet Sounds she drew from her instrument. Mr. Ilolford, the conductor, wielded the baton in his ' usual effective style, and Miss W. B. Kay was an efficient accompanist. COLLIERY ENGINEMEN AND THEIR WORKING Hams. A fully representative meeting of the colliery engine-winders of the St. Helens district, was held at the George Hotel. George-st., on Saturday night. The meeting was called for the purpose of consider- ing a proposal to agitate for a reduction of work- ing hours. In the course of the proceedings it was stated that some of the engine-winders had to work 84 hours per week and it was contended that they ought to be relieved from working on Saturday afternoons and on the Sunday, or in lieu of this that their wages be correspondingly increased. It was ultimately decided to send deputations to the employers and to again consider the subject at a future meeting. UMBRF.LLLS RE.COVERSD at an hours' notice.--J. & W. Dutton, Sankey-street.

MILTON CONGIIEUATIONAL CHAPEL WIDNES. In this chapel on Sunday the Rev. R. G. Hughes de- livered special sermons to good congregations. The sub- ject in the morning was " Robert Annan, or the Lion who became a Lamb ;4 and in the evening "Model Mothers."

MISSIONAgY MHETING AT WIDN'ES. The annual services in aid of the Wesleyan Homo Missionary Society were held in Victoria-road Chapel, on Sunday, when the 11,.v. T. Waugh, evangelist, preached both morning and evening. There was a good congre- gation at each service. On Monday evening the annual public meeting was held under the presidency of Mr. W. Clarke, of Hough Green. Addresses were delivered by the Hove. T. Waugh, T. Law and G. S. Meek. The collection realised a satisfactory sum.
