NORTHWICIi DIVISION LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. The annual meeting of the meinb.,lrs of the Runcorn district of this association, has been held under the pre- sidency of Mr. B. Kniveton. The customary business of organisation was carried out. The numper of vice- presidents allowed by the rules were elected, and the chairman of the different districts into which the town is mapped out were appointed. Members of the " 300 " and of the Exocutive Committee were also elected, seve- ral necessary changesbeing made. Mr. W. Handley, the secretary, was present. Fivraas.—J. S. Garland, ironmonger, Bridge-street. War- ringtott.—_4det. TRADESMEN'S BALL AT RUNCORN._

- The annual tradesmen's ball was held in Runcorn Public Hall, on Tuesday night. The hall had been taste- fully decorated for the occasion by Mr. Richard Morris, who had also supplied the stretcher which covered the floor. About 25 couples were present, but tickets for considerably more than that number has been disposed of, and there was a good number of spectators present. Signor Massa's band played the dance music. The duties of M.C. were ably fulalled by Mr. P. Smith, and Mr. J. Much performed the secretarial duties with every satis- faction.—Refreshments were provided by Mr. Cooper of Wilsons Hotel who also provided a recherche supper.

THE SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN YOUNG MAN. At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, Wm. Fredk. Hancock, a plumber, and well-known footballer, was brought up on remand, charged with criminally assault- ing Maria Barker, 19 years of age, daughter of the keeper of the Ferry Inn, Church-st., on the 29th January.--Superintendent Large said the girl was still unable to appear, and he asked for a further remand for a week. By that time the doctor thought she would be lit to appear.—Mr. A. Linaker, who appeared for the prisoner, did not object to this course, but applied far bail. After consideration, the magistrates decided to liberate the prisoner on bail, himself in £lOO, and two sureties of £75 each. The sureties were Mr. A. Riley and Mr. W. H. Rogerson.
RuNCORN PARISH Cau uca.

We gather from the Parish iia.-4-a-z-i-ne of this month hat the stipends of the assistant clergy for the present year are estimated at £520, and towards that sum it is estimated that the following amounts may be received : —from the additional Curates Aid Society, £BO ; Parish Church Offertory, £l3O us. Bd. ; St. Michaels, £37 Os. 2d.; Weston, £3 lle. Bd. ; Subscription list, (includ- log Christ Church Oxford, and Major Owed', £llO 16s. 4d. ; total, £361 193. Bd., leaving a deficiency of £l5B Os. 4d. The income of the living cannot be esti- mated at more than .£444. The deficiency upon the work of the Church Army for the past year lißtd been about £35. The Vicar appeals to the parishioners for liberal contributions, through the offertories to keep up the clerical staff. UMBRELLAS lIR-COVERED at an hours' notice.--J. X W. Dutton, Sankey-street. OLD MEN'S TREAT AT HALTON.

The Old Men's Annual Dinner was held at the Norton Arms Hotel, on Tuesdar. About forty sat down to an excellent spread provided by the host Edward Hadley. After the removal of the cloth the chair was taken by the vicar, the Rev. George P. Wray, M.A., who in a very neat speech expressed his pleasure at meeting. the old men belonging to his parish. The usual loyal and patriotic toasts were duly honoured and speeches followed by Mr. Thomas Wright, Mr. Joseph Stokes, Mr. Hugh Rowe, senior, Mr. John W. Haddock. During the even- in. songs were given by Messrs. Jones, Haddock, and Walton. A vote of thanks was given to Mr. Thomas Wright, as chief organiser of the "Old Men's Dinner fund," also to the host for the capital catering. The singing of the National Anthem terminated the pro- ceedings. PETROLEUM OIL.—J. S. Garland. 51, Bridge-street, War- , rington.—Adet.
WIDNES LIBERAL CLUB.

Under the auspices of this Club a concert was given in the Baths Assembly Room, on Monday evening in aid of the funds of that political institution. The special object of the concert was to wipe off the balance of a debt incurred in furnishing the Club. Mr. E. K. Muspratt, J.P., presided and delivered a brief address, speaking upon the position and prospects.of the Liberal party in the town in an encouraging strain. An admirable pro- gramme was presented, and was well sustained by the following vocalists :—Miss C. J. Wright, Miss Pierpoint, Miss Leatherbarrow, and Miss M. Dwyer ; Messrs. F. Wareing, F. Heyes, Caldwell, G. Kiddie, and Wilson Blackledge. The numerous audience who had assembled expressed their appreciation by frequent encores. Miss Muspratt recited " The Inch Cape Rock" in dramatic style and was enthusiastically applauded. CRITCHLET, Practical Tailor. Warrington.—Advt.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

A special meeting of the members of this Board was held on Tuesday morning, for the purpose of filling the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. J. B. Unison. Mr. T. S. Timmins presided, and the were also present Rev. J. Clark, Dr. McDonnell, Messrs. B. H. Davis, S. Quinn, and G. H. Hanby (clerk).—The chairman said it had always been the custom of the Board that the privi- lege of nominating a member should belong to the party with which the deceased or resigned member was con- nected, and he believed it to be a salutary rule. Under that rule it fell to the Church to nominate who should fill the vacancy caused by the death of Mr. Imison, and he had much pleasure in moving the ejection of Mr. C. E. Barlow,who was well knowri to them all as a former mem- ber of the Board, and of the important School Manage- ment Committee. As he came back with a knowledge of the work, his services would be doubly valuable to the Board. Mr. Barlow was also a prominent citizen and a leading manufacturer who had shown himself to be a very competent man of business, and he (the chairman) ventured to think that his name would be received with unanimity,—Father Clark seconded the motion, remark- ing that Mr. Barlow was a gentleman of great experience, and he wished him many years of successful work on the Board.—The motion was carried unanimously.

VIOLENT ATTACK ON POLICEMEN AT WIDENS. 'Ttichard Rollinson, of Victoria-st.. was brought before Mr. Pilkington and Mr. Timmis, at Widnes Police Court, on Monday, to answer a charge of having been drunk and disorderly and with resisting P.C. Hudson in the execution of his duty. The prisoner was further charged with unlawfully and maliciously wounding P.C. Holbrook and with damaging that constable's helmet to the extent of ss. From the statement of Inspector Keighley it appearcd that about half-past eight, on Saturday night, the prisoner and his brother, who were both drunk, were causinz a disturbance in the butcher's shop of a man named Travis, in Ann-st. As they refused to go the constable took the men into custody, but P.C. Holbrook who had charge of the prisoner allowed him to go because he knew his nail's and address. He thee assisted P.C. Hudson with the brother. After walking a short distance towards the Police Station, the prisoner came up and threw a couple of stones, one of which penetrated through Holbrook's helmet and caused a lacerated wound on the scalp.—Dr. McLennan, who had dressed the Wound, said the constable was not in a fit condition to attend court. The stone must have been thrown with great force to have gone through the helmet and had it not been for the helmet, the constable's skull would have been broken. The prisoner was remanded for a week. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED at an hour? notice.-3. W. Dutton, Sankey-street.

div.head: MINERS' WAGES.
div.p: MINERS' WAGES.

In accordance With the decision of the recent National Conference of the Miners' Delegates, at Birmingham, applications have been sent in to the colliery proprietors of the country asking for another advance of ten per cent in wages. In the St. Helens district the notices were forwarded last Friday and intimated that a deputation from the colliers would wait upon the employers on the following Friday in order to receive their answer. If the answer was unfavourable, the notices con- tinued that a 14 days' notice demanding the advance would be served. • If the applications are not complied with, it is anticipated there will be a general strike of colliers throughout the district. AN BAST WAY TO HELP THE PoOL—For erery half-pound of Collier's 2e. Tea purchased by persons whl attend St. Michael's or Old Parish Church. Walter Collier will give one ounce of this splendid Tea (neatly wrapped) to the District Nurse for distribution among her patients. Directions: The ,tinfoil wrappers to be sent to 6. Church-st.. with name and address of sender written oa the inside.— A drt. LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL.

The Lancashire County Council met on Thursday, at Preston. There was a large attendance. The various committees presented their reports for con- firmation. The agenda of business was a very formidable one, and occupied all the afternoon. Grants of £5OO in each case were asked for oppos- ing the Liverpool Corporation and Oldh am Extension and smaller sums for opposing other Bills, in- chiding the Manchester Ship Canal, the opposition to the group, including the latter Bill, being formal. A grant of £1,400 was asked for the purchase of land for the Prestwich Asylum. The Public Health Committee again urged the appointment of a medi- col officer for Lancashire, at a salary of £BOO per annum. The revised budget was presented along with the report of the Finance Committee, the , Chairman of which is Alderman Guthrie, of Man- chester.

„. Cometu.souY EntrcATioN.—A number of parents W.,ro fined ss. including costs for failing to comply with the Education Act, by not sending (heir children to school regularly. DRUNKENNESS.— Henry Carter, Tarbuck, W alter Harttes, 92, Kent-st.. Edward Matthews, Wareing-st., Margaret Redmond, Walmsley-st., William Wallace, Windermere-lane, were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly.—John Devereux of MOSS Rank, for a similar offence was fined 7s. 6d. and costs.—George Johnson, carter, of Cuerdley, pleaded guilty to being drunk whilst in charge of a horse and ca it in Lugsdale- road, on the 23rd ult. and a fine of 10s. and costs was imposed. BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Reuben Hewitt, Travis-st., was summoned for causing a breach of the peace at Widnes, on the 25th ult. The case was dismissed.— Mary Woods, of Walmsley-st., was also summoned for causing a breach of the peace at Widnes, on the 24th tilt. The defendant was bound over to be of good behaviour fora period of three months. BREACHES OF THE MUZZLING ORDER—George Richards, Mersey-road, and John Lyons, of Hough Green, were each summoned for a breach of the muzzling order. by . allowing their dogs to he at large unmuzzled on the nth ult. A fine of is. and costs was imptised in each case. PITCH AND TOSS.—CharieS Garghan, of 18, George-at., was summoned for playing pitch and toss at Widnes, on the 26th ult.—The defendant, who pleaded guilty, was ordered to pay a fine of 6d. and costs. ASSAULT ON THE RlVER—William Wilittalt,T, of 47, John-at., fiatman. was summoned for assaulting William Atherton on the 29th ult. Mr. Knowles, who appeared forthe complainant, said his client (Atherton) was cap- tain of the fiat Clement, and on the day in question he was going out of the West Bank Dock. The defendant, who was also a captain, was in charge of another flat, and Atherton requested him to get out of the way. The defendant, after making use of some words, croAsed another fiat and came on the one in charge of Atherton, ! and assaulted him, and had not someone come to his assistance the consequence wwild have been more seri- ous for had anything happened to Atherton his flat would have been washed against Runcorn Bridge and I been wree'ked.—The defendant was ordered to pay a fine ! of 10s. and costs, in all El 3s. 6d., or go to gaol for 14 days. CRUELTY TO A HORSE AT WlDNES.—Thornas Martindale, of Moorside, Widnes, was summoned by Inspector Wilson, ! of the Royal Society for ;he Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, for working his horse whilst in an unfit state at Widnes on the 23rd ult. Mr. Knowles defended, and pleaded not guilty.—lnspector Wilson stated that at 10.45 on the day in question he was walking along Victoria-road. Widnes, when he saw the defendant in charge of a bay mare which was attached to a cart. The mare was very lame on the fore leg and near the hind leg. There was a spaNiin on the near hind leg, and the tendons were swollen and inflamed. The animal kept lifting its leg up when standing, and appeared to be in pain. It was totally unfit for work.--Sergeant Strick- land, John Shaw Menzies, veterinary surgeon, of St. Helens, and John Yates, of Farnworth, gave evidence to this effect.—The Chairman said they were of opinion that the horse was worked in an unfit state, and the defend- ant would be fined ss. and costs, in all El. div.head: SC ENE.
div.p: SC ENE.

A special meeting of the members of Widnes I Local Board was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday morning for the purpose of considering certain Bills now pending in Parliament, and intituled "A bill to alter certain works authorised by the Manchester Ship Canal Act. 1885 and for other purposes ;" also " a Bill for incorporating and conferring powers upon the Widnes Brine Supply Company, and for other purposes." &lad if considered expedient of passing reso- lutions to oppose the said Bills. Mr. Gossage presided and there were present, Messrs. Carey Handley, Colk, 11. Tiinmis, Sadler, Houghton, Tavhir, Liddell, Hayle (deputy clerk) and Oppenheim (solicitor.) Mr. Carey as Chairman of the General Purposes Committee, which had had the matter in hand, explained ,hat the object of this proposed opposition was to place the Board in such a position that they could preserve the interest of the rate- payers of Widnes. The Ship Canal Company proposed to make certain alterations in the overflow slu ces which the Committee thought would be prejudicial to the interests of the town, and to the navigation of the river ; especially would they be prejudicial to the inter-

eats of Widnes And West Bank Docks. In all propability , they would not put the ratepayers to any expense in the matter, because they had good reason to think that before the Bill came on they would be able to make satis- factory arrangements with the Ship Carl Company.— The Chairman proposed that the Board oppose the Man- • chester Ship Canal Bill, in Parliament, and take all nee- cessary steps for the ~uti protection of the rights and interests of the district of %Widnes.—Mr. Carey seconded the motion which was carried unanimously. • The Chairman then moved a resolution, drawn up in similar terin4 in regard to the Widnes Brine Supply Company's Bill.—Mr. Carey seconded the motion, and explained that the Board had not the slightest desire to throw any impediunint in the way of bringing brine to Widnes. If brine were brought to Widnes in large quantities, it (night be a very important and useful thing for the town, and the opposition of the Board would be of the most friendly character, but it was necessary to , take these steps to secure the rights of the ratepayers. ' The opposition was mainly directed against the route it was proposed to take the pipes. The company intended to brim he pipes along the main roads, and thus inter- fere s% ith the gas and water mains, and the sewers, and the Committee considered that the pipes should be britight along the back streets.—Tlie resolution was car- ried unanimously. Subsequently a meeting of owners and occupiers was held with a view to obtaining their consent to the oppos- ition, of the Bills, and the application of the public funds for the purpose. The ratepayers present in addition to the members were Messrs. S. H. Muspratt, W. J. Har- greaves, S. Patin, and J. C. Routtedge. Mr. Gossage presided. Resolutions consenting to the opposition of the Bill by the Board were proposed by the Chairman Seconded by Mr. Muspratt and carried without dissent. —Mr. Patin said he had an intimate acquaintance with the tides awl current of the Mersey and he was of opin- ion that the overflow water of the sluices would not scour the river at all. and that the sluices would be more an encumbrance, than a benefit to the river. It would be a n d thing if the Board could compel the Company to remove the rock at the ferry slip better than they had do/le.—The Chairman said the committee had this matter tinder consideration with a view to getting the rock removed in a better fashion. Arrangements had been made for making the ferry in a manner which %you'd be a great improvement en the present system. The merting then concluded,

RUNCORN GAS COMPANY. The annual meeting of the shareholders of this Company was held at the Gas Works yesterday. Mr. F. chairman of the directors, pre- sioed, and proposed the adoption of the report and statement of accounts, and that a dividend of 10 per cent be declared. He said that owing to the rise in the price of coal, and because they had had to call up their additional capital in accordance with statute, he was afraid they would not be able to continua' to pay that amount of dividend; but the increased consumption of as was most satisfac- tory and he thought the shareholders might look forward in future to the continuerV prosperity of the Company.—The report was adopted.—The auditors (Slear.,. James Pritchard and W. Handley) stated that. their examination of the books proved how, well the financial affairs of the Company, were conducted.—The Chairman proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Frith for the care he always exer- cised over the interests of both the Company and of the public in the matter of gas lighting.—This resolution was unanimously agreed to and entered on the minutes.

BTT,T.IATIDA AT Tint CONS/CRVATIVR CLUE. n'l Saturday af7-ernoon a billiard handicap WM played off in the ConQervative Club, Penketh, between the respective teams of the Penketh and Rainhill Conservative Clubs. The visitors won by 85, after an interesting and exciting game. LF.CTURE ON "THE BLOOD." On Wednesday evening a lecture was delivered in the Elementary Day Schools, Penketh, by Dr. Murry on "The Blood." The occasion was the weekly meeting of the Penketh Mutual Improve- ment Association. Afterwards Mr. Gumersall (chair- man) thanked Dr. Murry on behalf of the associa- tion. 'Mr. D. Garnett and Mr. C. E. Parker also ex- pressed their thanks to Dr. Murry for his interest- ing lecture. LECTI7RE ST GREAT SANKEY. On Thursday evening the Rev. E. S. Jackson, vicar of Great Sankey, delivered a lecture in the Sunday Schools. Great Sankey, entitled "Some reminiscences of a trip to New Zealand." The lecture was interspersed with amusing anecdotes which cau.ed very much fun. There was an inter- val during which Mr. Winder sang "Botany Bay," Mr. Willie Jeans gave a banjo solo, and Miss Jeans sang. The lecture was given in aid of the Penketh mission, and was much appreciated. Captain Ridgway occupied the chair, and Mr. Jackson was ably assisted by Mr. Crosby, who manipulated the slides which, illustrated the lecture. Hearty thanks to th 3 Lecturer brought an interesting evening to a close.

div.head: BOY SHOT DEAD.
div.p: A BOY SHOT DEAD.

A terrible affair happened at Brighton, near Sheffield, on Thursday morning. Walter Dawson, aged 16, went to Mr. Dickenson's farm for some straw. Reginald Dickenson. a boy, went with him to the barn, and they commenced •• skylarking." Suddenly Dickenson picked up a gun, saying "I'll shoot you." He pulled the tr , and Dawson fell dead. It is supposed that Dickenson did not know the gun was loaded.
igger

THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY AN -OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT. A glance at the Police records of Widnes for the past few weeks would appear to show that the chemical metropolis is lapsing into that condition of savagery and brutality, which gained it such unenviable notoriety a few years ago. Violent assaults on constables, attacks upon women with criminal design, the half murdering of wives, un- lawful wounding of comrades—this is the weekly programme of the Court; and the business of Quarter Sessions is always largely augmented by committals from Widnes. In nearly every instance, the offences are committed in fits of drunken pas- sion and the local temperance organisations have much scope in their missionary work of teaching men, and women too, to curb their carnal appetites, but they do not touch more than the fringe of the great evil. A few Sundays ago temperance sernions were delivered from toe pulpits of nearly the whole of the churches of the diocese of Liverpool, but these appeals would not reach the people most ia want of conversion. If they wish todo the work thoroughly the clergy must carry their mission into the streets and alleys of the towns. As there is no highway connecting Runcorn and Widnes, the maintenance of the ferry across the Mersey is of the utmost importance to the inhabi- tants of those towns, and it is gratifying to learn that Widnes Local Board have made satisfactory arrangements for the ferry traffic to be carried on when the Ship Canal is completed. While the Widnes Authority has been upholding the rights of the ratepayers, Runcorn Board of Commissioners have stood idly looking on and the reason why, they do not deign to tell, but their attitude of passive non-interference has not been creditable. From the vigorous manner in which Mr. Howitt conducted his election campaign for a seat on Run- corn School Board, it was expected that he would not be a silent member, and at the first meeting of the Board on Tuesday he set the ball rolling by giving notice of his intention to move a resolution in favour of Free Education, somewhat in the terms of that passed by the London School Board. He also gave notice of several questions he required answer- ing effecting the welfare of the Board Schools, and a lively and interesting discussion will no doubt be the result at the next meeting. At the meeting referred to the Clerk presented an interesting report on the Technical Education Act, passed last year, and although speaking in favour of the principle of that Act, Mr. Moss ad- vised the Board not to adopt it, on the ground that the work was outside their statutory duties, and , that a committee of five gentlemen, organised to carry on science and art classes could adopt the Act and call upon the Commissioners to give aid from the rates. It may be doubted whether the Act bears out the conclusions drawn by Mr. Moss, but even if it does, it may be pointed out that there is no science and art class in the town, and that there is no institution set apart for such a purpose. On the other hand the Board have well appointed schools, and a staff of teachers at their command, and are altogether in a favourable position for adopting and carrying out the Act. The existence of Runcorn depends to a great extent upon scientific industries, which the Act was meant to improve by giving better instruction to the youths of our towns in subjects relating to such industries and it is to be hoped that the Committee, who have the matter in hand, will recommend the Board to immediately take advantage of the opportunity afforded by the Act of improving the educational status of the town. .

That the secretary's report was fiat stale and unprofitable, but the fact that h 3 had to deal with a balance of about £l5O on the wrong side was not calculated to make him cheerful. div.head: FATALITY AT A WIDNES WORKS.
div.p: FATALITY AT A WIDNES WORKS.

John Conroy, chemical labourer, 63 years of age, whose home was at Eleanor-st., died at Widnes Accident Hospital on Thursday from injuries received on the previous day. Conroy was wheeling a waggon to the hoist, and did not notice that the hoist had decended. The waggon fell upon the cage below, and the deceased followed, fracturing his skull, and putting his shoulder out of joint, and breaking a rib, the broken bone penetrating one of his lungs.—lle was conveyed to the Hospital ad attended by Dr. MacLennan but he died as stated.

div.head: OVER-LOADING A STEAMSHIP AT RUNCORN.
div.p: OVER-LOADING A STEAMSHIP AT RUNCORN.

At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. G. L. Davies. a sum- mons was heard against John Braithwargn Iligham, who was charged with having, at Runcorn, on the 9th Dec., while master of the British steamship Musgrave. unlawfully allowed the said vessel to be so loaded as to submerge in salt water the centre of disc contrary to section '2B of the Merchant Shipping Act, 1876.—Mr. Paxton, who prosecuted, said the action was taken under the Merchant Shipping Act, 1876, and the defendant was liable to a penalty not exceeding , £lOO. By a section of that Act it was provided that the master of a British ship must have a mark on the side of his vessel,a disc, through thich a line was drawn and it was ordered that the vessel should not be loaded to such an extent as to cause that mark to be under water, ' Under the present state of the law the owner of a vessel could place the mark on the vessel where he chose. On the 9th Dec. last year, the Board of Trade Surveyor visited the port of Runcorn, and saw the Musgrave, of which the defendant was master, in the dock and noticed that no part of the disc was visible. In consequence of the disc being so much below .water, it only left a clear 5-1 inches from the water to the deck, whereas there ought to have been a clear 11 inches. The Act referred to submerging in salt water, but in order that there might he no doubt in the matter the Surveyor took a sample of the dock water, and ascertained the density of it, and found the difference between that and salt water was 2.1. Allowing for this, the disc would be submerged 4 inches below the requirements of the Act.—Mr. English, who appeared for the defendant, who pleaded guilty, said it was purely a case of accident. The offence had been committed owing to the chief engineer, who had only been appointed to the vessel on that voyage, taking in an extra quantity of coal at Dartmouth without con- sulting the defendant.—Mr. Brundrit said this was a serious offence, and he did not see the slightest excuse, as the defendant must have known what the vessel would carry, and how much the mark ought to have been sub- merged. The defendant was fined £lO and costs.

div.head: CHEMICAL LABOURERS' UNION.
div.p: THE CHEMICAL LABOURERS' UNION.

A meeting of the Chemical Works' labourers con- nected with the Chemical Labourers' Union was held in the Public Hall, Hardshaw-st., on Sunday afternoon, for the purpose of selecting yard com- mittees. Mr. P. J. King, the organiser, said it was becoming 9. habit of several individuals to criticise him very severely, and, of course, adversely, because they were opposed to the interests of the men, not that they were large employers of labour themselves, but that they thought it fashion- able to denounce a man like him for haying pursued the course he had pursued. He urged the workingmen of St. Helens to get their names and addresses, and if they refused to give the desired information, well then they might apply their boot to that portion of the anatomy generally referred to when threatening to chas- tise cowardly, ruffianly, despicable individuals. (Laughter.) Humble as he was, he was determined to defend himself, and that no one should assail him with impunity. (Hear, hear.) He warned the men against internal treason and laid that as they were now 1,400 men strong, he wanted them to be aware of cranks and soreheads. (Laughter.) Those were the men who were continually going round finding fault with everything that was being done, lb they themselves were con,picunuA for the lack of constructive abilities. Ii conclusion he asked them to he firmly resolved that every man in connection with chemical and copper works, should become members of the union, and never cease pro- pagating the faith that was within them, and their faith in the justice of the claims of their fellow men, until they had made the union a greater and grander success than it was at the present moment. (Applause.) The yard committees, consisting of eight men in .each yard, were then elected and the • meeting terminated.

div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN
COUNCIL.

A monthly meeting of this Council was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday evening, The Mayor presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Davies, Harrison, Sutton, Wright, Crosfield ; Councillors Monks, Platt, W. Pierpoint, J. Shaw Green, Muir, Flood, Marsh, Ashton, Flem- ing, Perci v al, Blackhurst, Heaton, R. T. Fairclough, Fairclough, Hepherd, Garner, Tinsley, Greenall, Bolton, H. Roberts, Taylor, Jenkins; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Chor- ley (borough treasurer), and Longdin (borough surveyor). DHATHS OF Mn- BLECKLY AND MR. DICHINNIES. The MAYOR said that since they last met Warrington had sustained a great loss by the death of Mr. Blackly and Mr. McMinnies. Mr. Meekly came to Warrington many years ago, and took a great part in the building up of the Hallam and Bewsey forges. In fact, he be- lieved it was generally admitted that to Mr. 'Bleckly's great business ability was due very much of the success which had attended that , gigantic undertaking. Mr. Bleckly's time was very much taken np with e.his own busineaS, yet he managed to devote a considerable amount of time and energy to the duties of this borough. Twice he filled the office of Mayor with conspicuous ability, and throughout his public life he was respected by all classes, and was looked upon as an able, industri- ous and valued townsman. Mr. McMinnies also took a lively interest in. everything connected with the well- being of Warrington. He was one of its first Aldermen, and he (the Mayor) felt convinced that he must haye been a useful member of that Corporation. From 1880 to 1885 he represented the borough in Parliament, and did his utmost to give general satisfaction. He was a naost generous man, and his many acts of kindness mulit have made him a large number of friends. By the death of Mr. McMinnies they had lost a true friend, a generous- hearted townsman, and one who was ever ready to help forward every good and useful work. (Applause.) Alderman DAVIES moved "That the members of this Council earnestly desire to record their affectionate and deep regard to the memory of two W-arrington worthies, the late Henry Sleekly, Esq., S.F., who died on the 24th day of January, 1890; and John Gordon McMinnies, Esq., S.F., who represented Warrington in Parliament from 1880 to 1885, and died on the Ist day of February, 1890; and that the Town Clerk be requested to convey to both of their families the heartfelt sympathy and con- dolence of the Council with them in their bereavement." (Applause.) He added that he did not know that words were at all necessary to support such aresolution, know- ing how readily the members of the Tpwn Connell would support it, with a desire to keep in remernberance two such noble men. (Hear, hear.) Alderman BURGESS in seconding the motion, said he quite agreed with Alderman Davies that words were not necessary to recommend the adoption of the resolution. One observation, however, he might be allowed to make, namely, that be hoped it would be a very long time in- deed before Warrington would suffer such serious be- reavements as it had suffered during the last fortnight. (Hear, hear). Alderman SUTTON said Warrington had lost two of its greatest worthies, both of whom were well known and respected on account of their good qualities, excellent abilities, and valuable experience in local and other matters. Alderman CROSIGELD who, in referring to Mr. Me- Minnies, was deeply moved, said he should just like to say how heartily he supported the resolution. He thought that every word which had fallen from Alder- man Davies and the other speakers was perfectly true. They had lost two of the ablest men Warrington ever produced. He suppo-ed Mr. Bleckly was one cf the deepest thinkers and one of the best read men in Lan- cashire, a man of superior judgment, and one who raised himself by his own abilities to the high ' position of Chairman of Quarter Sessions. With regard to Mr. McMinnies they all knew his good qualities, his tender heartedneqs, his generosity, and nis memory would al- ways live with them. (Hear, hear). The resolution was then agreed to. - SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE. This Committee met on the 16th January, when the Inspector reported that 44 cases had been inquired into by the Board of Guardians, and school fees allowed in 41 cases for 92 children. Eighteen cases were brought before the Committee and dealt with. On the proposition of Councillor FLEMING, seconded by Councillor J. Saw-Gasss, the minutes were con- firmed.

ment under the Corporation of Liverpool. It had been a source of some gratification to find that there were so many applications for the vacancy. The appli- cant whom the Committee had selected was scatcely 20 years of age, and was willing to accept the position at a salary of 14s. a week. That, he thought, indicated tbitt young men appreciated the training and special educa- tion which work under a Corporation gave them. (Hear, hear.) He did not know how the Council would feel disposed to meet the resolution concerning the proposed increase in Dr. Gornall's salary. The Committee had furnished every member of the Council with a copy of the application msde by the Medical Officer, showing how long he had bren in the service of the Corporation and the amount of work which had fallen to him in the dischaige of his duties at the Infec- tious Diseases Hospital. I In Use statement referred to Dr. Gorr/ism. said :—lt is now twelve years since I entered upon the duties of Medical Superintendent of this hospital, being originally appointed in January, 1878, and reappointed in October, 1880, when I relinquished private practice to undertake the new responsibilities that were forcing themselves on municipal authorities. I think it was then generally understood that my duties were to be those of medical supervision, with occasional professional care and treatment of cases admitted. Since, however, the powers obtained under the Notification Act (1879) have come into force, there has been a large increase of patients from year to year, and I am now virtually the medical attendant of nearly all cases admitted (irrespective of position in the social scale) as well as the medical super- intendent. During the last three years nearly 1,000 patients were admitted, and in 1888 we had an average daily list of 70 patients in hospital, so that my time and whatever skill I possess were entirely taken up in the treatment and supervision of disease. I can also point with some little pride to the fact that no complaint has ever been lodged against the management, and as far as the hospital is concerned, it has escaped the popular iU- will that is often loitered against such an institution. Under these circumstances I think I may ask (with some little confidence) the Committee to take into con- sideration the question of an increase in my salary. Continuing, Alderman Burgess said that the Committee were of opinion that Dr. Gornall's application was not an unreasonable one. (Hear, hear.) They thought that he had given services to the borough for which he had not been overpaid, but which, on the contrary, the medical officer himself and the profession generally in Warrington considered underpaid. What they had to do was to put a proper value on his services, and remunerate him accordingly. Be had now a salary of £l.OO ES medical officer of health, £lOO as Superintendent of the Hospital for Infectious Diseases, and £5O as public analyst, making altogether £250 a year. After ten or twelve years' service, during which time Dr. Gornall had discharged his duties in a manner which had been so satisfactory that the Council would regret very much if anything brought about a change in the office—(hear, hear)—he was entitled to the increase He might mention that the death rate throughout the country was diminishing, and although he had not the returns for Warrington, he believed they showed a similar decrease. Alderman Sutton seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Alderman Burgess explained that about twelve months or two years ago Dr. Gornall made application to be allowed private practice, and his request was granted, but he had not undertaken any, and so remained in about the game position. Alderman Davies and the Mayor supported the Pro- posal of the Committee, and the minutes were confirmed. PAVING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTER.

The above Committee had resolved that the setts in front of the Infirmary in Kendrick-street betaken up and that portion of the street be relaid with wood pavensent, and that setts removed from Kendrick-street be used in the paving of Market-street ad Victoria- street, and at a subsequent meeting that the tender of Messrs. Darbi- shire and Company, to supply 200 tons of macadam at 9s per ton, at London andAorth-westorn Railway Station, be accepted. - Alderman Davies proposed the adoption of the minutes, and referring to the making of streets, said that the Com- mittee would shortly be coming forward with a new batch of streets, and he thought that they would be supported by the Council (Hear hear). Alderman Wright seconded the proposition, which was carried.
