LPPOINTED TOWN-CLERK.

At a meeting held on the 20th January, a letter was read from Mr.W.H.Brook, resigning his position as Town Clerk, when it was resolved, " That this Committee it) re- ceiving the resignation of the Town Clerk cannot refrain from expressing its deep regret that he cannot see his way to continue in the office he has so ably filled for the past twelve years with such conspicuous ability and integrity." —At a meeting held on the 27th January the Mayor Aldermen Burgess, Holmes, Harrison and Sutton, and and Councillor Monks, who had been, appointed a Sub:Coin- , mittee to consid-er the duties and salary• of the Town , Clerk's successor, presented their report, which was published in last Saturday's "Examiner." The com- mittee recommended the appointment of Mr. J. Lyon Whittle as Town-clerk under conditions stated in that report. The confirmation of the minutes 'was moved by the MAYOR, seconded by Alderman SUTTON. and agreed to. The Council then rose. , ,
Mr. Brooke: Did you then read Richard's state- ment?
Witness: Yes.
It was as follows :

The true statement of R. Davies.—l hereby confess that me and MS brother George made it up to kill father, on Saturday, *January 25th. (Sensation.) I left the shop at about eight o'clock to go home, but instead of going home I was to wait in Crewe-lane for father to come, and then I was to come out of the hedge, and seize the pony's head, while George, who was riding with him, and was bringing the axe with him, would jump up and strike him two or three times. I ran be- hind and caught hold of him and pulled him out of the trap, and then George got out of the trap, and I went home and left him there to wait until he was dead, and then he was to come running home saying they had been stopped up Crewe-lane by two men. I arrived home about eleven o'clock, and in ten minutes or a quarter of an haur George came and told us. .rran and got to him first, but he was on the 'opposite side to where I had left him, and quite dead. I took his money out of his pocket, and then Jack, my elder brother, came up. The cause we had for it was because he was such a bad father—not to me exactly, but to George and the rest, and a bad husband to mother, for they have been very nearly- starved sometimes, for he would neither buy them coal for the fire or meat to eat when he was in a bad temper, but may the Lord forgive us, we never thought what a crime we were committing, nor the consequences of it, and I hope the lase will deal mercifully with me. and George. We don't deserve it, I know,but let it be for the sake of mother and my little brothers. Spare one of us for them." The statement is signed "H. DAVIES." These statements were real over in the presence of both prisoners. Richard said, when lie heard George's state- ment, "Now, George, yours is not true. The first part is, but the last is nothing but lies. I did not say that, and I expected you, George, to tell the truth. The fast part is not true. You had the axe and you know it. You struck father first." The prisoner George replied, "No, I did not. It's all true what I have written. You came up with the axe-head in one hand and the stave in the other, and did you not say, 'What shall we do now ? You took the pistol with ypu and you said if you did not finish him with the hatchet your would with the pistol. You struck him from the side of the trap. Did you not 'go down the lane and over a style into Commer's Field, and say. 'Some one Is coming down the lane.' You said, " I will go home, and you must come in ten minutes, and say my father has been stopOd in Crewe-lane by two men.' I did so, and you know it. I never struck father with the axe at all. You took the axe into the trap." Richard said to Geroge, "You took the axe"; whereupon George replied, "I did not. You took it." Richard said to that "How could I take it when I was in the skating-rink and ether places before I went home ?" " Oh, George, you know you did. How can you say ;bat? I got hold of the pony's head, and you struck him whilstin the trap, and he fell backwards with the seat." He then conveyed both prisoners back to the cells. On Sunday morning the elder brother John came, and was told the prisoners had expressed a wish to see him. He brought Richard into his office, and on confessing to John, Richard said "John, I hope you will forgive toe for what we have done to father." John said, "Then it is true." Richard replied, " Oh, yes ; only too true, lam sorry to say. John said, "Well Dick, I forgive yon; but you have to ask someone else to forgive you." Afterwards George was brought into his brother's presence. John said to him "Welt George, this is a sad job." George replied "Yes, it is: but I am innocent." 'George did not say more. After some time had been spent in silence he was conducted back to the cells, and John went away. Emily Davis, deceased's daqghter, who keeps the house attached to the shop in Victdria-street, said that on the sight of the murder she saw both her brothers, Richard and George, having a conversation in the yard behind the shop. She did riot hear what it was. Richard left the shop about eight o'clock, and George followed about half-past ten, riding in the father's trap. Next day the chopper was missing from the yards She identified the handle produced as part of the chopper. [lt had been picked up with blood on it near the scams of the murder.] Early on Sunday morning, her brother Richard came to' tell her what had happened, and on opening the door to him his words were, " Fathet is killed.' The prisoners were remanded until Wednesday. WEDNESDAY.—THE PRISONERS AGAIN BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

At the Crewe Police court, on Wednesday, Richard' Davies, 18, ;and George Davies, 16, were again brought up before Mr. H. J. Tolletnache, M.P., and a full Bench of magistrates, charged with tho murder of their father, Richard Davies, at Hough. Mr. Stuart Brooke again prosecuted on behalf ot the Treasury ; and Mr. C. H. Pedley watched the case as executor to the will of Mr. Davies. The police were re- presented by the Chief Constable, Superintendent Leah, and Inspector Oldham. Mr. Stuart Brooke said that after certain evidence had been called it would be necessary, in the interests ef justice, to ask for an eight days' adjournment. , • Dr.7rederick Edward Matthews, surgeon, Nantwich, ' gave evidence, and said that he was called by the police , to go to Hough On the 26th ult. He went to the house , of Mr. Davies; and found the by lying in the back ' kitchen. Describing the results of the post-morten examination, he said he found 10 wounds on the heed, six being fractures of the skull. Either of three ef the ' fractures was sufficient to produce death. The back of the head was also smashed in, and the brain was exposed. There was one lear cut wound on the left side, about an inch above the ear, which was a little over two inches, the bone being exposed.. There was another au inch behind this having the same direction, and being about two inches long, also exposing the bone, a small piece of which had been cut out. Another run- ning transversely hail cut through the scalp. The eighth was star-shaped, having five angles, and was on the right side of the head. On the right temple there was a lacerated wound, and there was a contused wound running from the outside of the left eye to immediately above the left ear. There were six fractures of the skull. The outer covering of the brain was uninjured. A suf- fusion of blood covered the right side and the left pos- terior surface. There were three wounds on the right hand. the thumb being very nearly severed. The injuriewto the head were the cause of death. The cut wounds had probably been caused by is sharp cutting instrument, withan edge about two inches long. The lacerated wounds might have been caused by some blunt weapon. Considerable force must have been used, and he judged that- the cut wounds must have been caused by a man standing at the side of Mr. Davies and striking him from that position. He could form no opinion as to the direction from which the contused wounds were struck. Last evening he examined the handle ef the hatchet, now produced by Sergeant Pear- son, and found stains upon it. He believed those steins to be blood. By the Chairman—Witness theught any of the wounds might have caused death if Davies had been lying on the ground, and an assailant had struck him while standing over him. Prisoners did not ask any questions at the close of the examination of Dr. Mathews. Police Constable Pickford next gave evidence as to the prisoners desiring to make a statement, and described how they,were supplied with pen and ink, and wrote their confessions in the cells. He also stated that when their confessiohs were read over Richard said that some ef the-statements made by George were lies, and added, "You had the axe,George. and you know it. You struck father first." George denied this. The constable con- firmed the evidence given by Inspector Oldham, on Monday, as to the wrangle between the prisoners after their statement had been read over to them. • Sergeant Walley, of Nantwich, proved finding the knife belonging to deceased near a pool of blood in the road, and Sergeant Pearson said he found the hammer stave with blood marks upon it near the spot. Police Superintendent Leah testified to receiving- infor- mation of the murder from Inspector Oldham, and to immediately visiting the house, where he -took state- ments from members of the family and saw the prisoners. Richard made a statement saying he knew nothing of the occurrence until quarter-past eleven o'clock at night. when his brother George came running henne, and said their father had been stopped in Crewe-lane. George's statement was that when driving home with his father from the shop in Vietcria-st., Crewe, and when near Hough, they were attacked by two men: He (George) then got out of the trap and ran home. The witness made inquiries through Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday, and on the latter day went to Victoria-street, and, noticing chopped firewood in the yard, hc inquired of Richard, who said it had been chopped by his little brother with a small butcher' e cleaver. The,witness asked Richard to show it him, and the prisoner produced a small cleaver (produced), which did not appear to have been recently used, and told the witness that was the one always used, and there was no, other on the premises. Going after- wards to the Hough, the little brother, Freddy, made a I statement, in consequence of which the witness saw George, who repeated the story as to the attack by I strange men, but some of the details were inconsistent with what lie had said before. He described his father as sitting still in the trap, with the reins in his hands, while he (George) was running to and fro to get away from one of air; men who was pursuing him. Thrning to Richard, the witness said it was beyond a doubt that there was a hatchet other than the little cleaver,: and it was at the shop in Victeria-street as recently- as live o'clock on Satueday. Asked if he could tell anything about that missing hatchet, Richard said he could not. There was one, but (he had not seen it for a long time. Afterwards, examining some clothing of the prisoners, ' slight blood stains were found. Driving with the prisoners to Crewe, the witness with tbem made an unsuccessful search for the missing hatchet, and then taking them to the police-office placed them pnder arrest, charging them with murdering Richard Davies, their father. Richard, after a moment's hesitatien, said, "Oh, good heavens, I'm sure I'm innocent. Such a thought' never entered my head." George said," I'm sure I am." Albert Moseley, manager of a grocer's shop in Victoria- street, Crewe, said that on Saturday night, January 25, he heard Mr. Davies, who was in the back yard of his house, av, "Loose me, loose me, -loose my throat.' W itness went and tried the back door leading to theyard,

but he could not obtain admission. He heard Davies previously shouting angrily to both prisoners. Bolina Micklewright said that on the night in question, at about half-past nine, she saw both theprisoners stand- ing against the pony trap near the shop. They were together. She spoke to Richard, asking him to,keep an eye on her shop while she went to a neighbour's. The prisoners were there when she came back. . . . . .
The prisoner Richard said that witness was mistaken as to the time. It was half-past eight. Witness said that it was later than that.
Mr. Brooke then produced the bough of the tree found near the spot, with bidod upon it. He did not, however, think that it had been used in attack.
The case was then adjourned till Thursday next week, and the prisoners were subsequently removed to Stafford Goal.
THE DEMEANOUR OF THE PRISONERS.

A special correspondent telegraphed from Crewe on Wednesday that the police authorities there state that certaia reports have appeared calculated to excite pre- judice against the pnsoners. One of ,these was that Richard asked for a concertina on Monday evening, and another that during the night he whistled lively airs. It was also stated that the prisoners by their disorderly conduct kept a female prisoner in an adjacent cell awake. The first two statements are entirely baseless, and as to the third it was the woman who kept them awake by disgraceful noises. Much was said of the cool- ness of the prisoners when in the dock, but to a close observer their faces during the examinatiiin on Monday last bore an entirely different aspect. When the confes- sions were read both were moved to silent tears, and cold . . . . _ _

Sisveat on the forehead of Richard showed his' concern. George did not appear fully to comprehend his position. His brother is, however, alive to his terrible situation, and the police say that he exhibits every sign of being sincerely and deeply penitent.

div.head: CREWE MURDER.
div.p: THE CREWE MURDER.
ACCUSED BEFORE TUE MAGISTRATES.
THE FULL CONFESSIONS.

At Crewe on Tuesday afternoon, Richard Davies, aged 18, and George Davies, aged 16, were brought up charged with the wilful murder of their father, Richard Davies, in the parish of Basford, on the night of January 25th. The prisoners appeared in different attire to that worn at the last examina7

tion. both now wearing black suits.. They, seemed to take very little interest in the proceedings.—Mr. C. S. Brooke appeared for the Public Prosecutor; and Mr. C. H. Pedley watched the case for the prisoners. Mr. Brooke, in briefly opening the 'case, said he proposed to put Inspector Oldham in the boa first, and he would give the prisoners' statements. He regretted it would be his duty in this very painful case to call the mother and the prisoners' brothers and sisters as witnesses against them. Inspector Oldham said he was stationed at Crewe on Sunday morning, the 25th of January. Abbut ten minutes to one o'clock the prisoner Richard Davies came to him in a pony trap, in Victoria-st., Crewe. The prisoner asked "Are you the sergeant ?" and witness said "Yes." Prisoner said "Ms father has been stopped by two men in Crewe-lane." Witness knew prisoner and his father before. He was also aware his father was in the habit of going from his shop in Crewe to Hough every week. When the prisoner Richard came to him in Victoria-street he said his father had been attacked by two men while driving home with his , brother. He asked hint if his father was hurt, and Richard replied he did not know. Witness said he would go to the police-station and get some lights and assist- ance, and prisoner drove away, as he said to alarm his sister, who lived at the Victoria-street shop. The pri- soner afterwards overtook witness in Ectlestene-road with the trap. Witness again asked whether he knew if his father was hurt, and he said he did not. He did not know whether a doctor would be required. He got into the trap and they proceeded to the village. Prisoner spoke very little all the way. He was not wearing an overcoat. It was a' very cold, rough night. When they had got to the locality of the attack he found half-a- dozen villagers standing round the body of the deceased, who was lying on his back at the side of the road. He was quite dead. The head was terribly cut and the back of the head smashed in. His right-hand thamb was .cut off and the second and third fingers bad- ly cut. He found the seat of the trap near. Witness prodnced the murdered man's clothes, which he searched. In the pockets only 6d. was found. That was in the left hand trousers pocket. He did not find any keys upon the body. The deceased had a watch and chain, but it had been removed before he got there. There was considerable blood on the road. He had the body re- moved to the deceased's house. It was conveyed to the house in the trap. Neither of the prisoners assisted to remove the body. The place where the body was found was about three miles from Crewe. It was a lonely spot in the lane. The deceased's house was about a quarter of a mile beyond the scene of the murder. In the road about five yards from deceased's body he found a large branch of a tree of considerable weight. It had not been cut if recently. The thick part had blood upon it. He drove to Nantwich, and laid the case before Superintendent Leah. On Tuesday night, the 27th of January, the two prisoners were brought to Crewe by Superintendent Leah and locked up on a charge of murdering their father. The pri- soners had been under his witnesses care ever since. They had been confined in separate cells. About twelve o'clock (midnight) en Wednesday, January 29, in conse- quence of a cammunication received from the prisoners, he went to the cell where the prisoner George Davies was confined. Witness said to George Davies, " Do you want to see me ? " and he said, " Yes." Prisoner then said, " I want to see Dick," meaning his elder brother in a neighbouring cell. Witness asked him, "What, alone P" George said, "Yes." Witness replied, " I cannot allow you to see him alone. It must be in my presence." He added, "If you wish it, I will allow it." The prisoner answered "Yes," and witness brought them both out into the police-office. When they got into the office, witness addressing Richard, said, " george has asked to see you, and I must tell you both that what conversation you have I must take notice of, as it may be given in evidence aealost you:'!. George then turned to his brother Richard, and said "What are you going to say, Dick ?" The priscner. replied "I don't know what to say, I'm sure." Both prisoners then remained silent for some time. Sergeant Averssaid to them" Is that all ?" and they both replied "Yes." They were then conducted back to their res- pective 'cells. At ten o'clock the following morning he received another message from the prisoner George from the call. He went to the cell and saw the prisoner. The prisoner George said again, " I should like to see Dick," and he brought out both prisoners into his office. When they got into the office, George said, " Well, Dick, what are you going to say ?" Witness had just previously cautioned them that whatever they said might be given in evidence against them. George, turning to his brother, said, Well Dick, what are you going to say? The elder prisoner, replied, " I hardly know ; what are you going to say?" George answered, "You know Dick. There is my little brothers, sisters, and mother." Dick ,replied, "Yes," adding to his brother, "What are you going to say? Are you going to tell r George did not make any answer to that,and Richard went on to say, " If you will give me a piece of paper I will write it down." Witness gave Richard some paper and said to George," Do you want a piece cd paper too 11" George replied, can tell mine. I cannot write very well." Witness replied" The charge is so serious perhaps you had better have a piece of paper each." George replied, "Very well," and witness gave him a piece of papsr also. They were also supplied with pens and ink. Each prisoner was then taken back to his cell and left by him- self. About half-past twelve o'clock the same morning he received another message from the cell, and went and saw the prisoner Richard. Richard handed him a state- ment. After receiving the statement from Richard he went to see George, and he gave him the statement signed with his name. Witness then took both prisoners into his office. Police Constable Pickford was present. Witness asked of the prisoners. " Are these statements correct that you have written ?" and each prisoner said, " Yes." He cautioned them again and read over to them the statement of the prisoner George, which was handed to him first. The following is the statement. On Saturday, Jan. 25th, Dick got ready to go home first, and went the back way out. When he got ready to go into theyard he said to me, "George some here," and I went to him. He said, " I want you to get me a bex Of pistol caps. lam not going that way. I shall come here again before you go home. You need not say what I want you for," and then he went in. About half-an- hour afterwards I went down to get the caps, and when I got to the shop I stood looking through the window, when someone knocked against me. On looking round I saw Dick standing there, and he said, " Hive you got those caps ?" and I said " No" ; and he said "Go and get them." I went and got them, and came out of the shop and gave them to him. Then we both walked up Victeria-st., and went into John-st., and stood against bur trap. When we got there Dick said tome, "I tell you what. I think I shall have ago at our old chap to- night." I said. "Please yourself." He said " I meant to have a go at him on Monday night, but he picked somebody up and gave them a ride." Dick said, "I shall get the little chopper out of the yard," and I said, " I should not get it, because it would be missed," and he said, "No ; they would not miss it." Richard saki, " You will not see me again before I have hit him and I shall go home, 'and you must come running about ten minutes after me, and run into the house and sav some one has stopped my father up Crewe-lane." Then Emily came and called me, and we parted at that I thought no more about 'it and did not think he would do it. About half-past ten me and father started from the shop, driving home in the pony and trap. We stopped at the Banel at Nantwich-road and father stayed five or ten minutes. About a quarter or twenty minutes to eleven we started from the top of Mill-st., and we went on right till we got to Crewe-lane When we had got about half- way down the lane Dick hit father with somethina, and father said, "Oh, dear, dear I What's that? Ana then he said "Way, way," and Dick hit him again, and then father fell out of the back of the trap, and the seat as well. And then the pony went on a bit, and then I got but and went farther down the lane, and did not know what to do. Then Dick came running down, and he said he thought somebody was coming, so he went across the fields and went home, and I went round by the lane, and gOt home about ten minutes after Dick. I went running into the house, and said " Father has got stopped up Crewe-lane." Dick was then putting his shoes on, and ran out of the house, and he went to Maddock's and told them that father had been stepped, and then he ran up Crewe-lane to where father was, and found him dead. I think you know all the rest. (Signed) GEORGE DAVIES.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

*.* Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warringt,on, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.
Romolar HORNETS T. RUNCORN LILIES.—This match was played on the ground of. the latter on Saturday. Score: Hornets,three tries and five minors, to Lilies three minors.

HALTON LIBBRAL INSTITUTE V. RUNCORN WHITE ROSE. —Played on the ground of the latter, and resulted in a draw, the score being Rose 1 try' 6 minors, to Institute I try, 8 minors. Finlay scored for the Rose, and Marsh for the Institute. RUNCORN TURN BLUES V. Sr. HELENS HOLT CROSS.— This match was played on the ground of this former, and a pleasant game resulted in a win for the Blues by ' one goal, three tries, and four minors to Holy Cross nil. Hill (dropped goal), Povey (two tries), and Cousins were the scorers for the Blues.

RUNCORN RRCREATION v. FRODBHAIL-011 Saturday these teams met at Frodsham, in the presence of a "large number of spectators. Frodsham had the best'of the play throughout. In'the first half Runcorn obtained a try, and Frodsham two minors; but in the second half, A. Tudor, Webb, and W. Tudor obtained tries in rapid succession, Darlington following suit, and of these two were converted Into goals. The score at the termination of play was—Frodsham, '2 goals, 4 tries, 2 minors ; RecreaiLon,l try.

WIDNES Sr. MARY'S v. WIGAN ROVERS.—This engage- ment took place at Widnes. on Saturday, before a large number of spectators. Kelly kicked off for the Saints, and Hogan dribbled splendidly to the line, having hard lines for scoring. After splendid passing Pennington scored a try, but no goal resulted. Donoghue then passed to Cafferty, and the latter scored under the posts. IKelly kicked au easy goal. In the second half France started for Wigan and Jameson scored for the Rovers. Donoghue followed with another try for St. Mary's. Mailing failed at goal. Harding picked up, and after a dodgy run dropped a neat goal for the home team. Final score: Widnes St Mary's two goals, two tries, and six minors ; Wigan Rovers, two tries and one minor. RUNCORN v. SALFORD .! A " Taams.—Played at Run- corn, on Saturday, and an exciting game ended in favour of Runcorn by one goal and two tries to Salford one try two( miners. The victory for the home team was very popular, as they only played 14 men throughout the whole of the game, and reflects the highest credit on them for defeating so strong an "A "team as Salford. The visitors were represented the best by Saunderson, Mallinson, Oswald, and Beatty. Teams :—Runcorn May, full back ; Cawley, Woods and Houghton, three- quarter backs ; Pendlebury and Davies, half backs; Hughes, Hulse, Stubbs, Andrews, Clark, Evans, , Williams, and Moores, forwards. Salford : Blemley, full back; Mallitison, Bowker, and &undersell' three- ' quarter backs ; Oswald and Ditchfleld, half backs; Derbyshire, Haslam, Richards, Tonge, Walker, Gill, Foster, Knowles, and Beatty, forwards. WIDNES v. Tor:Jiff:Tex.—This match was played at Widnes on Saturday, oa the ground in Lowerhouse-lane. Parkinson kicked off against the wind, and no return being made, a scrimmage took place in the visitors quarter. Here Plumpton received a pass, and with his drop kick had hard lines of scoring. Two free kicks gave Tottington a temporary visit into the home quar- ters. A dribble by the home forwards proved a slight gain, but losing possession of the ball Tottington, assisted by the wind, and a free kick from kreturn by Hartles, carried play to the home line, where a number of well contested scrimmages took place' and a good prospect of the visitors sconng. Clarke, however, brought relief by a kick to touch near the 25 flag. Parkinson and Brennan were next conspicueus with a good run to, the visitors' quarters, and from a scrimmage which then took place Brennan passed to Clarke, who with some dodgy play crossed the line and registered a try. The place kick was not an easy one, and Plumpton's effort proved fruitless. From the drop-out Widne.s again pressed, and to save further disaster a minor was cell- ceded to them. At half time the score was Widnes one

_ - try and one minor to Tottington nil. Shortly before half- time one of the visitors' forwards, named Fogg, re- ceived injuries to his knee, which necessitated his retire- ment from the field. On changing ends Widnes had the wind in their favour. Some clever passing between Brennan, Drummond, Howard, and Clarke resulted inthe latter again crossing the line, but only a minor resulted. Drummond and Brennan were again conspicious, the former feeding his three-quarter back in capital style. Brennan received a pass and rushed through his Oppo- nents in fine style, scoring a try almost behind the posts. Plumpton took the place kick, which resulted in a goal. The attack on the visitors' line, after the kick off, was again continued, and subsequently Howard registered the third try, from which Plumpton landed a fine goal. A few minutes later a pass from Drummond to Plump- ton was ably taken, and the latter, after a long run almost from the centre, crossed the line; and with some dodgy play placed the leather opposite the posts, and afterwards kicked a goal. Operations having been recommenced, Drummond again broke up the scrim- mages by a neat pass to Howard and then to Plurnpton, the latter dropping a splendid goal amid enthusiastic cheering. The visitors next had a look in, and their full back would undoubtedly have scored but for the smart tackling of Drumtnond. A few minutes off the call of "No time," Daines succeeded in crossing the home line, but no goal resulted. One of the most iateresting games played on the Widnes ground this season ended in an easy win for Widnes by 3 goals, 2 tries, and 4 minors, to Tottington 1 try. The Widnes team was made up as follows :--Llartles, back; Clarke, Parkinson, Brennan and Plumpton' chrte-quarter backs.; Drummond and Howard, half backs; Laws, Gandy, Tickle, Gordon, Farmer, Pearson, J. H. Smith, and P. Whelan, for- wards. .

WARRINGTON "A "v. Switcrox "A."—This match was played at Swinton on Saturday, in the presence of a moderate nuilnber of spectators. Warrington commenced hostilities by kicking off down hill, when ,Valentine gaining hold, returned smartly into touch. The homes- ters, headed by Allen and Wallwick, eventually attacked, ' but Thornley and Mather saved rather cleverly, and for a time play rested in mid-field. Warrington now gradually worked towards their opponents' line, heeling out and dribbling in a scientific and combined fashion. The visitors penned their opponents, and later some ex- citing play in which the visitors' backs participated ended in Webster scoring after a smart and well-dodged run, a grand try, which he failed at converting. Jolley was now to the fore with some fine punting, and Mather, who got possession, passed beautifully across the field to Daniels, who mulled, and a splendid opportunity was lost. Later, however, he ran nicely along touch, and now fine open play on both sides was witnessed, Thorniley Byres, and Barnes being well to the front. Some good loose play, in which Jolley and Davies were seen to ad- vantage, now brought play to Swinton lines but Lord relieved to mid-field and here for a time play ensued. Eventally Mather ran to the Swinton 25, and passed to Daniels who struggled to gain ground by a tricky run, and was finally held in front of the hornester's goal. Here some exciting play ensued, which eventually ended in Webster dropping a magnificent goal. Jolley for his fine kicking was next rewarded applause as were Thornley and Davies for their fine and clever dribbling and tack- ling. Again good passing on the part of the visitors' backs placed theta on the aggressive, but Lord and &ego worked hard to neutralize and gain an advantage. Later a rare chance was given '-Holker by Edge, but Jolley speedily marred his progress, and the advantage was lost. As yet,however,the defensive tactics of the homesters pre- vented the visitors from again crossing the line Williams and Edge beingprominent by timely relief. Molyneuxand Berry, not to be denied, raced back, but Holker saved, and half time was brought about.with the score—Warringten onegoal, one try, one minor; Swinton, nothing. On resuming, the visitors, led by Eyre and Holmes, broke away, and thus forced the homesters to utilize their defensive tactics. Swinten forced relief, their resistance being well sustained by Tipler and Williams. Off-side tackling penalized the homesters somewhat consider- ably, Lord's nice play being of no advantage to his side, After some loose play, Swinton gained a slight advant- age, and gradually forced the visitors to defend, Jolley kicking dead, and thus the homesters scored their first and only point. Jolley dropped out, 'and Davies and Lawless were conspicuous in their endeavours in again forcing Lawton to assume an aggressive position. The visiting backs again exhibited some fine passing. Jolley

finally dropping at goal,a minor accruing. Swinton now struggled hard and endeavoured to force play, but the visitors were too combined for the homesters to gain any distinct advantage, Lawless and Mather, by a trick exhibition of half back play, attacked strongly, Bra - burn being mainly instrumental in preventing a tang- ible point being counted. However, play now rested for a time in Swinton, 25, and Bradburn, in endeAvour- ins' to relieve, had his kick charged down by Neild, the ball rebounding over the line and a scramble ensued. The leather, was, however, brought back by some in- fringement, and a series of scrimmages were now wit- nessed. Eventually Edge relieved, and Williams dribbled cleverly, Webster,however,saving. Lawless ran strongly but passed forward, and Holker, by some dodgy work, gained considerable ground; but BOSCOW relieved in fine style by a well-timed kick. After some give and take play, Eyre succeeded in securing the leather, and grounded it safely behind the posts; but Webster's attempt again failed. Some interesting play followed, aud at the call of time victory rested with Warrington after a good game. Score :—Warrington: 1 goal, 2 tries, 4 minors; Swinton: 1 minor. Teams ;—War- rington : Full back, Boscow ; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Webster, and Daniels ; half, backs, Lawless and Mather; forwards, Thornley, Isherwood, Eyres, Molyneaux, Barnes, -HolmeS, Davies, Neild and Berry. Swinton: Full back, Bradburn ; three-quarter backs, T. Valentine, Holker, and Lord ; half backs, Stopford and Edge •, for- wards, Allen Tipler, Hovey, Williams, Holland, Wall- wick, Howard, J. Hotchkiss, and Sackfield. Referee, Mr. Fogg, Tottington. RUNCORN v. Serzonn.7-The return match between ,these two clubs took place on Saturday, at Salford,in the presence of a large number of spectators, and amongst 'them were many from Runcorn, who had availed them- selves of the privilege which had been conceded by, the railway company to travel at a reduced rate. Runcorn's representatives were :.T. Brazendale, back ; T. H. Davies, J. 11. Crompton, Abrams, three-quarter backs) ; H. Hnghes and Evans that( back.); W. Faulkner, W. Hughes,l. Gayter, P. Riley, R. Dolan, Lee, A. Hampson, W. H. Broady, and W. Rigby, (forwards.) Salford : Mainwaring (back) ; Myles, Barrett, and S. Williams, (threequarter backs), Newton and Walsh (half backs), Roberts, McVittie, Shaw, king, Tune, Birch, Law, Craven, and Tongue (forwards.) A great amount of ' speculation was entered into as to the result,as when the teams met at Runcorn, in the early part of the season, Salford sustained a crushing defeat, only scoring a try to , one goal, one try, and three minors registered by Runcorn. Shortly after half-past three the ball was put into motion by the home team' and very early on Faulkner obtained possession. Ascrimmage ensued,in the centre of the ground, and the visitors 'made a deter- mined attack on the home team's quarters; but relief I was given by Mainwaring. A grand struggle for supre- macy was then observed, and the struggle was of some- what lengthy duration, during which smart passing was exhibited by Evans (Runcorn), Hughes and Crompton doing some smart work. Mainwaring, hoWever, twatched his opportunity, and, when it presented itself, • relieved the pressure, and the ball was taken back. Broady gained considerable ground owing to a tree kick, and W. Hughes stepped in and added his quota towards altering the position of the visitors. Exciting as the play had been up to this point, it became more so afterwards, arid neither side secured any parti- cular advantage. Birch dribbled to the Runcorn twenty- five, and the play was transferred to the other end of the ground, and a dead ball was registered for Runcorn. Williams' made some good punts for Salford • but Cromp- ton and Davies were by no means behindhand. Later on Hughes passed to Davies, who spurted away in splendid style, and succeeded in getting over near the touch line. Brazendale failed to improve matters. On re-starting Crompton and Davies kept up their reputation, and W. Hughes put in a neat drop, and Mainwaring obtained possession, but was immediately tackled. The. visitors continued to press, when Davies narrowly escaped drop- ping a goal, the ball striking the nost. Crompton almost i got n, and Salford had to touch down. In the first half the visitors certainly had the best of the play, and gave the spectators a splendid opportunity of witnessing some good organized football, and as the whistle was blown at half time the score stood--Runcorn, 1 try; Salford, nil. The homestem were put on their metal in the second half by this state of things. Faulkner re-started, and Salford at cure showed a thorough determination to alter the previous state; but Runcorn evinced an equal determina- tion, the forwards pushing their way right up to the Salford line, and the struggle was one which excited the admiration of the spectators, the home players having the greatest difficulty in relieving their quarters. Things for a time looked very awkward, but Salford' succeeded in obtaining three tries within ten minutes of the close of play; whilst Runcorn added nothing to their score. WARRINGTON v. SWINTON.

Saturday was a red-letter day in the annals of Rugby football in the Warrington district, the famous Swinton team making their first oppearance in the series of home and home matches' arranged between the above clubs. iCodsiderable interest had been taken in this match, con- sequent upon the defeat inflicted on the Warringtonians in the first engagement, and the improved form shown by them in the recent matches. The first match, as will be remerbbered, ended in a victory for Swinton by two goals and one try to nil, and when it is taken into ancount that all their major. points Were scored in the last fest? minutes of the game, it will be agreed that the Swintonians were blessed with no small amount of luck. After- this defeat by Swinton, things went from bad to worse for Warrington, and unexpected reverses were experienced week by week. It was not till the close of last year that the " wirepullers " pulled themselves together, with the ultimate result that victory after victory met their efforts, and they are now again looked upon as one of the leading organizations in the County Palatine. The mildness of the weather naturally had a tendency to draw a large crowd together, but much of the interest that attached to the match was negatived by theabsence of 'Valentine Bumhy, and Mills, the two formerhaving been selected to do duty for the North of England in the return engagement at Richmond. , Teams :—Warrington: Evans, hack; Massey, Barnes, and Lawless, three-quarter backs ' Antrobus and Bate. half backs ; Fair Thrner, Frank Turner, W. Dillon, Nevins. Bandies, Littlewood, Povey, E. Dillon, and Donohue forwards. Swintola : Roberts, back ; Murray, Marsh, and Okell, three-quarter backs; Smith and Buxton, half backs ; Hot-ley, Hotchkiss, Lomax, Nicholas Hallam, Clayton Walker, Astall, and Hall, forwards. Marsh kicked off, Evans replying to Okell, whose kick deposited the oval at the half-way. From the line-out a rush bylaw Swinton forwards was the means of taking the game to the Warrington quarter flag, where Bate cleverly saved, and from the succeeding pack Buxton I threw to Marsh, but Barnes was alert, and depriving the county centre of possession he changed the venue t o past the half-way flag. By neat combined play, in which Frank Turner, Dillon and Povey were prominent, the game was taken near to the Swinton goal, and a grand kick by Massey neutralized an effort by Honey. Evans responded to a movement in which Hallam and Hotchkiss were foremost, and then from a pack some passing between Bate, Antrobus, and Massey found the latter punting near the Swinton line. From a scrim- mage Turner made a fine effort to cross the line, but the defensive play of Marsh' was sound and danger was avoided. However, Warrington would not be denied, and another grand burst cf passing by Bate, Antrobus, and Barnes saw the latter crossing the line and placing first score to the credit of Warrington. Frank Turner made a good but successful bid for goal. The drop out found no relief for the Swintonians, and their energies were taxed to the utmost to prevent the Warringtonians from scoring. Lawless put in a grand kick to the Swinton line, and Roberts -was collared before he could return, and a tuition forced, Marsh put in some telling kicks soon after the restart, but all his endeavours to ease theyressure were fruitless, for the fine combined play of tilt; bointbacks compelled the game to be con- tested in the Swinton quarters. A drop at goal by Massey forced a secoad minor. A fine run and pass by Barnes to Lawless almost ended in a score, Marsh tack- ling and preventing. From a pack •Antrobus threw to Barnes, who dodged through and handedt the oval across to Massey, whose kick sent the oval beyond the dead ball line. Loose play followed, and those who came in for notice were Fair. Turner, Marsh, and Antrobus. Still no impression could be made on the home defence, and eventually another fine piece of pass- ing between Bate, Antrobus, and Barnes finally ended in, Lawless being pushed into touch in goal. Exchange kicks followed between Marsh and Lawless, and then iron' some fine play by Massey Roberts saved. Soon after the drop-out Marsh was collared near his line by Bandies, and from the succeeding pack another burst of, passing by Bate, Antrobus, Barnes, and Lawless resulted in the last-named wriggling his way through ad scoring a brilliant try. Frank Turner took the difficult place, and landed a fine goal. Roberts again saved from a rush of the home forwards, and then the whistle sounded for half-time, the telegraph beard showing the score-- Warrington. one goal, one try, six minors; Swinton, 'nil. After the usual interval Frank Turner re-started towards the pavilion goal, the kick off being responded to by Roberts, who along with Nevins exchanged kicks. Some loose play ended with advantage to the Swinton men, but from me pack near the home line, Barnes re- ceived, and dodging round, he wound up a grand effort by punting in touch near the half-way flag. Massey further improved his side's position by a smart kick ILO follow up, grassing Roberts before he could reply. Okell was now transferred to back. but Nevins With an accur- ate pass to Massey enabled that player to once more place his side on the aggressive. Some beautiful passing among the Warrington backs was now witnessed, and was intercepted by Marsh, who sent the oval to Evans. The home custodian had had little to do so far, and en receiving the leather he kicked to the half way flag, followed up, and secured possession once more, and put in another brilliant kick close th the Swinton quarter flag. Some more passing, was next witnessed among the Warrington backs and Lawless being hemmed in he kicked across and Massey racing up, secured possession; and although Marsh made a grand effort to collar his opponent, the fleetness of foot of Massey seraod him to advantage, and a pretty piece of play resulted in a try, Frank Turner failing at the place. No sooner had the restart been effected than another brilliant piece of play by Massey

- - again caused Swinton trouble. Bate threw low to Frank Turner a yard from the line out, and he dodged Nicholas and Hallam, and the fourth try was placed to the homester's credit, the kick at goal being unproductive of the major point. Soon after the restart a hasty visit was paid to the home quarters, and Evans was placed in a queer predicament near his own line. His kick found Roberts making his mark opposite the posts, and Marsh ' took the kick amidst breathless excitement. Luckily for Warrington, Donohue charged the kick down, and then another grand series of passing by the " wirepullers' back division found Lawless racing away at top speed, Marsh eventually knocking him in touch. An effort by Marsh forced Swinton their only minor. Barnes put in some grand runs towards the dose, but the previous exertions of the match, which had been of an extra- ordinary fast nature, told their tale, and all efforts to score were futile. Warrington remained on the attack the greater portion of this half, and the game taming down somewhat, the interest subsided. A finely con- tested game was eventually brought to a conclusion. the final score reading as follows : Warrington, 1-3-6; Swin- ton, 0-0-1. That the best team won there is no denying, and War— rington must be complimented on their all-round brilliant display. Their play in every detail was of 'a machine-like description, and not single fault could he found in any department or, style of play. Where the homesters excelled most was in the back division, wh° passed-with excellent judgment and kicked judiciously. The forwards, too, were never wanting. In making distinction Barnes, Massey, Antrobus, Bate, Littlewood, Nevins, Fair Turner, Frank Turner, and Dillon come in ' for special praise. Marsh was 'the best player on the Swinton side.

The broad-acred county has undoubtedly won the honour in the matches it has played though its pre-aminence over other counties, and espeoially Lancashire has not been so marked this year as last. Indeed, there has been either a distinct decline in the prowess of the Yorkshire Rugbyites, or a great ior provenient on the part of Lancashire, and it would IYA be surprising to see the relative positionof the two coun- ties changed next season.

- WARRINGTON CHAMBER OF COM- MERCE. ' • ' ANN CAI MEETING. The adjourned annual meeting of the Warrington Chamber of Commerce, was held at the Chamber in Bewaer-street, on Monday, the president Coun- cillor P. A. Roberts, C.C.,) presiding.' There were also present Councillors Monks, C.C., W. Pierpoint, J. H. Fleming, W. Tinsley, Mr. John Fairclough, and Alderman Davies and Mr. J. Tunstall (honorary Secretaries.) • The Chairman Said he had received Messages from Mr. Dun, Mr. John Rylands, Mr. • Stubs, Mr. J. Winser, Mr. W. Owen, Mr. Naylor, and Mr. W. Long ' expressing regret at their in- * ability to be present. 'THE COUNCIL'S neront. The Council reported as follows : be "The attention of the Council during the past year oas been occupied chiefly by two subjects, in connection With which numerous meetings have been held.—Railway 1443 : —The revised classifications and schedules of Maxi:alum rates and charges published by the Railway 'C• ompanies were earnestly considered, and the Council, that seer cat i . - es mg, t was incumbent upon them to ascertain • see views of those most interested in the matter, called ' !,• Ineeting of the traders and manufacturers of the dis- rot to meet the members of the Chamber. This meet- mg was held in the Council Chamber of the Town Hall on the 25th February last, and on the motion of Mr. !Sleekly, seconded by Mr. Carson, it was unanimously 1 ' lesolved—" That this meeting objects to any addition .I_,)eittg made to the rates and charges specifically author- , istnTera .i,by Railway the Acts of Parliament incorporating the Companies." It was arranged that each '' Irade should look to its own classification and interests, Ishilst the Chamber as a whole is represented by Mr. ) Veckly as its delegate to the Lancashire and Cheshire Con- Zrenee on Railway Rates and Charges. FACTS FOR " SAMORTNEDE." Sir,—l am not surprised that " Samohtnede "is ashamed to own his name to his disgusting epistle, which must appear so to men of ordinary intellect ; be repeats a lie, even if it was said by a Vicar. I cannot entertain his rubbish, the events occurring in the country (ad_ vancing Romeward) are to be read of almost daily. Now we have a wish expressed at Saint Paula', on Sunday last, by the head master of Harrow for the services of the festival of the Virgin Mary, and an order of Monks. If he can express himself so in public, what are the lads learning under him? Then Bishop Jayne demurs to the Vicar of Wakefield coming into Cheshire withoutconsult- ing him. Poor fellow Does he imagine Cheshire folk are going to tolerate boycotting liberty of speech? Nonsense. The Bishop signed the paper in favour of the order of Monks, attended an E.C.U. meeting in London to support Bishop King,the notorious lawbreaker and defier. Did he get permission from the Bishop of London ? He declines to reply to the inquiry for one verse out of the Bible in favour of Infant Baptism. Why? Because it is not to be found therein. Bribes are being offered to parents of Nonconformists to withdraw their children from Sunday School, and send them to the Church Schools. Is this the way to promote unity and kind feelings? They tell Nonconformists their parsons not having had the Bishop's hands laid upon them they can do no good, and no Sacraments in their 'chapel. Well, Archbishop Whately wrote, "That there •was not anything to prevent a layman from administering the Lord's Supper. 'rhey who say different are proceeding without any Scriptural authority." ROBERT 701.1LICES.
Frodsham, February sth, 1890.

CHRISTIAN UNITY. Sir,—What Unity did the great founder of Christianity intend there should be among his followers.? 'Such a question might well be occasioned by the sermon Of the Bishop of Chester in Trinity Church,Runcorn, last Thurs- day evening. Is not the unity spoken:of and enforced in Holy Scripture—the unity, not so mach of those who agree in certain facts and doctrines, as of those who having a firm faith in Jesus Christ and a steadfast adherence to his precepts, agree in that as the only essentialto give a rightto the name of Christian? "The Kingdom of God is within you "—net visible to all men's eyes is the Christian Church. Let all those then who have the one faith in the one Lord, and the one baptism of the spirit, learn to regard one another as equals. This is the principle which, if borne in mind by Christians, will afford the best clue to, as it is the only Solution of, "our unhappy divisions." The Lambeth conference was successful as far as it went, but its propositions could never be accepted ia tote by Nonconformists. If such conferences do any good, why not have one, lay and clerical, of all denomin- ations? Another question raised by the Lord Bishop's sermon seems to me to be; what influence was Christianity intended to have upon the world, or rather how was that influence to be exerted? Like the leaven, or the grain of mustard seed, were not the precepts of Jesus Christ intended to take firm root in the hearts of individuals and spread from one to another, 2radually permeating and levening the whole world of life and thought? Not by establishments therefore, and though a member of the Church of England I have no hesita- tion in saying it, is this work to be carried forward. When the religion of Christ has become the religion of the world, that may be possible, but meanwhile let believers in the Bible use Bible means and methods to further its teachings. Trusting you will pardon so long an incursion in your space, I ask leave to place these thoughts before your readers.
FIDES.

OUR NATIONAL POVERTY AND GOVERN- MENT EXTRAVAGANCE. Sir,—l think I have shown in former letters that cer- tain individuals receive from the public funds enormous sums annually as salaries for nominal work; that is an office or sinecure is created to which a large salary is attached with no work to do, and the person drawing the pay is an ornamental pauper. No matter what his rank in life may be, that is his social status, and,until men are sent to Parliament determined to put down this legalised dishonesty, it will continue to disgrace our national character. I am not against persons in high positions obtaining public employment in any branch of the public service they may choose, but first let them be qualified for the duties they undertake, and then faithfully per- form them. Lads at 17, who have never seen service, cannot be qualified to be generals, nor men of 35, who have never seen anything beyond a review, be compe- tent as Field Marshals. Vast sums are annually spent upon us?less appliances for warlike purposes—ships that will not swim, except at a very slow pace, carrying engines that break down and boilers that will not generate steam ; guns that break off and burst, calculated to do the greatest amount of damagetD our own sailors i n killing and wounding—but doing nothing to a possible enemy. Lavish and extrava- gant in bestowing places and pensions on certain individuals as our Government may be in some cases, in others they are mean and shabby in the extreme. They save at the spigot and waste at the bung hole. A few weeks since there died Lord Napier, of Magclala ; he was accorded a public funeral and a grave in Westminster Abbey. He was a brave man, a gallant and competent general, who deserved all he received; his name was in every mouth, and he was mourned by the nation at large—peace to his memory! About the same time there died at Pontypool, Monmouthshire, Benjamin Stewart West, at the age of 106 years; he, too, was a soldier, was in the army in 1809, serving under Sir John Moore, was present at Corruna, and witnessed the death of Sir John Moore in that disastrous retreat, served under Welling- ton throughout the whole of the Peninsular War ; took part in all those desperate battles—and was present at Waterloo—and in these engagements was twice wounded; was discharged from the army in 1817, re-enlicted in 1825, and was finally discharged in 1845, after serving and fighting in India. and doing garrison duty in North America. He, poor man, thought that his king service would entitle him to something extra in the way of pension, hut he was sadly mistaken. He got the regula- tion shilling a day, and, but for a small fund which some charitable people got together to smooth his path to the grave, his lot after so many years of arduous services would have been a hard one. In cases like this mean- ness and cruelty on the part of the Government become conspicuous. Our volunteers give their services gratuit- ously, and vet how shabbily they are treated! They give their time and no little money in making themselves efficient, and, in order to become efficient so as to earn the capitation grant, they, must know and learn how to shoot ; and to do this they must buy land or lease it for a shooting range (this is generally what they cannot afford to do), and yet the War Office cannot or will not assist them, and so resignation or a resort to begging must be the result. Few people outside the Volunteer movement know the shifts and expedients that many volunteer officers have to resort to—to raisethe needful; begging letters for subscriptions, coacerts, lectures, bazaars, and theatrical performances are among the expedients resorted to to keep together our citizen soldiers. Such expedients instead of inspiring patriotism must create disgust, and repel instead of alluring young men to join the force where they may become a factor in protecting our country from insult or invasion in any part of its dominions.—i am, sir, yours respectfully, CYMRO. Sankey Bridges, February 3rd, 1890. [lt has been discovered that the soldier West referred to by our correspondent was not over 100 years old, and could not have witnessed the death of Sir Thomas Moore, but that does not affect the main argument.] ED. Er.

Lord Salisbury travelled to London, on Wednesday from Hatfield, being accompanied by Mr. Balfour. A Cabinet rneetirg was afterwards held, but the details have not transpired. Lord Wolseley, addressing a gathering of military men at Aldershot, on Tuesday evening, said the British army was certainly small, but, as far as his observation went, it was better than any other.
THE MANCHESTER LIVERPOOL, MI.,
AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

Yesterday an adjourned meeting of this Society was held at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, Mr. G. C. Wale, of Liverpool, in the chair. It had been ad- journed from the 23rd ult. to consider a reselution passed at the general meeting in Decembdr last, and to make arrangements for the nomination and final election,at future meetings of a nev secretary,l The resolution in question. which had reference to th.• appointment of a successor to Mr. Rigby the retiring secretary, having been carried. Mr. John White proposed that a committee of eight members of the Council, with the Chairman and Secretary, be elected, to consider and define the future arrangements, and duties of the secretary-ship, and also to consider the future working of the Society generally. Mr. Nevett seconded the motion which was carried. The following gentlemen were appointed a carry the resolution. into effect :—Northern division, Messrs. Brockholes and Catterall; Western division, Messrs. Halsall and Scotson Eastern division, Messrs. Warburton and Robinson; Southern division, Messrs. Smith and White. The Com- mittee will meet in Liverpool on the 21st. inst. The Secre- tary informed the meeting that 180 members were in arrear with their subscriptions. A vote of thanks was passed to the retiring auditor. Mr. Lonsdale, who was atso pre- sented with the Society's gold medal in recognition of his , long services. Mr. Rigby produced a gold medal vithich he said he had had in his position for twenty years, it having been handed to him by his predecessor. The medal was from the Emperer of the French, Napoleon 111., ad was an acknowledgment of a Cheshire cheese that the Society presented to him in 1855, on the occasion of theirshow at Warrington.

div.head: ST. PETER'S TEA PARTY.
div.p: ST. PETER'S TEA PARTY.

The annual congregational tea party in connection with St. Peter's, Warrington, was held in the school- room, John-st., on Monday Evening. Nearly 200 parishinners sat dowli to tea, tile tables being pre- sided over by Mrs. W like. Mrs. Blease, Mrs. Green, Miss Jones, Miss Green. Miss Balshaw, Miss Edgar and Miss Roberts. The Vicar, the Rev. Thomas Rigby, occupied the chair at the subsequent enter- tainment, and was supported by the Rector of War- rington (Rev. F. W. Willis), Rev. E. C. E. Cadet:Gni Rev. E. T. Beatty, and the Rev. D. S. llodgson. The Vicar, in opening the proceedings, observed that when he occupied the position of Chairman it the last annual gathering, the history of the parish was in the future; now, however, some of it was in the past. (Hear. hear). Tracing the growth of the mission, Mr. Rigby spoke in terms of eulogy of his predecessors. During the past year the people of Warrington bad been very kind and generous in assisting the realization of the object which the parishioners had in view, the erection of a church. That object was so far attained that the contract for building had been signed with Messrs. Statham and Sons, Salford ; and he thought all the parish- ioners owed a deep debt of gratitude to the good- will and help of their neighbours, and not least to the Rector of Warrington, who took such a deep interest in St. Peter's parish. (Applause). He had a letter from the architect the other day, in which the writer told him that the seats were being made and that the orders had been given for the bricks and terracotta, and that in March workmen would be engaged on the site (Applause). The Sunday school was in a flourishing condition ; the day I school also was in a prosperous condition, which was indicated by the fact that the debt was 2,30 less than it was at the beginning of last year, and that was something to be thankful for in these times,when every school was more or less in debt. (Hear, hear.) An admirable programme, consisting of songs, iecita- tions, instrumental selections, &c., followed, the various items being contributed by Miss Fanshaw, Miss Jones, Miss Dagnall, Miss J. Ratcliffe, Rev.T. Rigby, Mr. T. A. Longdin. Mr. Furness, Mr. C. H. Ward, Mr. H. Buckton, Mr. Rose,. Mr. Whitehead, and Mr. J. Richardson. The accompaniments wer played by Mr. George Riley.—On Tuesday evening the scholars attending St. Peter's Sunday School had their annual tea party in the schoolroom. Be- tween 300 and 400 were present to tea, the tables being presided over by the teachers and others. Afterwards a miscellaneous collection of magic lantern slides were exhibited be Mr. Chorley, and at intervals Mr. Sykes contributed pianoforte solos.
THE ST. BARNABAS' SCHOOL DISPUTE.
THE ACTION IN ,THE COUNTY COURT.

At the, Warrington County Court, on Thursday, Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins made an application to his Honour, Judge Ploulkes, in an action for detinue which had been entered in the Court by the man- agers of thi St. Barnahas' School against the late schoolmaster (Mr. R. T. Woollacott), and mistress (Miss Parsons), from whom damages are claimed for the alleged detention Of school registers and other articles. Mr. Jenkins explained that the application he wished to make was on behalf of the defendants, his clients, for further and -better answers to interrogatories. Unfortunately, dissen- sions had taken place between the Board of Man- agement at St. Barnabas' School; and the result was that Mr. Woollacott and Miss Parsons, whom he re- presented— .—His Honour at this point intimated that Mr. Jenkins need not go into the nature of the dispute. lie asked whether the interrogatories had been filed. It transpired that that bad not been done, and his Honour asked why it was so; the

enswers had been tiled. It was very irregular. The answers were unintelligible in the absence of interrogatories.—Mr. Tomlinson (Preston), who was present on behalf of the plaintiffs, put in a copy of the interrogatories which had been served on him. —Hie Honour (to Mr. Jenkins) : Now what is the interrogatory. The one answer to which you object.— Mr. Jenkins : We object that there was no answer what ever from the Rev. George Allton.—His Honour: To which interrogatory ?—Mr. Jenkins: " At each of the said times."—His Honour: There are eleven interroga- tories. Which of them is it ?—Mr. Jenkins : o 3.—His Honour : That is, " At each of the said times who were the then existing managers of the schools." There seem to have been interrogatories on both sides.—Mr. Jenkins: Yes.—Mr. Tomlinson: The answer to that is.—His Honour: They are all lumped together. I cannot see why you could not have answered them separately.— Mr. Toinlinson:'lt is so connected with the others.—Hi Honour: No, surely ; look at the question. "At each of the said times who were the then existing manage r of the schools." The time related to is explained by other interrogatories.—Mr. Tomlinson : Nos. 1 and 2.— His Honour: I don't see any explanation of the word "time."—Mr. Tomlinson : I have taken it that he referred to the times of the appointment of the plaintiff's Pilkingtou and Proud as inanagers.—His Honour: There , is nothing to show that.—Mr. Tomlinson: It is the only 'explanation I could find of the interrogatory.—His Honour : The interrogatory is perfectly vague in itself. There is no explana,ion of the "said times."—Mr. Percy Davies said. that he appeared on behalf of Mr. Allton, one of the managers cf the school.—His Honour (to Mr. Tomlinson) : Whom do you appear for ? —Mr. Tomlinson said he represented the plaintiff's, the managers of the school. His Honour: The managers are not a corporation; therefore, they must be individually put.—Mr. Davies said that he appeared for the Rev. George Allton, who was the chief manager of the schools.—Mr. Tomlinson: I appear for the other four then, who are a majority.—His Honour (to Mr. Jenkins) : What is your objection to the an- swer P—Mr. Jenkins: Our objection is that it is not sufficiently full.—His Honour expressed the opinion that the intlrrogatories were wanting in clearness.—Mr. Jen- kins said that his clients wished to know also when and upon what terms Mr. Brown was appointed master of the school. That question, the plaintiffs declined to an- swer, on the ground that it was irrelevant.—Mr. Tomlinson: This, is art action for detinue.—Mr. Jen- kins said that his clients contended that they were still the master and mistress of the school. They had been forcibly ejected.—His Hor.our pointed out that a matter of that kind might come in as evidence, but he saw no necessity for it being put as an interrogatory.—Mr. Jen- kins said that they also asked for the production of the minute book, which, he believed, it would be admitted, was in the possession of Mr. Allton.—Mr. Davies said that on behalf of Mr. Allton he might admit that he had received notice as a witness to appear there that dev to produce the minute book. That was the first notice which Mr. ATlton had received of any action in any court, and in the particulars of the claim he was called ene of the plaintiffs. He now objected to being thus included, as he had never given instructions to any solicitor in conjunction with the other plaintiffs. He knew nothing of those proceed- ' ings, and now applied to his Honour to make se order upon the plaintiffs to idemnify him for costs if they were unsuccessful.—His Honour said he was afraid he could not make an order of that kind. —Mr. Davies said he simply gave his Honour notice that Mr. Allton knew nothing about these proceedings, until a subpcena was served upon him. Therefore, he asked his Honour te say that Mr. Anton was not a plaintiff.— His Honour said that was rather premature. To have that done, Mr. D4vies would have to appear at the trial and ask to have Mr. Allton's name struck out, on the ground that no authority had been given to enter the taint in his naine.—Mr. Tomlinson wa.s understood to say that Mr. Allton would be indemnified.—His Honour observed that if the other plaintiffs admitted that the action was brought without Mr. Allton's sanction, his name ought to be struck out.—Mr. Tomlinson asked for costs against the defendant's in the present application. His Honour complied with the request. The action for detenue has been fixed for hearing next Thursday.

div.head: LY3III.
div.p: LY3III.

EREENIASONRY.—On Thursday night, at the Earl of Chester Lodge, at Lvmm, Bro. Obadiah Burrow, of Altrincham, vras raised to the degree of a Master Mason by Bro. Lewis. TEMPERANCE CONCERT.—A well attended concert took place, on Monday night, in the Parochial Schools,Lymm, the proceeds of which were in aid of the funds of the Church of England femperahce Society's Brass Band. CONGREGATIONAL COXCERT.—A concert took place, on Thursday night, in the Congregational School, the pro- ceeds of which were for the funds of the Sunday school. Mr. Midgley had charge of the entertainment, and placed a well-selected programme'before the audience Tun LATE Ma. GEORGIA FORREST. —On Tuesday after- noon the remains of the late Mr. George Forrest, of Rush-green, were buried at the Higher-lane Baptist Chapel. The service- was conducted by the Rev. Mr. Hughes, student from the Manchester Baptist College. The deceased wata mAnb n. of a very old Lymm his father,the late Mr. John Forrest, having ocupid the old Dairy Farm, on Rush-green, for many years, and at which George was b-prn 71 years ago. NARROW ESCAPE : GALLANT Itzscue.—On Thursday night as Mrs. Milliard was going to a concert at the Con- gregational Schools, when by the canal bank at the Bridgewater Arms, she unfortunately through the absence of any light, walked toe far and stepped into the water. A cry of alarm was at once raised by her, which quickly brought those in the neighbourhood to her assist- ance. Amongst the first to arrive was Mr. C. Brazendale and hie brother Willie, the latter of whom, seeing the danger of the lady who was immersed, at once jumped into the water. In a few minutes he sucCeeded in bring- ing her to land, after which she was taken to Mr. Brazen- dale's where fresh clothing was found and every possible . assistance rendered. Dr. Williamson was quickly in attendance, and after-stimulants were administered she was removed to her residence in Statham-avenue in a cab. LIBERAL MEETING..—On Tuesday evening a meeting took place, at the Plough Hotel Assembly Room, under the auspices ofthe Altrincharn Division Liberal Associa- tion, and in connection with the Lymm Polling District. The meeting was very largely attended. Mr. J. A. Swan. wick, chairman of the Lymm Liberal Association, occu- pied the chair, and was supported by Dr. J. F. Fox, M.P. for King's County, Ireland ; Mr. I. S. Leadatn, the Liberal candidate for the division; and Mr. G. L. We!- ford. Before the proceedings, the audience joined in singing heartily several Liberal songs, amongst which were "Tie Liberal March," " Should old achievements be forgot," and "God bless • the Grand Old Man." When Dr. Fox rose "We're brothers evermore," was heartily sung. Addresses were given by the chairman, and Mr. G. L. Welford moved a resolution in favour of Home Rule. This was seconded by Mr. T. H. Evans, supported by Dr. Fox, M.P., and Mr.Leadam, and enthu siastically carried. The meeting broke up with cheers for the "Grand Old Man."
LYNN! LOCAL BOARD. - The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day evening. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—IR the course of his

annual report, Dr. Fox said the number of births in the year was 175, giving an annual birth- rate of 30.5, which though above the local average, corresponds with that of England and Wales. The number of deaths was 82, giving an annual rate of mortality of 149 which is three per 1,000 below the low death rate of England and Wales for the same period. The zymotic death rate was the lowest with one excep- tion attained during the -12 years of which records had been kept, namely. 0-72;per 1,000, that for England and Wales being 210.—The CHAIRMAN said they might con- gratulate themselves and Dr. Fox on his favourable report. It was gratifying to find that the death rate was below the average.—The report was adopted. THE COMING ELECTION—The CLERK was empowered to make the usual arrangements for the coming Local Board election. It was stated.that the retiring members were Messrs. Dutton, Harrison, and Appleton. A WARNING. —lt was decided to prosecute three young men who were charged with breaking the public gas lamps. 11111 i was all the business.

Mr. John White presided. Mr. Wm. Tinsley was selected to be pre- ; sident of the Ward Committee, and the following were appointed vice-chairmen :—for No. 14 polling district, Messrs. John White, Wynne Jones, Joseph Davies, I). Jones, and J.Hartley ( Woodbine-terrace); ; for No. 15 polling district, Messrs S. ;Reynolds John Coxon, J. Lee. and Edward Greenall, junior. Mr. John Hartley was re-elected secretary, and the following delegates to the Council were appointed : • —Messrs. Thomas Knight, J. H. Clerk, .Jos. div.head: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.
div.p: WARRINGTON UNION ASSESSMENT COMMITTEE.

The monthly meeting of this Committee was held at the Workhouse, yesterday morning. Mr. G. Blackhurst presided, and there were also present, the Rev. G. F. Roberts, Messrs. Balharry, Ratcliffe, J. Houghton, Kilshall, Heaton; S. Sutton (assistant clerk), and W. Owen (valuer). TEA BLUE COAT ScnooL.—Mr. OWEN said noti cehad been given him by the overseers of additions to the Blue Coat School, but as this was a charitable institution in which there was no beneficial occupation they had hitherto kept the school exempt from assessment. He presumed,therefore, that he would have to deal with the assessment as heretofore.—The report was adopted. BILL-POSTING STATIONS.—Mr. OWEN reported with re- gard to bill-posting and advertising stations, that the overseers would be able to deal with advertisements at- tached to houses and buildings. In the case of railway ' stations he was of opinion the overseers should increase the gross and retteable values so as to include the increased value for their use for the purpose of advertising. Mr. Owen added that if these assessments were made as 'ho suggested there would probably be an appeal, and the matter could then be gone into thoroughly.—This suggestion was approved, the Chairman remarking that it would he an advantage if it led to fewer advertise- ments being displayed at railway stations. This BECTOIC'S Times.—The Clerk said that Mr. E. J. Nicholson had appealed, on behalf of the Rector of Was- nington, against the assessment of the tithe due to the Rector from Great Sankey. He had taken the oppor- tunity of obtaining a statement of the tithes from different townships received by the Rector so that tho whole matter could be dealt with. The statement showed as follows i—Burtonwood, total tithe £341 18s. lid.' deduction for cost of collection, poor rate, &c., £5B 17s. 4d.. net tithe to be inserted in the valuation list, £283 is 7d •, Rixton, total tithe £209 16s. Bd., deductions £32 13s. Od., net tithe £177 4s. Bd. ; Poulton-with- Fearnhead, total tithe. £64 15s. 5d., deductions £lO 03. 9d., net tithe £54 14s. Bd. ' • Woolston-with-Martins- croft, total tithe £56 9s. 2d., deductions £8 15s. 6d., net tithe £47 13s. Bd.; Great Sankey, total tithe £52 Bs. 9d., deductions, £9 Os. 7d.. net tithe £43 6s. 2d. On the motion of Mr. Heaton, seconded by the Rev. G. F Roberts, this list was adopted. This was all the business.

div.head: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT THE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.
div.p: PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT THE BLUE COAT SCHOOL.

The annual distribution of prizes to the success- ful pupils at the Warrington Blue Coat School took place, on Thursday evening, in the presence of a large company. Alderman Joseph Davies presided, and there were also present the Rev. S. Wilkinson, Mrs. Wilkinson, Mr. Charles White, the Misses White, Mr. 11. Greenall, Mrs. Carleton, Mr. J. and Mrs. Dewhurst, Miss Shaw, Mr. arta Mrs. A. Brime- low, Mr. J. Hatton, Mr. J. Craik, Mr. and Mrs. E. Rose, master and matron. A chorus of the scholars sang three anthems, "Great is the Lord." "0, Praise the Lord," and "Be joyful in the Lord," in a very pleasing manner, and a girl rendered the solo "There is a green hill" with admirable taste. Alder- man Davies next distributed the prizes, but before so doing he delivered a most interesting address, in which he related a number of amusing incidents of his school life. He referred to the great change that had taken place in the system of educa tion, and said that whatever progress or revolu- tion had taken place the best education was tha- in which religion was brought to bear. (Applause.)t He urged the children to take full advantages of tlseir opportunities, and however successful they might be to remember the religious instruction they had received.— The list of the prize winners was as folio :—Girls— senior girls : A. Hemingway, M. Hardy, E. Hazelhurst, E. WEtedall, J. Runcorn, E. Tomlinson; Class 1., R. Hayes, S. A. Whitlow, E. A. Jefferson ; Class 2, E. Hill, H. Williamson, M. Mather ; Class 3, E. Lamb, C. M. Harding. E. Jones, M. J. Williams ; Class 4, L. Smith, M. A Atherton. Boys—Class 1, W. H. Harding, G. Looker, T. Campbell, J. W. Dykes, J. Lowe, R. Dutton, J. A. Clare ; Class 2, J. Moss, J. Atherton, A. G. Tavler, T. Meek, J. Crozier, J. Jackson ; Class 3, F. H. Allison, J. Battersby, E. Hoult, W. Mason ; Class 4, E. Johnson, J. Peer.—An excellent programme of selections by the hand, part songs, recitations, and quartetts by the children, was then gone through. A number of dumb-bell exercises were also performed with admirable precision. Mr. E. Rose officiated as conductor to the children, Mr. Armstrong conducted the band, and Mr. F. Rose efficiently played the accompaniments on the har- monium —Mr. C. White proposed a vote of thanks to Alderman Davies, and to Mr. and Mrs. Rose, for the capital arrangements they had made for the enjoyment of the visitors.—The motion having been carried with cheers, the proceedings were brought to a close with the singing of the National Anthem.

div.p: WARRINUTON RURAL SANITARY
AUTHORITY.

---- • The monthly meeting of this authority was held at the Workhouse yesterday morning. The Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. 11eaton.Owen,j3mith, A. Jolley, J. Hough - ton, Kilshall, Swinton, Sutton (clerk), Dr. Sepliton (medical officer), W. Owen (surveyor), and F. Her- foot (nuisance inspeCtOi.) THE PROPOSED EXTENSION OF THE BORODOW.—The resolution passed at a meeting of ratepayers in Padgate and Poulton. protesting against the proposed extension of the Borough in that direction, was submitted by the Clerk, who also stated that he had just received a copy ot the Bill, but had not time te go through it.—Mr. J. Houghton : Are they going on with the extension of the Borough:" The CLERK could not say; there seemed to be no certainty. The Corporation might go on with it or not.—The CHAIRMAN did not think they coutd take any ' action on the resolution of the inhabitants until the Clerk further advised them after a perusal of the Bill. Further consideration of the subject was left over till the next meeting. MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.—Dr. Sephton rororted that during the month there had been 45 births and 23 deaths. The death-rate was 179 against 174 in the corresponding month of the previons year. DISEASED MEAT.—The Inspector reported a case in which the meat of cows which had died of disease was Sound cut up and dressed on the premises of Mr. Cook, farmer, Thelwall. It appeared that the attention of the Inspector had been called to the matter by an anony- mous letter received by Mr. Norman,the Warrington Cor- poration Inspector. It was stated that one of Mr. Cook's cows had died of anthrax and another taking ill, was killed, and it was afterwards found that it had been suffering from tuberculosis. The Inspector seized the meat and afterwards had it destroyed. As it ap- peared that Mr. Cook had given notice to the police and and called in a veterinary surgeon before the visit of the Inspector, it was considered that there was no grounds for a prosecutien. NEW HOUSES.—The Surveyor reported that the follow- ing plans had been submitted and being in accordance with the bye-laws might be approved :—Warrington Land and Property Company, Limited, new streets and Passages on the north side of Liverpool-rd., Sankey; Mr. Win. Bostock : 30 houses on the north side of Liver- pool-rd.' Sankey ; and Mr. James Baker: 4 houses in Penketh; Mr. Rodgers : 5 houses in Penketh. The report was adopted.
A Vienna telegram states that smokeless powder is at once to be introduced into the Austrian Army, which is already provided with the new eightemillemetre Mann- licher rifle. _
The remains of Sir -William Gull were on Monday re- moved from London to Thorpe-le-Soken' Essex, for in- terment. Many distinguished medical men attended the funeral.
