div.head: TERRIBLE COLLIERY DISASTER.
div.p: TERRIBLE COLLIERY DISASTER.
EXPLOSION IN A MONMOUTHSW RE PIT.
LOSS OF ONE HUNDRED AND S'XTY LIVES.
RESCUE OF SURVIVORS.

Monmouthshire has again been startled and shocked by a terrible colliery explosion. The disaster this time occurred, on Thursday morning,at the Llanerch pit, near Abersychan, Monmouthshire, and in it 160 men and lads have lost their lives. The colliery is one of the oldest in the district. Between 300 and 400 men have been constantly employed principally upon the day shift, the only one really worked, though from 50 to 60 men would go down during the night. About this number came up at six o'clock, on Thursday morning, and at seven o'clock the day shift, numbering at the lowest computa- tion more than 200, were lowered to the bottom of the shaft, whence about 80 of them made their way to what is known as the long slope of the Meadow vein and the Rock vein, the remaining men going into what is called Cook's meadow vein slope. It was in the latter that the explosion occurred, the fire, it is believed, killing almost every man there. The shaft is about 250 yards deep, but there is a dip to the end ef the Meadow seam which gives a maximum depth in the colliery of about 300 yards from the surface. The colliery was put in full working order,but at seven o'clock on Thursday morning, when the work of raising coal had been going on for some time in the Meadow vein seam, the 2xplosion occurred. Its fearful character may be imagined from the fact that out of the first ten bodies recovered six were utterly unrecognisable. The bodies were calcined masses with but a resemblance to human shape, while only two or three of the bodies brought to the bank had succumbed to the effects of a ,ter-damp, thus showing that fire had done the greater part of the dread work. The report, it is said, was heard at Abersychan, two miles away. The blast swept the cage to the bank, smashing the timber work at the top, and throwing the works out of gear. The banks- man, a man named Harvey, was standing near a brick structure some five feet high, in which a huge fire is kept. He was blown completely over this, and down the tip. In about half an hour after the shock, tappings from below were 'ward. At length the downcast shaft was got to work, and the cage was sent down. In a few minutes three strokes of the bell announced its rise again, and the cage was brought to the bank. The first to step forth was Mr. Moran, certified manager of the mine. He brought with him the glad intelligence that there were many yet alive belew, but with it was the news of the havoc that had been wrought in the Meadow vein seam. Mr. Morgan called for volunteers to descend, and gallantly led the way with the first exploring party. Amongst the first to go down were Mr. Llewellyn, Mr. W. P. James Mr, W. Davies, Mr. Bruce, and Mr. Williams. Mr. Edward Jones, managing director of the Com- pany. was also soqn at the pit, being closely followed by some of the other directors—Mr. Pritchard (chair- man), Mr. P. A. Williams, and Mr. A. C. Jones. The , strength of the exploring body was soon reinforced. A ' number of locked up lamps were sent for from the Varteg colliery, and with these the explorers were able to make their way to the face. Prior to this, however, the liv- ing, about 50 in number, who had been working in the other two veins, and who, when thri explosion occurred had made the best of their way to the shaft, were sent to the bank. In the slope itself about forty bodies were discovered, many of them scorched beyond recognition. These as quickly as possible were sent to the bank, and taken to the engine-house. The news of the disaster reached Abersychan shortly after nine o'clock, and a large number of people at once made their way to the colliery. The impossibility of communicating with those below made the suspense terrible. Fathers andlnothers sisters and brothers of the men below crowded round: and their grief was pitiful to witness. It was with breathless excitement that the appearance of the cage above the mouth of the pit was watched, and, as the well-known faces of the men were recognised a sigh of relief escaped from those who were so anxiously waiting for them. But those who were alive—numbering about 80—did not all come up without injury. Many were badly hurt. An old man named Beard, who had been employed at the colliery for about forty years and performed the work of a hitcher, was brought up alive, but both his legs had been blown away. Between three and five o'clock the bodies were brought up rapidly, and it was then seen how great must have been the force of the explosion. Most of the men were charred. Others were badly cut about the head. One of the worse cases was that of a boy whose brains had been blown out.

A special correspondent of the Central News, tele- graphing from Newport, says 300 men, forming a full mining shaft, went down the pit at seven o'clock in the morning, and the last man had scarcely settled to work when the explosion took place. There is every reason to believe that 160 men have lost their lives by the dis- aster. The colliery belongs, with half-a-dozen others, to Messrs. Partridge and Jones. Only a few days ago an explosion by which five men were killed occurred in the adjoining Glynn pits, which afterwards became flooded, and there is reason to believe that the gas dislodged by the water found its way in large quantities into We Llanerch pits. The shall machinery at the pit mouth was almost entirely destroyed by the explosion, which was accompanied by flames add followeel by clouds of smoke. _ _

A Press Association telegram says :—About 400 men and boys are employed in the pit, which is stated to have been well managed. A miner, who was working not far from the bottom of the shaft, some distance from the locality of the explosion, had one of his legs blown away, and died on being taken to the bank. A collier and two sons, who had only resumed work that morning after the recent accident at the Glynn pit, are entombed. At the time of the accident there were nearly 300 men and boys in the pit. Over 100 escaped at the time of the explosion, and in the course of the afternoon eighteen men were brought eut alive. A telegram from Pontypool on Thursday night says: —Her Majesty's Inspector, Mr. Martin, has received the following message of inquiry and sympathy from the Horne Office : I have to express through you the deep regret and sympathy of the Secretary of State for Home Affairs at the disaster at Llanerch Colliery, and request further information as speedily as possible.— (Signed), "UNDER SECRETARY OF STATE, Home Office. CAUSE OF THE DISASTER.

div.head: MARKETS.
div.p: MARKETS.

MANCHESTER TRADE, FRIDAY. There is no improvement in the market, and the business doing in any department is very moderate. Cotton has not been in a buoyant mood, notwithstanding that quotations were twi points up at the opening. Yarns are not brisk, and spinners are getting few offers that they are disposed to accept. Cloth is not any better. There is some Egyptian business still going through. A few South American inquiries are men- tioned. The Glasgow demand for printers is slow,and at low prices. The home houses are taking delivery free, but new orders are Pearce. _ _ _

div.head: MISSING STEAMER ERIN.
div.p: THE MISSING STEAMER ERIN.

..... Lloyd's agency says a mail from Azores arrived at Madeira,on Wednesday, put brought no news of the miss- ingsteamer Erin, which is now 40 days out from New York. There were 72 men on board. • RUMOURED RETIREMENT OF SIR RICHARD MOON.

The ".Dublin Express" says—We understand that Sir Richard Moon, Bart.; is about to retire from the chairmanship of the London and North-Western Railway. Company, which he has filled with remarkable ability since the year 1861, and that his successor will probably be Mr. Findla,v, the general manager. Sir R. Moon is now in his 76th year. ELECTION INTELLIGENCE. THE PARTICR DIVISION.

Mr. John Parker Smith (Liberal Unionist) and Sir Charles Tennant (Gladstonian Liberal) were nominated. en Thursday, as candidates for the Plirtick division. The polling takes place next Tuesday. It is stated that at the next election Mr. W. J. Davis I will be the Liberal candidate for West Birmingham.

Mr. Ralph Darlington, Town Clerk of Wigan, died at his house atSouthport on Monday night, at the age of 75. The death is announced at San Lucar, Andalusia, of the Due de Montpensier, who was at one time a candi- date for the Spanish throne. It was resolved at a conference of Scotch miners' eele- gates held at Glasgow, on Wednesday, to demand an advance in wages of 12i per chit. equal to ed. per day. ' Mr. Gla.dstone,on Wednesday, delivered an address be- fore the Oxford Debating Society Union, on the points of contact between Homer and Assyrian literature, as shown by recent research. The right hon. gentleman. who has been on a visit to Oxford, was enthusiastically applauded. The "Cologne Gazette" publishes a despatch from Lisbon referring to the suggestion that a Conference should be held for the settlement of the Anglo-Portu- guese dispute. It is said that Spain, France, Italy, Austria and Russia are" inclined" to such a Conference, but that Germany is" more reserved." It is reported that the Tories opposed to free education will hold a meeting at the House of Commons immedia- tely after the meeting of Parliament. It is added that Mr. Howarth and Lord Cranborne are taking the lead in the movement, and that they are assured of the support of at least 100 Conservative members.

div.head: AT EARLESTOWN.
div.p: AT EARLESTOWN.
ALARMING OUTBREAK OF INFLUENZA

SERIOUS RAVAGES. During the last two or three weeks, influenza, cohls,.&c., have been extremely prevalent in Bevies- town, Newton, and the Surrounding districts. Though the epidemic is not of the " Russian " tyPe' most of the cases are of a more malignant character than the ordinary run of such cases. In consequenct of the unusually large number of suers, mans Ot tile works in the district have • been seriously affected. At the printing and stationary works of Messrs. George McCorquodale and Co., Newton, ovel 100 people have had to leave work; at the Visdlici' Wagon Works, Earlestown, belonging to the Londoa_ and North-Western Railway Co. it is stated that zixol! 80 of the men in one department are unable to folio!, their occupations, there are 50 similarly afflicted ~h!. another 'shop," and 40 and 30 respectively in two of tn° other departments of the Waggon works. it 15 al off. stated that at the Vulcan iron foundry over 70 are . work" suffering from the same complaint, and at tn! Sankey sugar works, as well, a considerable number 01. , the hands have had to temporarily leave their emploP • meat; twelve being the number who had to op i 1 day. Smaller works and manufactories have b afflicted, but in a lesser degree. The worst feature 0 ,the epidemic is that the disease generally runs through the family of the household after any one individual ha° been attacked. The children in these circurnsta suffer to the greatest extent. It is currently stated about 500 children are" laid up," but he school at' ance officer asserts that about 400 is nearer the m The visitation of the disease is the most extensive in recollection of the oldest residents. Happily no de' I have been directly attrinuted to the epidemic as 0'

The horse Ingram had ridden was standing iL Lll.l door-steps, cropping the grass. The man dashed at it, seized the reins, and mounted. Then he rode 4, bowing gravely to the faces at the window. Ingram rushed out after him opened the ball d.r, and fled across the park, bareheaded, x but in a e,cm- trary direction to that the man had taken. Ingestre laughed hoarsely. "If they come to a hand to hand fight, I'll back the Englishman to win. The creole i.e a coward." Lina clasped her hands tightly together, and her ,faoe became a leaden colour. "If Ingram Ingestre is killed, I shall feel like his murderess, since I first set him on the track of that bad man. God forgive me for it !" And she went up to the baroness, and laid her head on her bosom. Madame Bernstein put her arms round her, but staggered beneath the weight of the girl, for she had fainted. Then all was confusion for an instant. The barones3 was alarmed, and IngestreAad to lift the girl to the sofa, and there support her, while they applied re- storatives. While Cleland, the baroness, and Ingestre stood round the fainting girl, that forlornwoman, Catherine, rose up to leave the house for ever. No one saw her glide from the room, no , ne guessed her purpose and, unperceived, she left the house, and stole away like some guilty creature, beneath the avenue GE wintry elms. THE SHIP CANAL. TIIE FLOODS. The damage occasioned by the recent flocding of the Ship Canal at Thelwall, has to a great extent been recti- fied. Many of the railway lines have had t 3 be repaired, and in many instances almost reconstructed. All the water has not vet been got out of the cutting, but in its present state it offers no impediment to the progress of the general work in the vicinity of the locks. Many repairs have had to be done consequent upon the floods, which have been the means of delaying the ordinary work for several days. ENTERTAINMENT AT THELWALL. An enjoyable entertainment was given at Thelwall on Tuesday evening, in connection with the Ship Canal mission. Mr. W. Davidson, of Grappenhall, was the chairman, and there was a good attendance, including the new missionary of the section, Mr. J. Moore, Mr. R. Bushel', and other gentlemen from the Ship Canal offices. The Misses Price and E. (Heave were the accom- panists. Songs were contributed by Misses Bushell, Manning, and Silverton. The Misses engin played the pianoforte duet : and Messrs. H. Rigby, J. Moore. and H. Price also sang. Mr. Manning delivered an address, and the meeting closed by the Chairman wishing Mr. Moore every success in his new duties on the No. 6 section.

CRITICAL ILLNESS OF LORD AUCKLAND. Lord Auckland was seized with paralysis yesterday, when about to cut the first sod of the new railway between Bakewell and Chesterfield. His condition is critical. TWO CHILDREN BURNED TO DEATH. Two children were burned to death on Thursday night at Southampton, through the accidental capsizing of a paraffin lamp by a tailor, who, being deaf and dumb, could not give an alarm in time. A third child was injured. MILL FIRE AT BOLTON. Early yesterday morning, a fire broke out in the Carlton Mills, Bolton, belonging to the Rothwell Hosiery Company,. Limited, and before the flames were extin- guished damage was done to the extent of £lO,OOO, which is fully covered by insurante in several societies. THE ACTION AGAINST THE BISHOP OF LINCOLN. Sir Walter Phillimore, yesterday, continued his ad- dress to'the Archiepiscopal Court, at Lambeth Palace, on behalf of the Bishop of Lincoln. The learned counsel now addressed himself to the subject of light. The Court afterwards adjourned until Thursday week. THE GOVERNMENT PROGRAMME. A London weekly contemporary, in giving a forecast of the Government programme, states that a sum of £20,000.000 will be devoted to the extension and dove- lopmrnt of the Ashbourne Act ; that £1,000,000 of Mr. Goschen's surplus will be given to assist free education ; and that a portion ot the surplus will also be devoted to reduce taxation and to helping the volunteers. ALARMING BOILER EXPLOSION. • TEN PERSONS INJURED. A Sheerness correspondent telegraphs that H.M.S. Barracouta resumed her steam trials yesterday morning, but when off Margate one of her boilers exploded with a terrific report. Ten of her crew were injured, one of them, it is believed, fatally. They were brought back and sent to the hospital. A second man is reported in a critical state. The mishap is supposed to be due to the bursting of the port boiler, causing the flamc to rush into the stokehole. TWO WOMEN BURNT TO DEATH. Yesterday morning, the residence of Mr. Dm:a Robertson, Onslow Gardens, South Kensington, was the scene of a fatal fire. Two female servants, Leonard and Holder, and an aged woman named Dunn, were the sole occupants at the time. Holder coming downstairs early yesterday morning to light the fire found the lowest floor of the house in flames. She alarmed the others, who were at the top of the house, but they were unable to escape before the fire overtook and killed them. Holder escaped through a window and scrambled down a water pipe. THE JUBILEE PLUNGER. NICE, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—Benzon was taken before the examining magistrate to-day, and remanded for another week. He wept in court. THE DUKE OF MONTPENSIER. MADRID, FRIDAY AFTERNOON.—The remains of the late Duke of Montpensier were conveyed on a hearse drawn by eight horses from the Southern to the Northern rail- way station and thence by train to the Escurial for inter- ment.

quantity of gas, it is said, issued out of a fissure sud- denly. It was fired by the naked lights carried by the I men. This really is, it is conjectured, the true cause of the disaster. It should be added, in justice to the pro- prietors of the colliery, that the reason why naked lights were used there was because the ventilation was "super- excellent." IDENTIFICATION OF TFIE BODIES. As the bodies were identified they were removed on ambulance stretchers to a train of trucks, to which a special engine was attached, for conveyanceltotheir homes at Abersychan, Pontnewvndd, and Talywain, were most of the men, if not all, lived. Frequently, as these poor fellows were being carried out, the ambulaxce-bearers had to stand on one side to make way for a further number just brought out of the pit, while crowding around were weeping women, the sight of whose woe- stricken faces and the sounds of whose lamentations will haunt those who were witnesses for many a day. Mr. Edward Jones, managing director of the colliery, stated that the loss of life would probably reach 150. The total number of bodies recovered yesterday up to 3.10 p.m. had reached 161. HOW AN ENGINEMAN WAS KILLED. , The explosion indirectly caused one of the enginemen to lose his life. He was on duty in the engineroom adjoining the shaft, and when the explosion occurred the poor fellow seemed to lose his head with fright. He • incautiously approached the edge of the pit, and falling down was dashed to pieces at the pit bottom. THE INTERMENTS. The majority of the men will be buried on Sunday, and at every carpenter's shop in the neighbourhood men are busily engaged in making coffins. RELIEF FUND. The Lord Mayor of London has opened a Mansion House Fund for the relief of the sufferers.
